teile.einleitung: Carnivorous plants catch small animals and digest them. That sounds eerie, but it is a clever adaptation to nutrient-poor soils. Some of these meat-eating plants also grow in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Carnivorous plants often grow on nutrient-poor soils, for example in bogs.
The prey supplies mainly nitrogen and phosphorus.
They get their energy like other plants, through photosynthesis.
There are sticky traps, snap traps, pitfall traps and suction traps.
In Switzerland, sundew, butterwort and bladderwort grow.
The Venus flytrap comes from North and South Carolina in the USA.
Charles Darwin wrote a book about these plants in 1875.

abschnitte.text: Carnivorous plants often grow in **bogs** and on acidic, poor soils. There, important nutrients are lacking. The prey supplies them mainly with **nitrogen** and **phosphorus**. They get their energy themselves, like other green plants, through **photosynthesis**. The animals are thus more a fertiliser than a food.

**Sticky traps** have sticky glands to which insects cling. The **Venus flytrap** has a **snap trap** that shuts in a flash. Pitcher plants form **pitfall traps** with a smooth rim into which insects slide and are digested at the bottom. The **bladderwort** has small bladders under negative pressure. If a small animal touches the flap, it is sucked in within fractions of a second. This is a **suction trap**.

In Swiss raised bogs grows the **round-leaved sundew**. It bears red glandular tentacles with glistening drops of glue and is protected. On damp alpine meadows you find the **butterwort** with greasy, shiny rosettes of leaves, for example the alpine butterwort. In pools and ditches lives the **bladderwort**. Many of these plants have become rare because bogs have disappeared.

The **Venus flytrap** grows wild only in a small area on the coast of **North and South Carolina** in the USA. There it settles damp, nutrient-poor sandy areas. **Pitcher plants** grow mainly in South-East Asia. On Borneo, **mountain tree shrews** lick sap at the pitcher lid and in doing so let droppings fall into the pitcher. These give the plant a lot of nitrogen.

The naturalist **Charles Darwin** studied the sundew and other species in many experiments. In 1875 he published the book **“Insectivorous Plants”**. In it he showed that these plants really do digest their prey. Before that, many experts had doubted it.

gewusst: Since 1987, bogs in Switzerland have been protected by the Federal Constitution. This also helps sundew and butterwort.
The trap of the Venus flytrap usually only shuts when its trigger hairs are touched twice in quick succession.

teile.einleitung: Sepals are the outermost leaves of a flower. Usually they are green and inconspicuous, but they have an important job: they protect the bud. In some plants they are even colourful and eye-catching.
wichtigste: Sepals form the outermost circle of the flower envelope.
They are usually green.
They protect the young flower bud.
All the sepals together form the calyx.
In the dandelion, the calyx is changed into a crown of hairs.
In the fuchsia and the Christmas rose, the sepals are strikingly coloured.
Strawberry and mallow also have an epicalyx.

abschnitte.text: A typical flower is built in circles. Right on the outside stand the **sepals**. Inside follow the coloured **petals**, then the stamens and, in the middle, the carpels. All the sepals together form the **calyx**. It can consist of free sepals or of sepals **fused** together.

As long as the flower is still a **bud**, the sepals wrap around the inner parts. They protect them from **cold**, **drying out** and from animals that want to eat them. When the flower opens, the sepals fold to the side. In some plants they then fall off, in others they stay for a long time.

In the **strawberry**, the calyx stays after flowering. It sits as a green wreath on top of the fruit. Strawberry and **mallow** have a second circle of small leaves below the real calyx. This is called the **epicalyx**. In the **dandelion** the calyx is changed into a crown of hairs, the **pappus**. It works like a parachute, so that the wind can carry the fruits far away.

Not all sepals are green. In the **fuchsia**, the four spreading sepals are coloured a strong red or pink. In this way they help to attract pollinators. In the **Christmas rose**, the large white leaves look like petals. In reality they are **sepals**. The real petals are changed into small nectar containers.

gewusst: In the Chinese lantern plant, the calyx grows after flowering into an orange husk that surrounds the fruit like a lantern.
In the corn poppy, the two sepals fall off as soon as the flower opens.

teile.einleitung: The honey bee is an insect that lives in large communities, the bee colonies. It makes honey and wax and pollinates many plants, which is why it is very important for nature and farming.
wichtigste: Every bee colony has a queen, who lays all the eggs.
The worker bees are female and do almost all the jobs.
The male bees are called drones.
Bees show the way to flowers with a dance.
A honey bee has five eyes.
When it stings a person’s skin, the sting is often left behind.

abschnitte.text: A bee colony consists of a **queen**, many **worker bees** and, in summer, also **drones**. The queen is the largest bee and lays all the **eggs**. The workers are females. The drones are the male bees. They have no sting and do not collect nectar. In summer a colony can have many thousands of bees.

The **worker bees** have many jobs. They clean the cells, feed the larvae and build **honeycombs** from wax. Later they guard the entrance. Last of all they fly out and collect **nectar** and **pollen**. In doing so, they carry pollen from flower to flower. In this way they **pollinate** many fruit trees and other plants.

When a forager has found good flowers, she flies back to the hive. There she **dances** on the comb. With the dance she shows the other bees the **direction** and the **distance** to the flowers. If the flowers are further away, she does a **waggle dance**. The researcher Karl von Frisch decoded this bee language.

A honey bee has **five eyes**. Two large **compound eyes** sit at the sides of the head. In addition there are three small **simple eyes** on top of the head. The worker’s **sting** has small **barbs**. If she stings a person, it stays stuck in the skin and tears off. That is why the bee usually dies afterwards.

gewusst: For one jar of honey, bees together fly a very long way and visit millions of flowers.
Karl von Frisch received the Nobel Prize in 1973 for his research on bee language.

teile.einleitung: German chamomile is one of the best-known medicinal plants. Its small white flowers with a yellow centre have a strong scent and have been used for tea for a long time. It is often found in fields and at the edges of paths.
wichtigste: German chamomile has white flowers with a yellow centre.
For chamomile tea, the dried flowers are used.
Chamomile tea is an old household remedy, for example for tummy ache.
If you cut the yellow centre in half, it is hollow in German chamomile.
It likes to grow in fields and at the edges of paths.
Chamomile and daisies belong to the same plant family.
It blooms mainly from May into the summer.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of German chamomile look like small stars. Around a yellow centre stand white petals. Each little head actually consists of many tiny individual flowers. This puts chamomile, like the **daisy**, in the **daisy family**. The plant has finely divided leaves and usually grows knee-high.

There are several plants that look similar to German chamomile. A simple test helps: if you cut the yellow centre in half lengthways, the **flower base** inside is **hollow** in German chamomile. In similar species it is filled. In addition, German chamomile has a strong, typical scent.

German chamomile likes sun. It likes to grow in **fields**, on farmland and at the **edges of paths**. It blooms mainly from May into the summer. During this time the flowers are collected. For sale, chamomile is also grown in fields.

For **chamomile tea**, the dried flower heads are used, because the scent is in them. Many people traditionally drink the tea for **tummy ache**. For a cold, you lean over a bowl of hot chamomile tea and breathe in the steam. This is called **inhaling**. With strong or long-lasting complaints, however, you should go to the doctor.

gewusst: The oil of chamomile contains a substance that colours it deep blue, even though the flowers are white and yellow.
The word chamomile comes from Greek and means roughly “ground apple”, because of its apple-like scent.

teile.einleitung: Food waste means that edible food is thrown away or lost along the way. This happens in the field, in shops, in restaurants and at home. Worldwide and in Switzerland there are plans to reduce the waste.
wichtigste: With the goal SDG 12.3, the UN wants to halve food waste by 2030.
The best-before date is a quality guarantee, not a throw-away date.
Easily perishable foods carry the note “use by”.
Food loss is loss between harvest and retail, food waste is the waste after that.
Rotting waste in landfills produces the greenhouse gas methane.
Leftover food should first be passed on to people.

abschnitte.text: A large part of food is never eaten. The UN has therefore set itself sustainability goals. Goal 12 concerns sustainable consumption and production. The sub-goal **SDG 12.3** demands that waste per person in retail and among consumers be **halved** by 2030. Switzerland also pursues this goal and has an **action plan** of the federal government for it.

The Food and Agriculture Organization, the **FAO**, distinguishes two kinds. **Food loss** is loss between harvest and retail, that is in storage, transport and processing. **Food waste** is the waste in retail, in the catering trade and in households. Even in the field a lot of vegetables are sorted out. Crooked carrots or too small potatoes often do not meet the **trade standards** for size and appearance, although they would be edible.

On many packs it says **“best before”**. Up to this date the manufacturer guarantees the quality. Pasta, rice or tins are often still good after it. You check them with your senses: look, smell, taste. It is different with easily perishable goods such as **minced meat**. There it says **“use by”**. After this date you should no longer eat them, for safety reasons.

It is best if no leftovers arise at all: **prevention** comes first. If food is already left over, it should first feed **people**. In Switzerland, organisations such as “Tischlein deck dich” or the “Schweizer Tafel” distribute surplus goods to people in need. Only after that come animal feed, energy from biogas and disposal. If waste rots in landfills without oxygen, **methane** arises, a strong greenhouse gas.

Some people take still edible food out of the waste containers of supermarkets. This is called **dumpster diving**, in German “Containern”. They want to draw attention to the waste in retail. This is distinguished from **gleaning**, the picking of leftovers in fields after the actual harvest.

gewusst: Per molecule, methane has a clearly stronger effect on the climate than carbon dioxide.
A large part of the waste happens not in the shop but at home, in households.

teile.einleitung: The **ragged robin** is a pretty pink meadow flower. Its petals are so finely slit that they look like fringes. It likes to grow best on damp meadows.
wichtigste: The ragged robin blooms pink.
Its petals are deeply slit like fringes.
The cuckoo is in its German name, because it blooms when the cuckoo calls.
It usually begins to bloom in May.
Butterflies and bumblebees pollinate it.
It is becoming rarer, because damp meadows are being drained.

abschnitte.text: The ragged robin belongs to the **pink family**. It grows about 30 to 80 centimetres tall. Its **pink** flowers have five petals. Each of them is **deeply slit into narrow strips**. That is why the flowers look a little tousled, like small fringes. On a meadow you can easily recognise it by this.

The plant usually begins to bloom **in May**. This is the time when you hear the **cuckoo** call. That is how it got its German name, “Kuckucks-Lichtnelke”. The white foam on the stem is also linked with the bird. In everyday speech it is called **cuckoo spit**. It has nothing to do with the cuckoo, though.

Often you find **small blobs of foam** on the stem. In them lives the larva of the **froghopper**. It sucks plant sap and blows a foam from it. In it, it is protected from drying out and from enemies. This hardly harms the plant.

The nectar of the ragged robin lies deep in a narrow tube. That is why mainly insects with a long tongue can reach it. These are especially **butterflies** and **bumblebees**. They pollinate the flowers while drinking nectar. The plant is thus an important part of species-rich meadows.

The ragged robin loves **damp meadows**, bogs and the banks of streams. Such habitats have become rare in Switzerland and in the whole of central Europe. Many damp meadows were **drained** and turned into fields or heavily fertilised meadows. Frequent mowing also harms it. That is why it has become rarer in many places.

gewusst: The froghopper blows its protective foam from plant sap and air.
In Germany, the ragged robin was chosen as Flower of the Year 2017.

teile.einleitung: In integrated pest management, farmers protect their plants with many different means. Chemical sprays are used only when it is really necessary.
wichtigste: Preventive measures come first, chemical products only as much as necessary.
Control starts only once the economic damage threshold is reached.
A varied crop rotation keeps disease organisms in the soil low.
Forecasting models such as Agrometeo show the right time for a treatment.
Flower strips encourage beneficial insects such as hoverflies and lacewings.
Changing active ingredients prevents resistance.

abschnitte.titel: Prevention is the most important thing
abschnitte.text: The principle is: **preventive measures first**, chemical products only as much as necessary. These include robust varieties, healthy soil and a **varied crop rotation**. If something different grows in a field each year, disease organisms in the soil cannot build up as strongly. They then do not always find their favourite plant in the same place.

Not every pest is a problem straight away. First you count and observe. Only when the infestation goes above the **economic damage threshold** is control worthwhile. Then the damage would be greater than the cost of the treatment. **Pheromone traps** help with this: they use scents to attract certain moths and show when these are flying.

In Switzerland, many farmers and winegrowers use the **Agrometeo** platform. It uses weather data to calculate when, for example, a fungus could attack the vines. With such **forecasting models**, spraying is done only when it is really necessary. This saves products and protects the environment.

**Flower strips** are laid out at the edge of fields. They encourage **beneficial insects** such as hoverflies, lacewings and ladybirds, whose larvae eat aphids. In Swiss viticulture, the **confusion technique** is used against the **grape berry moth**. In it, many scents of the females are spread around in the vines. The males therefore cannot find the females, and there are fewer caterpillars.

If the same product is always sprayed, a few disease organisms that are insensitive sometimes survive. They multiply, and the product no longer works. This is called **resistance**. That is why people alternate between **active ingredients with different modes of action**.

gewusst: With the confusion technique, small scent dispensers hang in the vines, with no poison at all.
A single lacewing larva can eat a great many aphids in its life.

teile.einleitung: With its bright blue, the cornflower is one of the most beautiful wild flowers. In the past it bloomed in almost every cornfield, but today it has become rare there. In gardens and flower strips, however, you can often see it again.
wichtigste: The cornflower gets its name because it often grows in cornfields.
It belongs to the daisy family.
A cornflower lives for only about a year.
Its outer flowers look like small funnels.
Through weedkillers it has become rare in many fields.
At the edge of a field it often grows next to the corn poppy.

abschnitte.text: The **cornflower** has its name because it often grows in the **corn**, that is, in cornfields. Its flowers shine a strong **blue**. The outer flowers are large and look like small **funnels**. Inside sit smaller, darker flowers. Together with the red **corn poppy**, it once coloured the edges of many fields.

The cornflower belongs to the **daisy family**, like the daisy. What looks like one flower is therefore a head of many individual flowers. The plant lives **only about a year**. It germinates, flowers, forms seeds and then dies. Its seeds fall to the ground and grow into new plants the next year.

In many fields the cornflower is rare today. One important reason is the **weedkillers** that farmers spray on their fields. Because seed grain is now cleaned very thoroughly, hardly any cornflower seeds reach the fields any more. That is why cornflowers are sown specially, in **gardens** and in **flower strips** at the edge of fields. There they offer bees, bumblebees and butterflies food.

Dried cornflower petals are a popular **ingredient in tea**. They give tea blends touches of blue. The cornflower is also popular in bouquets, because it lasts a long time. Anyone who sows it in the garden needs a sunny spot and rather poor soil.

gewusst: The cornflower probably came to central Europe thousands of years ago together with the grain from the Mediterranean region.
The cornflower is a good bee plant, because it produces a lot of nectar.

teile.einleitung: Chestnut blight is a tree disease caused by a fungus. In North America it wiped out almost all American chestnuts. The sweet chestnuts in Ticino are affected too, but here the disease runs a milder course thanks to a virus.
wichtigste: The pathogen is a sac fungus called Cryphonectria parasitica.
It comes from East Asia.
It enters the tree through wounds in the bark.
In North America it almost completely wiped out the American chestnut.
In Ticino it attacks the sweet chestnut, not the horse chestnut.
A virus can weaken the fungus, which is called hypovirulence.
Typical signs are orange-red fruiting bodies and dead shoots.

abschnitte.text: Chestnut blight is caused by the **sac fungus** Cryphonectria parasitica. It comes from **East Asia**. The chestnut species there are largely resistant. With plant material the fungus reached North America and Europe. Its spores are spread by wind, rain and animals.

The spores enter through **wounds in the bark**, for example after hail, frost or a cut. The fungus destroys the bark and the **cambium**, the growth layer. It forms orange **fruiting bodies**. Because it constricts a branch in a ring, the parts above it wilt. Their brown leaves often stay hanging.

From **1904** the fungus spread out from **New York**. It killed billions of **American chestnuts**. This tree species was once very common in the forests of the eastern USA. Today it mostly survives only as **coppice shoots**: young shoots grow from the root stock, which often fall ill again later.

In southern Switzerland the **sweet chestnut** shapes the landscape. Its light groves are called **selve**. Around the middle of the 20th century the fungus also reached **Ticino**. It attacks only true chestnuts. The **horse chestnut** is not botanically related to them and is spared.

The **Cryphonectria hypovirus 1** infects the fungus and makes it less aggressive. This is called **hypovirulence**. Infected bark wounds heal over, and the tree survives. In Europe such weakened strains of the fungus spread on their own and dampened the disease. In North America, among other things the greater variety of fungal strains hindered the transfer of the virus.

gewusst: The American chestnut is today regarded as almost gone from its former range, although many root stocks are still alive.
Researchers in Switzerland have been studying for decades how the helpful virus spreads in the chestnut forests.

teile.einleitung: The cambium is a wafer-thin layer in the trunk of trees and shrubs. It makes sure that a tree gets a little thicker every year. Without cambium there would be neither wood nor tree rings.
wichtigste: The cambium is a growth tissue with cells that can divide.
It lies as a thin sleeve between the wood and the bark.
Inwards it forms wood, outwards it forms inner bark.
In the inner bark, sugar and other nutrients are carried.
Because the cambium rests in winter, tree rings form.
Palms have no such cambium and therefore no true tree rings.
In grafting, the cambium layers must touch.

abschnitte.text: The cambium surrounds the wood like a thin sleeve and lies directly under the bark. Often it is only a few cell layers thick. Its cells can divide again and again. Such tissues are called **growth tissues** or **meristems**. The cambium is responsible for the **thickening** of trees and shrubs.

Most of the new cells are given off by the cambium inwards. From them forms new **wood**, which carries water up from the roots and supports the trunk. Fewer cells move outwards and become the **inner bark**. In the inner bark, sugary sap flows from the leaves to the roots. The inner bark is later pushed outwards and then belongs to the bark.

In spring and summer the cambium is active, and in winter it rests. In spring it forms light wood with wide cells, and in late summer darker, denser wood. In this way a visible **tree ring** is laid down each year. The method of dating wood by means of these rings is called **dendrochronology**. The Greek word dendron means tree. With it, wood can often be dated to the exact year.

Palms belong to the **monocotyledons**, like grasses and bamboo. They have no ring-shaped cambium. That is why their trunks do not grow thicker year after year, as trees do. That is why palms also have no true tree rings.

In **grafting**, gardeners place a small twig of a good fruit variety, the **scion**, onto another plant, the **rootstock**. For the two to grow together, their cambium layers must lie exactly on top of each other. Only the cambium can form new cells and join the wound. This is how many apple and pear trees in Switzerland bear the desired variety.

gewusst: If a ring of bark and inner bark is removed all around a trunk, no more sugar can flow to the roots. The tree then often dies after some time.
With dendrochronology, experts have already been able to date the wooden piles of pile-dwelling settlements on Swiss lakes exactly.

teile.einleitung: An insect hotel is a nesting aid for wild bees and other insects. You can build one yourself and put it in the garden or on the balcony.
wichtigste: An insect hotel is a nesting aid.
It should stand in a sunny spot.
A roof protects it from rain.
Hollow bamboo tubes and holes in hard wood are good nesting places.
The holes must be smooth inside and free of splinters.
Mason bees especially like to move in.

abschnitte.text: Many wild bees live alone and lay their eggs in small hollow spaces. In tidy gardens they often find no such places. An **insect hotel** is a **nesting aid**: it offers many small tubes. The bee puts pollen in as food and lays an egg, then seals the chamber. The next spring a new bee hatches.

Insects love warmth. That is why the insect hotel should face **the sun**, ideally south or south-east. A **roof** protects it **from rain**, because wet tubes can go mouldy. The hotel should stand firmly and not sway in the wind. Very important: nearby there must be **plenty of flowers**, otherwise the bees find no food.

**Hollow bamboo tubes** or reed stems are well suited. You can also drill holes **in hard wood**, for example in beech or ash. The holes should be of different widths. It is important that they are **smooth and free of splinters** inside, otherwise the bees hurt their wings. Pine cones and loose straw are hardly used by wild bees.

**Mason bees** especially like to move in. They seal their tubes with clay. Other species use pieces of leaf or resin. From the sealed entrance you can tell that a tube is occupied. Wild bees are peaceful and hardly ever sting, so you can watch them from close by.

gewusst: Many wild bees fly only a few hundred metres, which is why flowers must be close by.
Some of the wild bees nest in the ground and need open, sandy spots instead of tubes.

teile.einleitung: Some plants build themselves a pantry: a thick tuber. In it they store nutrients to survive the winter or to sprout again. The best-known tuber is the potato.
wichtigste: A tuber is a thickened plant part that stores reserves.
Potatoes grow underground and store mainly starch.
The “eyes” of the potato are small buds.
You should not eat green patches on potatoes.
Kohlrabi is a tuber that grows above the ground.
Sweet potatoes and dahlias also form tubers.

abschnitte.text: With the potato, you eat the **tubers**, which grow underground on the plant. They are thickened parts of the shoot and full of **starch**. The small dents on the skin are called **eyes**. They are buds from which new shoots grow. That is why whole potatoes are put into the soil in spring, to harvest new ones in autumn.

If potatoes lie in the light, they turn **green** in some places. There the poison **solanine** forms. A lot of it is also in the sprouts. Green patches and sprouts are therefore cut away generously. The parts of the potato plant above ground, that is, leaves and berries, are poisonous and are not eaten.

Not all tubers grow in the ground. **Kohlrabi** forms a thick tuber directly above the soil. It is a thickened stem, from which the leaves grow at the top. You can eat it raw as a snack or cook it. Celeriac also belongs to the tuber vegetables, but grows for the most part in the ground.

The **sweet potato** tastes sweetish and often has orange flesh. It is not closely related to the potato but belongs to the bindweed family. The **dahlia**, a popular garden flower, also grows from tubers. Because these cannot stand frost, they are dug up in autumn and stored in the cellar. In spring they are planted again.

gewusst: The potato comes from the Andes in South America and reached Europe in the 16th century.
The dahlia also comes from America, namely from Mexico.

teile.einleitung: The cherry laurel is a popular evergreen hedge plant. It comes from south-eastern Europe and western Asia and is also spreading into woods in Switzerland. That is why it may no longer be sold here.
wichtigste: The cherry laurel is evergreen and opaque.
It comes from south-eastern Europe and western Asia.
Birds eat the fruits and spread the seeds into the woods.
Leaves and seeds are especially poisonous.
It is of little value to native insects.
Hedges that were planted before the sales ban may stay.
The hornbeam is a native alternative.

abschnitte.text: The cherry laurel has large, **leathery** leaves that stay green all year. So it is **evergreen** and grows densely. In this way it gives **privacy** even in winter. That is why it was planted as a hedge in many gardens. In spring it bears white spikes of flowers, later black fruits.

The cherry laurel belongs, like the **sweet cherry**, to the genus **Prunus**. It is not related to the true **bay laurel**, whose leaves are used as a spice. Originally it is native from the Balkans through Asia Minor to the **Caucasus**. From there it came to central Europe as an ornamental plant.

Especially **poisonous** are the **leaves** and the **seeds**. They contain substances from which poisonous **prussic acid** can form. The flesh of the fruit is less poisonous, but should not be eaten either. Care is needed with children and pets.

abschnitte.titel: From the garden into the woods
abschnitte.text: **Blackbirds** and other birds eat the black fruits. Later they pass the seeds out again in another place. In this way the cherry laurel gets into the **woods**. There it forms dense stands and pushes out native plants. For native **insects** it is of little value, because only a few can use it as food.

In Switzerland the cherry laurel counts as an **invasive neophyte**. Since 1 September 2024 it may no longer be **sold, given away or imported**. Plants that already stand in gardens are not affected and may stay. Anyone planting a new hedge can choose native species, such as the **hornbeam**. Its dry leaves often stay hanging until spring.

gewusst: Together with the cherry laurel, other invasive plants were excluded from sale in Switzerland, for example the butterfly bush.
Native hedges such as hornbeam, privet or hawthorn offer birds and insects much more food.

teile.einleitung: Agriculture means growing plants and keeping animals in order to obtain food and other raw materials. Farming families supply milk, cheese, meat, grain, vegetables and fruit, and in doing so also look after the landscape. In Switzerland, green meadows, alpine pastures and cows shape the image of agriculture.
wichtigste: In agriculture, plants are grown and farm animals are kept.
Agriculture began about 10,000 years ago in the Near East.
In the Middle Ages the three-field system was used, in which one field lay fallow every third year.
With crop rotation, farmers spare the soil and reduce pests.
Meadows and pastures make up the largest part of Switzerland’s farmland.
The time when cows spend the summer on the alpine pastures is called summering.
In organic farming, chemical-synthetic plant protection products are forbidden.

abschnitte.text: Agriculture covers **arable farming**, that is, growing plants such as wheat, maize, potatoes or sugar beet, and **livestock farming** with cows, pigs, hens, sheep and goats. It also includes fruit, vegetable and wine growing. Farmers produce food, but also fodder, wood or wool. Without agriculture, more than eight billion people could not be fed today.

About 10,000 years ago, people in the **Fertile Crescent** in the Near East began to grow grain and tame animals. This change from hunting and gathering to settling down is called the **Neolithic Revolution**. In the Middle Ages the **three-field system** became established in Europe: one field bore winter grain, one summer grain, and one lay fallow to recover. From the 19th century, machines and fertiliser made agriculture much more productive.

Farmers alternate the plants grown on a field from year to year, which is called **crop rotation**. In this way the soil is spared, and pests and diseases that attack only certain plants can spread less. Legumes such as clover or peas are gladly grown as **green manure**, because their nodule bacteria fix nitrogen from the air. A healthy soil full of earthworms and micro-organisms is the most important capital of a farm.

In Switzerland in 2023 there were just under 48,000 farms, many of them family businesses. The largest part of the farmland is made up of **meadows and pastures**, because in the hilly and mountainous regions grass thrives better than grain. That is why dairy farming is especially important, and from the milk come well-known cheeses such as Emmental, Gruyère or Appenzeller. The federal government supports farms with **direct payments** if, for example, they look after the landscape or keep animals particularly well.

In summer, many cows, young cattle, sheep and goats are driven up to the alpine pastures in the mountains. In Switzerland this time is called **summering**. On the alps, alpine cheese is often made on the spot. In autumn the animals return to the valley in the festive **alpine descent**, often decorated with flowers and large bells.

In **organic farming**, chemical-synthetic plant protection products and artificial fertilisers are forbidden. Instead, organic farmers rely on crop rotation, beneficial insects and mechanical weed control. In Switzerland, the **Knospe**, the bud, of Bio Suisse is a well-known organic label. Agriculture can also harm the environment, for example through too much fertiliser in waters, which is why farmers lay out flower meadows, hedges and wildflower fallows to protect biodiversity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The planned change of the plants that are grown on a field one after another.
The summer period in which the livestock live on the alpine pastures in the mountains.
A field on which nothing is grown for a time, so that the soil recovers.
Money from the federal government to farms for services such as landscape care and animal welfare.

gewusst: A dairy cow eats roughly 50 to 100 kilograms of grass or fodder per day and drinks many litres of water with it.
Switzerland produces about half of the food that is eaten in the country and imports the rest.
At the alpine descent, the finest cows sometimes wear a magnificent headdress of flowers and fir twigs.

teile.einleitung: How much forest does Switzerland have, and how is it doing? The **National Forest Inventory** gives the answer. It is a large survey of the Swiss forest that is repeated regularly.
wichtigste: The National Forest Inventory is carried out by the research institute WSL and the federal government.
The first inventory was taken from 1983 to 1985.
The data come from measurements on sample plots.
The timber stock per hectare is among the highest in Europe.
The forest area has increased, mainly in the Alps.
The Swiss forest belongs for the most part to public owners.

abschnitte.text: An **inventory** is a list of everything that is there. The **National Forest Inventory**, **NFI** for short (in German **LFI**), records the state of the Swiss forest. It is carried out by the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (**WSL**) together with the Federal Office for the Environment. The first inventory was taken **from 1983 to 1985**. Since then it has been repeated several times. In this way you can see how the forest changes over the decades.

You cannot measure every tree in Switzerland one by one. That is why the NFI gets its data through **measurements on sample plots**. These are spread over the whole country in a regular grid. Experts visit the plots and measure the trees. The diameter of a trunk is measured **1.3 metres above the ground**, which is roughly at chest height. In addition, aerial photographs are evaluated and foresters are surveyed.

The **timber stock** gives the **volume of all living trunks**. In the Swiss forest there is a great deal of wood per hectare. The stock is **among the highest in Europe**. The NFI also records the amount of **deadwood**. Dead trees are important for **biodiversity**. Many beetles, fungi, mosses and birds such as woodpeckers need dead wood to live.

The **forest area** of Switzerland has **increased** in recent decades. This happened **mainly in the Alps**. Many alpine pastures and mountain meadows are no longer used. There, shrubs first and then young trees grow in. On the Central Plateau, by contrast, the forest area is fairly stable, because the forest is well protected by law there. Today forest covers just under a third of Switzerland.

The Swiss forest belongs **for the most part to public owners**. These are mainly **municipalities**, citizen communities and corporations as well as the cantons. A smaller part belongs to private individuals. Regardless of the owner, in Switzerland you may in principle enter the forest freely. This is laid down in law.

gewusst: The diameter at a height of 1.3 metres is called the diameter at breast height.
In Switzerland, anyone may enter almost any forest, even if it is private.

teile.einleitung: If you leave a piece of land in peace, its plant life changes over many years. At the end of this development there is often a fairly stable community of living things, which experts call a climax community.
wichtigste: A climax community is the relatively stable end stage of a succession.
Frederic Clements held that climate alone determines the final community (monoclimax).
Arthur Tansley showed that soil and terrain also produce different final communities (polyclimax).
Permanent communities never reach the climax because of extreme soils.
Replacement communities such as hay meadows come about through humans.
The potential natural vegetation is the imagined plant cover without human influence.

abschnitte.text: The step-by-step change of the plant life in a place is called **succession**. On open ground, herbs and grasses grow first, then shrubs and fast-growing trees such as birches. Later come trees that tolerate a lot of shade. The relatively stable end stage is called the **climax community**. In large parts of central Europe this would usually be a deciduous forest, often with beeches.

The American ecologist **Frederic Clements** put forward the monoclimax theory. According to it, in one area the climate alone leads to a single final community. The Briton **Arthur Tansley** disagreed with the **polyclimax theory**: soil, water and relief also help to decide which plants grow in the end. That is why different stable communities can stand side by side in the same climate zone.

Some sites are so extreme that the climax never arrives. A **pine wood** on dry rock stays permanently, because beeches do not thrive there. This is called a **permanent community**. Other plant communities exist only because humans intervene. A hay meadow in beech forest country is a **replacement community**: if it were no longer mown, forest would come back in time.

Even a natural forest is not the same everywhere. The **mosaic cycle concept** describes it as a small-scale patchwork of different phases. In the **regeneration phase** young trees grow, in the **optimum phase** strong trees stand, and in the **decay phase** old trees die. In the process a lot of deadwood forms, and in the gaps the cycle starts again from the beginning.

Experts often ask what vegetation would establish itself without humans under today’s conditions. This imagined plant cover is called the **potential natural vegetation**. It helps in planning nature conservation and afforestation. For the Swiss Central Plateau it would be mostly beech forests, although today fields, meadows and settlements dominate there.

gewusst: The word climax comes from Greek and means “ladder” or “high point”.
Centuries can pass before a mature forest forms again on bare ground.

teile.einleitung: The dog rose is the most common wild rose here. It grows in hedges and at the edge of woods, blooms pale pink in early summer and bears red fruits in autumn, the rose hips.
wichtigste: The dog rose is a wild rose.
It is also called the hedge rose.
It blooms mainly in June.
Its flowers are light pink to white and have five petals.
Its shoots bear curved prickles.
Its fruits contain a lot of vitamin C and make tea.

abschnitte.text: The **dog rose** grows wild in **hedges**, at the **edges of woods** and along paths. That is why it is also called the **hedge rose**. It is the most common **wild rose** here. The shrub can grow several metres tall. Its long shoots often bend downwards in an arch.

The dog rose blooms in **early summer**, mainly in **June**. Its flowers are **pale pink to white** and have a light scent. As with other wild roses, they have only **five petals**. In the middle sit many yellow stamens. Bees and bumblebees like to visit the flowers.

The shoots of the dog rose bear curved **prickles**. With them it holds on to other plants and climbs upwards. Strictly speaking, these are prickles and not thorns, because they sit only on the bark and can be broken off easily. In the dense thicket, birds find shelter and build their nests.

After the flowering, the red fruits form, the **rose hips**. They contain a lot of **vitamin C**, often more than lemons. Dried, they make a red, slightly sour **tea**. You can also make jam or purée from them. In winter, rose hips are food for birds.

gewusst: The seeds inside the rose hip are surrounded by fine hairs that children used to use as itching powder.
Many garden roses are grafted onto dog rose roots, because these are very robust.

teile.einleitung: A legume is a special kind of fruit that you know from peas and beans. Many legumes are important foods because they contain a lot of protein.
wichtigste: A pod is a fruit that opens along two seams when ripe.
Pods are typical of the legume plant family.
Peas, beans, lentils, chickpeas and soya beans are legumes.
The peanut is also a legume, and its fruits ripen in the ground.
Siliques, as in rape and mustard, have a partition in the middle.
Tofu is made from soya beans, and hummus from chickpeas.

abschnitte.text: A **pod** forms from a single carpel. The seeds sit in a row along the seam. When the pod becomes ripe and dry, it opens along **two seams**, the ventral seam and the dorsal seam. In some species the two halves spring open so forcefully that the seeds are flung away. Anyone who opens a pea pod sees the seeds neatly lined up.

Plants with pods belong to the **legume family**, one of the largest plant families. It includes pea, bean, lentil, clover and also trees such as the false acacia. Many have small nodules on their roots with **nodule bacteria**. These take nitrogen from the air and make it usable for the plant. That is why legumes improve the soil.

abschnitte.titel: The peanut, a bean in the ground
abschnitte.text: Despite its name, the **peanut** is not a true nut but a legume. After flowering, a stalk grows downwards into the earth. There the pods ripen in the ground. The net-like shell that you break when cracking it open is the pod.

In everyday speech people often say “pea pod” for any such fruit, but in botany a pod and a silique are different things. True **siliques** are formed, for example, by rape and mustard. They arise from two carpels and have a thin **partition** in the middle. When one opens, the two valves come away, and the partition with the seeds stays standing.

Legumes are rich in **protein** and fibre. **Soya beans** are made into tofu and soya milk. **Chickpeas** are used to make hummus. The **runner bean**, with its bright red flowers, grows in many gardens. Raw beans are poisonous, and you must always cook them well.

gewusst: The peanut pushes its young fruits into the earth itself so that they ripen there.
Thanks to nodule bacteria, legumes need less nitrogen fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: With its thick, gnarled trunk and its tuft of thin rods, a pollard willow looks like a tree with a hairstyle. This shape does not arise by itself, but because people cut off the branches regularly.
wichtigste: A pollard willow is a willow whose branches are cut back regularly.
In the past its rods were used mainly for weaving baskets.
Cavities often form in old pollard willows.
Pollard willows typically grow by streams and in damp places.
If a pollard willow is no longer cut, the heavy crown can split the trunk.
Willow catkins are an important food for bees in spring.

abschnitte.text: In a **pollard willow**, the branches at the top of the trunk are cut off every few years. This is called **pollarding**. At the cut, the trunk gradually grows into a thick **head**, from which new, straight rods sprout every year. Pollard willows typically grow by **streams**, ditches and on damp meadows. Willows love water and grow very fast.

In the past, pollard willows were very useful. Their flexible **rods** were used for **weaving baskets**, for fences and for tying. Farmers cut the rods regularly and so always had a fresh supply. Today pollard willows are mainly looked after because they are valuable for nature and for the look of the landscape. If you stop cutting, the crown becomes too heavy and the trunk can **break apart**.

In the trunk of old pollard willows, **cavities** and rotten spots often form. In them live birds such as the little owl, but also bats and many insects. A special resident is the **musk beetle**. This shimmering green beetle smells of musk, and its larvae develop in the wood of old willows. In spring the **willow catkins** supply pollen and nectar for bees very early.

Willows are particularly easy to **propagate**. If you push a fresh branch into damp soil, it soon forms roots and grows into a new tree. In **willow bark** there is the substance **salicin**. It eases pain and fever. It was the model for a well-known painkiller that is now made artificially.

gewusst: The name salicin comes from the Latin word for willow, “Salix”.
A pollard willow can live to be over a hundred years old if it is cut regularly.

teile.einleitung: Jan Ingenhousz was a doctor and naturalist of the 18th century. He discovered that plants give off oxygen only in light, and so laid a foundation for the understanding of photosynthesis.
wichtigste: Jan Ingenhousz came from the Netherlands.
He was a doctor by profession.
He discovered that plants give off oxygen only in light.
Only the green parts of plants give off oxygen.
In 1779 his book “Experiments upon Vegetables” appeared.
He was friends with Benjamin Franklin.

abschnitte.text: Jan Ingenhousz was born in **1730** in Breda in the **Netherlands**. He studied medicine and worked as a **doctor**. Later he lived in England. There he learned about a method of protecting people against **smallpox**. At that time smallpox was a very dangerous disease.

In **1768** Ingenhousz travelled to **Vienna**. There he protected members of the imperial family of Maria Theresa against smallpox. The success made him famous, and he became personal physician at the court. Besides medicine, he worked on many scientific questions, such as electricity and plants.

Ingenhousz put plants under water and observed small bubbles of gas. He found that plants improve the air and give off **oxygen**, but **only in light**. And only the **green parts** do this. In the **shade** or at **night**, by contrast, plants make the air worse. Today we know that in light, green plants carry out **photosynthesis**, but they always have to breathe.

He published his results in **1779** in the book **“Experiments upon Vegetables”**. In it he built on the experiments of the Englishman Joseph Priestley. Ingenhousz was good friends with the American scientist and statesman **Benjamin Franklin**. The two wrote each other many letters about their research.

gewusst: As early as 1785, Ingenhousz observed the trembling movement of tiny specks of charcoal in alcohol, long before it could be explained.
That plants make the air worse in the dark is due to their breathing, which goes on day and night.

teile.einleitung: The coffee plant is a shrub or small tree from the tropics. From its seeds, the coffee beans, one of the world’s most popular drinks is made.
wichtigste: The original home of Arabica coffee is in Ethiopia.
Arabica and Robusta are the two most important kinds of coffee.
The fruits are called coffee cherries and usually contain two beans.
Brazil has long been the largest coffee producer in the world.
Vietnam is the second largest and grows mainly Robusta.
The coffee plant belongs to the madder family.

abschnitte.text: The **coffee plant** belongs to the plant family of the **madders**. The original home of **Arabica coffee** is in the highlands of **Ethiopia**. From Africa, coffee reached Arabia and later the whole world. Today it grows in many countries around the equator, in the so-called coffee belt.

Two kinds are the most important worldwide: **Arabica** and **Robusta**. Arabica likes to grow at cooler altitudes and is regarded as especially aromatic. Robusta is hardier, also grows in lower, warmer areas and contains more caffeine. Often the two kinds are mixed.

abschnitte.titel: From the flower to the bean
abschnitte.text: The coffee plant has white, fragrant flowers. From them, red **coffee cherries** develop. In each cherry there are normally **two seeds**, the coffee beans. They lie with their flat sides together. After the harvest, the flesh is removed and the beans are dried. They are then greenish and do not yet taste of coffee.

Only during **roasting** do the green beans turn **brown** and develop their typical **aroma**. Hundreds of aroma substances are produced in the process. Switzerland does not grow coffee itself, but a lot of coffee is roasted and traded here.

**Brazil** has long been the **largest coffee producer** in the world. In second place comes **Vietnam** in South-East Asia, which grows mainly **Robusta**. Colombia, Indonesia and Ethiopia are also important coffee countries. Many families in these countries live from growing coffee.

gewusst: A coffee cherry with only one round bean is called a peaberry.
Green, unroasted coffee beans can be stored much longer than roasted coffee.

teile.einleitung: The timber stock is the total amount of wood contained in the living trees of a forest. Switzerland measures it regularly with the National Forest Inventory and therefore knows exactly how much wood grows back and is used.
wichtigste: The National Forest Inventory (NFI) records the condition of the Swiss forest.
In the survey of 2018 to 2022, the timber stock was around 420 million cubic metres.
The spruce has the largest share of the stock, at around 42 per cent.
On the Central Plateau, the share of spruce is falling because of drought, storms and bark beetles.
Hans Carl von Carlowitz set out the idea of sustainability in 1713.
The Forest Police Act of 1876 laid the foundation for forest protection in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: How much wood stands in the forest?
abschnitte.text: The **National Forest Inventory**, or **NFI** for short, measures the Swiss forest on many sample plots. In the survey of 2018 to 2022, it found around **420 million cubic metres** of wood in living trees. This makes the Swiss forest one of the **richest in timber stock** in Europe. For a single piece of forest, you work it out like this: 12 hectares with 350 cubic metres each give 4,200 cubic metres of timber stock.

According to the 2025 forest report, around **42 per cent** of the stock is **spruce**. It used to be planted a lot because it grows quickly and supplies good building timber. On the warm, low-lying **Central Plateau**, however, the shallow-rooted spruce suffers from **heat and drought**. Weakened trees are easily attacked by **bark beetles** or blown over by storms. That is why their share is falling there, and broadleaved trees are becoming more important.

According to the NFI, around **10.6 million cubic metres** of wood grow each year in gross terms. After deducting the trees that die naturally, around 8.0 million remain in net terms. So around 2.6 million cubic metres die, and they often stay in the forest as **deadwood**. Around 7.1 million cubic metres are used, which is about **67 per cent** of the gross growth. So less wood is harvested than grows back.

In 1713, the Saxon chief mining officer **Hans Carl von Carlowitz** wrote the book “Sylvicultura oeconomica”. He demanded that no more wood be cut than grows back. He is regarded as the originator of the term **sustainability**. In Switzerland, clear-cutting and major floods led to the **Forest Police Act of 1876**. It first applied to the high mountains and was later extended to the whole of Switzerland.

gewusst: Deadwood is not waste: many beetles, fungi and birds depend on it.
The word sustainability, which is used everywhere today, originally comes from forestry.

teile.einleitung: The cacao tree grows in tropical rainforests. From its beans, cocoa and chocolate are made, for which Switzerland is world-famous.
wichtigste: Chocolate is made from cacao beans.
The fruits grow directly on the trunk.
The cacao tree comes from Central and South America.
It grows best in the warm, humid tropical forest.
Côte d’Ivoire harvests the most cocoa.
The Aztecs also used cacao beans as money.

abschnitte.text: The **cacao tree** originally comes from **Central and South America**. It grows best in the **warm, humid tropical forest**, in the shade of larger trees. It likes neither cold nor dryness. That is why it grows only in a narrow belt around the equator. In Switzerland it can only thrive in a greenhouse.

What is special is that the flowers and **fruits grow directly on the trunk** and on thick branches. The fruits are large, oblong and yellow, orange or reddish. In each fruit there are many **cacao beans**, surrounded by white, sweetish pulp. These are the seeds of the tree.

After the harvest, the beans are left to **ferment** with the pulp for a few days. This produces important aroma substances. After that they are **dried** in the sun. Only in the factories are the beans roasted and ground. From the cocoa mass the fat is also extracted, the **cocoa butter**. **White chocolate** contains only cocoa butter, but no dark cocoa mass.

The peoples of Central America already knew cacao. The **Aztecs** made a bitter drink from it. Cacao beans were so valuable that they also served as **money**. Spanish seafarers brought cacao to Europe in the 16th century.

Today **Côte d’Ivoire** in West Africa harvests the most cocoa. Switzerland gets its cacao beans **from tropical countries**, because no cacao grows here. Even so, Switzerland is famous for its chocolate. In the 19th century, the Swiss Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate.

gewusst: A cacao tree often bears flowers and ripe fruits at the same time.
The scientific name Theobroma means “food of the gods”.

teile.einleitung: Even in winter, trees and shrubs carry the leaves and flowers of the next spring inside them, well packed in buds. If you look closely, you can even recognise many trees by their buds.
wichtigste: A bud is a young, still closed shoot or a closed flower.
The buds for spring form as early as the year before.
Bud scales protect the buds in winter.
From a leaf bud come young leaves, from a flower bud flowers.
The bud at the tip of a twig is called the terminal bud.
Cloves, capers and broccoli are flower buds that people eat.

abschnitte.text: In a **bud** there are young leaves or flowers, folded tightly together. From a **leaf bud**, new leaves and shoots grow in spring, and from a **flower bud** flowers open. The bud right at the front of a twig is called the **terminal bud**. At the sides of the twig sit the **lateral buds**. From them grow new side branches.

The buds that open in spring are formed by the tree as early as the **summer before**. In winter they rest. Hard **bud scales** cover them like small roof tiles and protect them from cold and drying out. The **horse chestnut** has especially thick, sticky buds. The sticky coating also keeps off wet and small animals.

In winter, deciduous trees have no leaves. Even so, you can recognise them by their buds. The beech has long, pointed, brown buds. The ash has black buds. In many species the buds sit opposite each other, that is, in pairs, in others alternately, that is, one after the other left and right on the twig.

Some buds end up in the kitchen. **Cloves** are dried flower buds of the clove tree. **Capers** are pickled flower buds of the caper bush, which grows by the Mediterranean. In **broccoli** you eat mainly the many green flower buds. If broccoli is left standing too long, they open into small yellow flowers.

gewusst: The clove got its German name, “Nelke”, because it looks like a little nail, formerly called “Nägelein”.
Some buds stay dormant for years and sprout only when a branch breaks off.

teile.einleitung: The cryosphere includes all the frozen regions of water on Earth, that is, ice, snow and permafrost. It includes the huge ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland, the glaciers of the Alps, sea ice and the snow in winter. The cryosphere is an important part of the climate system and reacts especially sensitively to the warming of the Earth.
wichtigste: The cryosphere includes all the frozen regions of water on Earth, such as ice, snow and permafrost.
The name comes from the Greek word kryos for cold or frost.
Most of the Earth’s fresh water is stored in ice.
The largest masses of ice lie in Antarctica and on Greenland.
Light ice and snow throw back a lot of sunlight and so cool the Earth.
The glaciers of Switzerland are shrinking strongly because of climate change.
Melting ice sheets make sea level rise.

abschnitte.text: Besides air, water, rock and living things, the cryosphere is one of the great parts of the Earth’s **climate system**. It includes **glaciers** and ice sheets, sea ice, frozen lakes and rivers, the snow cover and permanently frozen ground. Some parts exist only in winter, like the snow on the Central Plateau. Others are hundreds of thousands of years old, like the deep ice in Antarctica.

The **Antarctic ice sheet** is the largest mass of ice on Earth and in some places over 4 kilometres thick. If it melted completely, sea level would rise by many dozens of metres. The Greenland ice sheet is also enormously large. **Sea ice**, by contrast, floats on the ocean, mainly around the North Pole and Antarctica, and when it melts it hardly raises sea level.

**Permafrost** is the name for soil or rock that stays frozen without a break for at least two years. Huge areas of it exist in Siberia, Canada and Alaska. There is also permafrost in the Swiss Alps, mostly above about 2,500 metres. When it thaws, rockfalls and debris flows can occur, because the ice no longer holds rock and rubble together.

Ice and snow are light and throw a large part of the sunlight back into space, which is called a high **albedo**. When the ice melts, darker surfaces come to light, which warm up more strongly. The cryosphere also stores a large part of the Earth’s fresh water. Glaciers act like **water stores**, which in the hot summer release meltwater to rivers such as the Rhone and the Rhine.

Switzerland has about 1,400 glaciers, and the largest is the **Great Aletsch Glacier** in the Valais, about 20 kilometres long. Since the 19th century, Swiss glaciers have lost a large part of their ice. In the very hot years of 2022 and 2023 they melted faster than ever since measurements began. The **GLAMOS** measuring network watches the Swiss glaciers closely every year.

Shrinking glaciers change landscapes, water supplies and tourism in the Alps. Where the ice disappears, new **glacial lakes** can form, which become dangerous if they burst. In May 2025, an enormous collapse of ice and rock at the Birch Glacier buried large parts of the village of **Blatten** in the Lötschental. Worldwide, the melting of the ice sheets leads to rising sea level.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large mass of ice made of compressed snow that moves slowly down the valley.
A huge blanket of ice that covers a whole country or a continent.
Frozen seawater that floats on the ocean.
Soil or rock that has been permanently frozen for at least two years.

gewusst: In the ice of Antarctica, tiny air bubbles are trapped that tell researchers what the air was made of hundreds of thousands of years ago.
Glacier ice often looks blue, because the dense ice swallows red light and lets blue light through.
In summer, white sheets are laid out on some Swiss glaciers to slow the melting.

teile.einleitung: A tadpole is a young frog or toad. It lives in water and looks quite different from an adult animal. In an astonishing transformation it becomes an animal that can also live on land.
wichtigste: Tadpoles are the larvae of frogs and toads.
They live in water.
Young tadpoles breathe with gills.
They swim with their paddle-like tail.
They eat mainly algae and plant remains.
In frogs, the hind legs grow first.
The change into a frog is called metamorphosis.

abschnitte.text: Frogs and toads lay their eggs in water. These eggs are called **spawn**. From them hatch tiny larvae, the **tadpoles**. They have a roundish body and a long **paddle tail**. At the beginning they still have no legs. Tadpoles can live only in **water**.

Young tadpoles breathe with **gills**, like fish. With them they take oxygen from the water. Later they get **lungs**. With their mouths they rasp off **algae** and soft **plant remains**. Some also eat dead little creatures. Many tadpoles are eaten themselves by fish, dragonfly larvae or birds.

After a few weeks, legs grow on the tadpole. In frogs, the **hind legs** appear first. Later the **front legs** are added. At the same time the head changes, and the mouth becomes wider. The tadpole now looks almost like a small frog.

The change into a frog is called **metamorphosis**. The whole body changes in the process. The body slowly breaks down the **tail** until it disappears completely. A water animal becomes an animal that also lives on land. The little frogs then leave the water. In Switzerland, ponds and pools are therefore important for amphibians.

gewusst: The tadpoles of the common toad taste bad to many fish and are therefore often spared.
In the midwife toad, some tadpoles spend the winter in the water and turn into toads only the next year.

teile.einleitung: The **Great Basin bristlecone pine** is among the oldest living things on Earth. Some of these trees are almost 5,000 years old. They grow high in the dry mountains in the west of the USA.
wichtigste: The oldest known tree with a single trunk is about 4,800 years old.
It is called Methuselah and is a bristlecone pine.
Its exact location is kept secret, so that nobody harms it.
The trees grow high in dry mountains and very slowly.
Ancient bristlecone pines are gnarled and partly dead.
In Sweden grows a spruce whose root system is said to be about 9,500 years old.

abschnitte.text: The Great Basin bristlecone pine is called Pinus longaeva in scientific terms. In German it is the “Langlebige Kiefer”, and “Kiefer” is another word for **Föhre**, pine. It grows **high in dry mountains** in the west of the USA, mainly in California and Nevada. There it is cold in winter and dry in summer, and the ground is stony. That is why the trees grow **very slowly**. As a result their wood becomes very dense and resistant.

The most famous tree of this species is called **Methuselah**. It is about **4,800 years old**. So it was already growing when the first pyramids were being built in Egypt. Methuselah is the oldest known tree with a **single trunk** whose age was determined by counting the tree rings. It is named after a figure from the Bible who is said to have lived to a very great age.

The **exact location** of Methuselah is **kept secret**. People want to prevent visitors from damaging the tree, for example by breaking off pieces or trampling the ground around the roots. Visitors can, however, hike through the forest where it stands.

Ancient bristlecone pines often look **gnarled**. Their trunks are twisted by the wind and **partly dead**. Often only a narrow strip of bark is still alive, supplying the few green branches. In this way the tree saves energy. This is exactly what helps it to get so old.

abschnitte.titel: Even older: a spruce in Sweden
abschnitte.text: In **Sweden** grows a spruce called **Old Tjikko**. The trunk that you see today is not very old. Its **root system**, however, is said to be about **9,500 years** old. Again and again a new trunk grew from the same roots. In Switzerland, too, there are very old trees, such as Swiss stone pines, larches and yews that are several hundred years old.

gewusst: Methuselah sprouted even before the great pyramids of Giza were built.
From the tree rings of old pines you can read what the climate was like thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: **Gilled mushrooms** have thin little plates under their cap, the gills. They include popular edible mushrooms and some of the most poisonous mushrooms of all. Anyone who collects them must know them exactly.
wichtigste: Gills increase the area on which spores are formed.
Many gilled mushrooms are deadly poisonous, which is why identifying them is tricky.
Webcaps have a cobweb-like veil when young.
Milkcaps give off a milky sap when injured.
The shaggy ink cap dissolves in old age into a black liquid.
The parasol mushroom has a ring that slides and a cap like an umbrella.

abschnitte.text: On the **gills**, the mushroom forms its **spores**. Many thin little plates side by side give a large area. The gills therefore **increase the area for spore formation**, without the cap having to be huge. The ripe spores fall downwards and are carried off by the wind. The gilled mushrooms also include the **brittlegills**, which are very common in Swiss woods.

In the **webcaps**, a **cobweb-like veil** stretches between the cap edge and the stalk in the young mushroom. Later often only fine fibres remain on the stalk. The webcaps are a very species-rich group, and some are dangerously poisonous. The **milkcaps** can be recognised by the fact that they give off a **milky sap** when injured. It can be white, orange or otherwise coloured.

The **oyster mushroom** grows **sideways on wood** and looks like a shell. It is also **cultivated** on straw or wood and is often available in shops. The **parasol mushroom** is a large gilled mushroom. Its cap looks like an opened **umbrella**. On the stalk it carries a **ring** that you can **slide** up and down.

The **shaggy ink cap** often grows on meadows and at the edges of paths. When young it is white and elongated in shape. In old age the gills turn black from the edge. Then the mushroom **dissolves** into a black, **ink-like liquid**. People really did write with this liquid in the past. That is how it got its name.

Identifying gilled mushrooms is **especially tricky** for beginners. They include many **deadly poisonous** species, for example the **death cap**. It can be mistaken for edible mushrooms. So the rule is: always have collected mushrooms checked by a **mushroom inspection service**. In Switzerland, many municipalities offer this service.

gewusst: The death cap is responsible for most deadly mushroom poisonings in Europe.
In the past, people wrote with the liquid of old shaggy ink caps.

teile.einleitung: In February, when hardly anything is blooming yet, a yellow shrub already glows at the edges of woods and in hedges: the cornelian cherry. In late summer it bears red fruits that you can eat.
wichtigste: The cornelian cherry blooms yellow as early as February and March.
It blooms when there is still little food for bees.
Its ripe fruits are red and sourish.
In German-speaking Switzerland it is also called “Tierlibaum”.
Its wood is very hard and heavy.
It is related to the red dogwood.

abschnitte.text: The **cornelian cherry** is a large shrub or small tree. It is among the first plants to bloom in the year, often as early as **February and March**. Its small **yellow** flowers appear before the leaves grow. That is why the whole shrub glows yellow. For **bees** it is very important, because there is still little food at this time.

In late summer the elongated fruits ripen. They are bright **red** and recall small cherries, but are not related to them. You can **eat** them. Fresh, they taste rather **sour**, while very ripe fruits are milder. They are made into jam, jelly, juice or syrup. Birds also like to eat the fruits.

The wood of the cornelian cherry is **very hard and heavy**. In the past it was used to make tool handles, cogs and walking sticks. The cornelian cherry belongs to the **dogwood family**. Its relative, the **red dogwood**, often grows in hedges and has strikingly red twigs in winter. In German-speaking Switzerland the cornelian cherry is also called **Tierlibaum**.

gewusst: Cornelian cherries can live to a great age, some shrubs over a hundred years.
The cornelian cherry is often planted in hedges and gardens, because it tolerates pruning well.

teile.einleitung: The **pumpkin** is seen everywhere in autumn: at markets, in soup and as a carved lantern. There are small ornamental pumpkins and giant pumpkins heavier than a car. For plant scientists a pumpkin is really a berry.
wichtigste: Pumpkins are harvested in autumn.
Botanically a pumpkin is a large berry.
Besides the flesh, you can also eat the seeds.
The Hokkaido pumpkin is usually orange.
Ornamental pumpkins should not be eaten, they can be poisonous.
The biggest giant pumpkins weigh more than 1,000 kilograms.

abschnitte.text: The pumpkin originally comes from **America**. There it was grown thousands of years ago. The plant grows along the ground with long tendrils and has large yellow flowers. For plant scientists the fruit is a **berry**, because the seeds lie in the flesh. Because of the hard rind, it is also called a **pepo**, an armoured berry.

Pumpkins are harvested **in autumn**, mostly from September to October. A pumpkin is ripe when the stalk is dry and woody and the rind sounds hollow when tapped. Many whole pumpkins can be stored **cool and dry for several months**. That is why they used to be an important winter vegetable.

From the flesh you make soup, gratin or cake. The **Hokkaido pumpkin** is usually **orange**. Its skin gets soft when cooked and can be eaten as well. The **seeds** are edible too. Roasted, they are a fine snack. From them dark green **pumpkin seed oil** is also pressed.

**Ornamental pumpkins** are colourful and have funny shapes. But they should **not be eaten**. They can contain **bitter substances** that are poisonous and cause severe stomach ache. Even an edible pumpkin that tastes very bitter does not belong in the pot but in the bin.

At **Halloween** at the end of October, faces are carved into hollowed-out pumpkins and a candle is put inside. This custom comes from Ireland and North America and has become popular in Switzerland too. At competitions, **giant pumpkins** are weighed. The biggest weigh **more than 1,000 kilograms**. In Switzerland there are large pumpkin exhibitions in autumn, and weighing competitions take place here too.

gewusst: A giant pumpkin can gain more than ten kilograms in a single day in summer.
Pumpkins belong to the same family as cucumbers, courgettes and melons.

teile.einleitung: Daisies, dandelions, sunflowers and edelweiss look very different, but belong to the same plant family: the daisy family, or composites. Their secret: what looks like a single flower is made up of many small flowers.
wichtigste: The “flower” of a composite is a flower head made of many individual flowers.
In the middle there are often tubular florets, at the edge ray florets.
The dandelion has only ray florets.
With the pappus, a parachute of hairs, the fruits fly through the air.
Edelweiss, arnica, sunflower, lettuce and cornflower are composites.
The composites are among the most species-rich plant families in the world.

abschnitte.text: If you look at a **daisy** with a magnifying glass, you discover a surprise: it is not a single flower but a **flower head** made of many tiny flowers. They sit tightly in a basket-like base, hence the German name **Korbblütler**, basket-flowerers. In this way the whole group looks like one large flower and attracts insects better.

In the **ox-eye daisy**, many yellow **tubular florets** sit in the middle. They are small and have the shape of tiny tubes. At the edge stand the white **ray florets**, which look like petals. Not all composites have both kinds. The **dandelion** has **only ray florets**, which is why its head looks so dense and yellow.

Many composites have a special trick for spreading. Their fruits carry a fine parachute of hairs, the **pappus**. In the **dandelion** you can see it well: the white dandelion clock consists of many fruits with small parachutes. The wind carries them far away. In this way the plant can spread to new places.

The family includes **edelweiss**, a symbol of the Swiss mountains. **Arnica** of the mountain meadows is also a composite. It is used externally for bruises. The **sunflower** supplies oil and seeds, and the **cornflower** blooms blue in cornfields. Even vegetables such as **lettuce** belong to it.

gewusst: The composites include over 20,000 species worldwide.
In edelweiss, the white, star-shaped “petals” are in truth felty bracts around the small flower heads.

teile.einleitung: The coconut is one of the best-known fruits of the tropics. It grows on the coconut palm and provides water, flesh, oil and even fibres. It is also a true seafarer.
wichtigste: The coconut grows on the coconut palm.
Botanically it is not a nut but a stone fruit.
Young coconuts contain clear coconut water.
Coconuts can float in the sea and in this way reach new islands.
A coconut has three dark “eyes”.
From the fibres, doormats among other things are made.

abschnitte.text: The **coconut palm** grows on tropical coasts all around the world. It has a slender trunk and at the top a crown of long leaves. The fruits hang in bunches under the leaves. For many people in the tropics the palm is very valuable, because almost all its parts can be used: fruits, leaves and wood.

For plant scientists, the coconut is a **stone fruit**, like the cherry or the peach. On the outside it has a smooth skin, and under it a thick **layer of fibre**. Inside follows the hard brown shell that we see in the shop. On it sit **three dark eyes**. Through one of them the seedling can later sprout. Inside are the white flesh and, in young fruits, the clear **coconut water**.

Thanks to the airy layer of fibre, a coconut can **float** in the sea. In this way it sometimes drifts for weeks over the water. If it is washed up on a foreign beach, a new palm can grow there. In this way coconut palms have spread to many islands. People, too, took them along on their travels and planted them.

For **coconut milk**, the grated flesh is pressed out with water. It is important in many Asian kitchens, for example in curries. From the dried flesh, **coconut oil** is obtained. The coarse fibres from the husk are very tough. **Doormats**, ropes and brushes are made from them.

gewusst: Coconut water is not the same as coconut milk: it flows out of the young nut by itself.
A coconut palm can bear fruit for many decades.

teile.einleitung: **True mosses** are the largest group of mosses. They form soft green cushions and carpets in the forest, on stones and on walls. If you look closely, you discover small capsules on fine stalks.
wichtigste: The spore capsule sits on a stalk called the seta.
A hood, the calyptra, covers the young capsule in many species.
At the opening of the capsule there is often a ring of teeth, the peristome.
The leaflets of most true mosses are only one layer of cells thick.
Many true mosses have a midrib in the leaflets.
In Switzerland there are over 1,000 species of moss.
The science of mosses is called bryology.

abschnitte.text: True mosses have a small **stem** with many tiny **leaflets**. The leaflets of most species are **only one layer of cells** thick. That is why they can take up water directly over the surface. Many true mosses have a **midrib** in their leaflets. By this you can often tell them from the leafy **liverworts**, whose leaflets have no rib. Mosses have no roots, but fine anchoring threads, the **rhizoids**.

True mosses multiply with **spores**. These form in a **spore capsule**. It sits on a thin stalk called the **seta**. In many species the young capsule is covered by a **hood**. This hood is called the **calyptra**. When the capsule is ripe, the hood falls off, and a little lid opens.

At the opening of the capsule in many true mosses there is a **ring of teeth**. It is called the **peristome**. The fine teeth move depending on the moisture. In dry weather they open and let the spores out, and in wet weather they close. In this way the spores are spread by the wind in good weather.

A well-known true moss is the **haircap moss**, called “Frauenhaarmoos” in German, “woman’s hair moss”. It is among the largest mosses here and can grow many centimetres tall. It gets its name from the **hairy hood** above the spore capsule. It looks like a small tuft of hair. You often find it in damp woods and bogs.

In **Switzerland** there are **over 1,000 species of moss**. The science that deals with mosses is called **bryology**. The word comes from the Greek word for moss. Mosses are important for nature. They store a lot of water, protect the soil and offer tiny animals a habitat. The **peat mosses** in the raised bogs also belong to the true mosses.

gewusst: Peat mosses can store many times their own weight in water.
Some mosses can dry out completely for a long time and turn green again after a rain.

teile.einleitung: A very long time ago there were plants only in water. Then the first **land plants** conquered the land. For this they needed new inventions against drying out and for gas exchange.
wichtigste: According to fossil spore finds, plants settled the land from the Ordovician onwards, about 470 million years ago.
The cuticle protects against drying out.
Stomata regulate gas exchange.
Sporopollenin protects spores and pollen.
Mosses have no woody conducting tissue.
Even early land plants lived in symbiosis with fungi, the mycorrhiza.

abschnitte.text: Land plants descend from **green algae** that lived in fresh water. The oldest evidence of land plants is tiny **fossil spores**. They show that plants settled the land **from the Ordovician onwards**, about **470 million years ago**. At that time on land there were still no animals bigger than tiny arthropods. The first land plants were small and grew close to water.

On land, plants are threatened by **drying out**. That is why land plants have a waxy protective layer on their parts above ground, the **cuticle**. It lets hardly any water through. So that the plant can still take in carbon dioxide and give off oxygen, there are small openings in the epidermis. These **stomata** regulate **gas exchange** and can open and close.

The spores and pollen of land plants are protected by a very resistant substance. It is called **sporopollenin**. It survives drought, UV radiation and even millions of years in rock. That is why such old fossil spores are found. Because in all land plants the young plant is first nourished by the mother plant, they are called **embryophytes** in technical language.

Land plants are divided into two large groups. The **mosses** have **no woody conducting tissue**. They therefore stay small and need damp places. Mosses in the wider sense include **true mosses**, **liverworts** and **hornworts**. The **vascular plants** have conducting tissues that carry water and nutrients. They include ferns, conifers and flowering plants. Thanks to them, plants were able to grow tall.

The soil at that time was hardly developed yet. Even early land plants received help from **fungi**. This partnership is called **mycorrhiza**. The fungal threads fetch nutrients and water from the soil and give them to the plant. In return they get sugar. Even today most land plants live together with mycorrhizal fungi.

gewusst: Most land plants today live together with fungi on their roots.
Sporopollenin is so stable that fossil spores are still preserved after hundreds of millions of years.

teile.einleitung: Climate change brings hotter summers, longer dry spells and new pests. So that the Swiss forest stays healthy, foresters help it to adapt to these changes.
wichtigste: Mixed forests with many tree species spread the risk better than forests of only one species.
In a selection forest, young and old trees grow side by side.
In thinning, individual trees are removed so that the others have more room.
In dry summers the danger of forest fires rises, especially in Ticino and the Valais.
