The WSL in Birmensdorf ZH researches forest, snow and landscape.
Young oaks need a lot of light and often suffer from browsing by game.
Deadwood offers habitat to many animals, fungi and plants.

abschnitte.text: Different tree species react differently to heat, drought and pests. The **spruce**, for example, suffers badly from drought and is then easily attacked by the bark beetle. If beech, oak or silver fir also grow beside it in a **mixed forest**, the forest survives when one species fails. That is why foresters today deliberately plant and encourage many different trees.

In **thinning**, individual trees are taken out deliberately. The remaining ones then get more light, water and space and become stronger. In a **selection forest**, as is widespread in the Emmental, only individual trees are ever felled. In this way young, middle-aged and old trees stand mixed together, and the ground is never completely bare. For **oaks**, small gaps are made, because young oaks die in the shade.

Roe deer and red deer like to eat the buds and shoots of young trees. This **browsing by game** hits oaks and silver firs in particular, that is, species that could cope well with the climate of the future. With fences, protective sleeves and regulated hunting, people try to protect the young trees. In this way a new, mixed generation of forest can grow up.

When it does not rain for a long time, dry leaves and brittle branches burn easily. On the south side of the Alps and in the Valais, the **danger of forest fires** then rises clearly. In such times the authorities often issue fire bans in the forest and at its edge. A forest fire is especially dangerous when it destroys a **protection forest**, which shields villages from avalanches and rockfall.

The Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research, the **WSL**, in Birmensdorf studies how the forest reacts to climate change. It also includes the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos. Today, dead trees are often left standing or lying in the forest as **deadwood**. In it live beetles, fungi, mosses and woodpeckers. A varied forest is also a resilient forest.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest.
Since the 19th century, a federal law has protected the Swiss forest from clear-cutting.
In a single dead tree trunk, hundreds of different species can live.

teile.einleitung: Lettuce is one of the most popular salads in Switzerland. Its tender green leaves form a round head, which is how it got its German name, “Kopfsalat”, head salad. You can also grow it in your own garden.
wichtigste: With lettuce, you eat the leaves.
It is called head lettuce because its leaves form a round head.
Lettuce is usually eaten raw with a salad dressing.
Slugs especially like to eat lettuce in the garden.
In long heat it shoots up and flowers.
Lettuce is related to the dandelion.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of **lettuce** grow close together and form a loose, round **head**. On the outside they are usually a strong **green**, and inside paler and more tender. Only the **leaves** are eaten. Lettuce contains a great deal of water and is therefore light and refreshing.

In spring, young lettuce plants are put into the soil. They are called **seedlings**. After only a few weeks you can harvest. Unfortunately **slugs** also like lettuce very much and eat whole leaves away in a single night. If it is **hot** for a long time, the lettuce begins to **bolt**: it grows tall, forms a stem and **flowers**. Then the leaves become bitter.

Lettuce belongs to the **daisy family**. It is related to the **dandelion**. You can see this when it flowers: the small yellow flowers recall the dandelion, and the seeds also fly with little parachutes. If you cut into the stalk, a white **milky sap** comes out, as in the dandelion.

Lettuce is mostly eaten **raw**. You wash the leaves, let them drain and mix them with a **salad dressing** of vinegar, oil and seasonings. The dressing is added only shortly before eating, otherwise the leaves go soft. In Switzerland a green salad goes with many lunches.

gewusst: The Latin word for lettuce, “Lactuca”, comes from “lac” for milk, because of the white milky sap.
Lettuce is more than 90 per cent water.

teile.einleitung: A “living fossil” is a species that today still looks very similar to its relatives of millions of years ago. Well-known examples are the ginkgo, the dawn redwood and the horsetails. The term is, however, disputed.
wichtigste: Charles Darwin first used the expression “living fossil” in 1859.
The ginkgo is the only living species of its class of plants today.
Ginkgo leaves from the Jurassic look very similar to today’s.
The dawn redwood was at first known only as a fossil.
The Wollemi pine was discovered in Australia in 1994.
Living fossils too have developed further genetically.

abschnitte.text: The expression was coined by **Charles Darwin** in 1859 in his book “On the Origin of Species”. He spoke of “living fossils”. By this he meant species that have preserved old forms to this day. A **fossil** is a petrified remnant of a living thing from earlier times. A living fossil therefore looks almost like its petrified ancestors.

The **ginkgo** is the last representative of a class of plants that was widespread in the Mesozoic. Its leaves are **fan-shaped** and have forked veins. Even from the **Jurassic** there are ginkgo leaves that strongly resemble the tree today. So the genus has survived well over 150 million years. In **Hiroshima**, several ginkgos survived the atomic bomb in 1945 and sprouted again. Today they are regarded as a symbol of hope.

The **dawn redwood** was described in 1941 by the researcher Shigeru Miki from fossils. Soon afterwards, in the 1940s, living trees were found in central China. Even more astonishing is the **Wollemi pine**: it was discovered in 1994 in a remote gorge in Australia. Before that only similar fossils were known. The exact site in Wollemi National Park is still kept secret today in order to protect the trees.

The **horsetails** (genus Equisetum) are the only survivors of an ancient plant lineage. In the **Carboniferous** there were tree-sized relatives, the calamites, which grew up to 20 metres tall. Today horsetails are small, herbaceous plants. In Switzerland you can find, for example, the field horsetail at the edges of paths and in fields.

Living fossils too have not stood still. Their **form** may stay similar for a long time, but their **genes** and their adaptations keep changing. Many experts therefore find the expression imprecise. Today people often speak of **relict species**. These are species that are left over as the remnant of a formerly larger group.

gewusst: Ginkgos today stand in many Swiss parks and along streets because they tolerate exhaust fumes well.
The site of the Wollemi pine is secret so that nobody brings in diseases or takes plants away.

teile.einleitung: Why do many animal species live on some islands and only a few on others? The theory of island biogeography gives an answer. Today it is important for nature conservation too.
wichtigste: Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson published the theory in 1967.
The number of species comes from a balance between immigration and extinction.
On large islands, fewer species die out than on small ones.
The further an island is from the mainland, the fewer species arrive.
Even at equilibrium, species keep changing.
Krakatau is regarded as an open-air laboratory of recolonisation.

abschnitte.text: In **1967**, **Robert MacArthur** and **Edward O. Wilson** published the theory of **island biogeography**. It says: on an island, new species keep arriving, while others die out. The number of species settles at a **balance** between **immigration** and **extinction**. Even then, which species are present keeps changing. This exchange is called **species turnover**.

On **large islands** there are more habitats and larger populations. That is why the **extinction rate is lower**, and more species live there. If an island lies **far from the mainland**, fewer animals and seeds reach it. The **immigration rate falls**. Mathematically, the relationship is described by S = c · A to the power z. With z = 0.3, the number of species grows by about a **factor of 2** when the area becomes ten times larger.

In the 1960s, **Daniel Simberloff** and Edward O. Wilson carried out a famous experiment. On small **mangrove islands** in Florida, they removed all the **arthropods**, that is, insects, spiders and their relatives. Then they observed how the islands were colonised again. A natural example is the volcanic island of **Krakatau**. After the enormous eruption of **1883**, almost all life there was wiped out, and researchers followed how plants and animals returned.

The theory does not apply only to islands in the sea. A wood between fields, a mountain lake or a **protected area** is also a kind of island. In the **SLOSS debate**, people ask whether **one large or several small protected areas** are better. Many experts today stress that protected areas should also be well **connected**, so that animals and plants can get from one to another. This applies in densely used Switzerland too.

gewusst: SLOSS is an English abbreviation for “single large or several small”.
On Krakatau, the first plants were growing again only a few years after the eruption.

teile.einleitung: Bumblebees are round, furry insects that belong to the bees. They fly even in cool weather and are therefore important pollinators in spring and in the mountains.
wichtigste: Bumblebees belong to the bees.
Their bodies are round and densely hairy.
They fly even in cool weather.
Only the young queens survive the winter.
Many bumblebees nest in holes in the ground.
A bumblebee colony is much smaller than a honey bee colony.

abschnitte.text: Bumblebees are a group of **bees**. Like other bees, they collect **nectar** and **pollen**. Their bodies are **round** and have a thick **fur**. The fur keeps them warm. When they fly, their wings beat fast, which makes a **deep buzzing**. Bumblebees are peaceful and only very rarely sting.

Honey bees often stay in the hive in cool weather. Bumblebees fly anyway. They **shiver** with their **flight muscles** and warm themselves up that way. That is why they are out and about early in spring. They visit flowers high up in the **mountains** and in rainy weather too.

Many bumblebees build their nest in **holes in the ground**, for example in old **mouse holes**. A bumblebee colony usually has only **a few hundred** animals, while a bee colony is much bigger. In autumn the bumblebee colony dies. Only the **young queens** hibernate, often in the soil. In spring each of them founds a new colony.

Bumblebees can shake flowers with **vibrations**. This makes the pollen fall out. It works especially well with **tomato flowers**. That is why vegetable growers use bumblebees in the **greenhouse**. This means more tomatoes form. For this, bumblebee colonies are specially bred and delivered in cardboard boxes.

gewusst: Several dozen different species of bumblebee live in Switzerland.
By shivering, bumblebees can raise their body temperature to over 30 degrees, even when it is cool outside.

teile.einleitung: The corncockle is a pretty field flower with purple-red blooms. In the past it grew in many cornfields and was feared by farmers, because its seeds are poisonous. Today it has become very rare in the wild.
wichtigste: The flowers of the corncockle are purple-red to violet.
It belongs to the pink family.
Its poisonous seeds used to get into the flour.
Through the cleaning of seed grain it has almost disappeared.
The plant is annual, and its seeds are black and warty.
Today it is often found in sown wild flower mixtures.

abschnitte.text: The **corncockle** grows about as tall as grain. Its large flowers are **purple-red to violet** and have five petals with dark lines. The plant belongs to the **pink family**. It is **annual**: it grows, flowers, forms seeds and dies in the same year. Its seeds are **black and warty** and sit in a capsule.

In the past the corncockle typically grew in **cornfields**. Its seeds are about as big as grains of corn. At harvest they therefore easily got in among the grain and were milled along with it. But the seeds are **poisonous**. If they got into the **flour**, the bread could make people and animals ill. That is why the corncockle was feared by farmers.

With the thorough **cleaning of seed grain**, the corncockle seeds were reliably sorted out. Because the plant multiplies only by its seeds, it almost completely disappeared from the fields in central Europe. Today you often meet it again in **sown wild flower mixtures**, in gardens and flower strips. There it is a nice source of food for butterflies. But you should not eat it.

gewusst: The corncockle has become so rare that in some countries it counts as threatened with extinction.

teile.einleitung: A deciduous forest is a forest in which mainly broadleaved trees such as beeches, oaks, maples and ashes grow. It changes greatly with the seasons: in spring the forest floor blooms, in summer it is shady, in autumn the leaves glow in bright colours. In Switzerland the beech is the most common broadleaved tree in the forest.
wichtigste: In a deciduous forest, mainly broadleaved trees grow.
The beech is the most common broadleaved tree in the forests of Switzerland.
Broadleaved trees drop their leaves in autumn so as not to dry out in winter.
In autumn many leaves turn yellow because chlorophyll is broken down and yellow pigments become visible.
Early bloomers such as the wood anemone flower early because a lot of light reaches the ground before the leaves come out.
A deciduous forest is divided into layers, from the moss layer to the tree layer.
Deciduous forests are a habitat for many animals such as woodpeckers, squirrels and roe deer.

abschnitte.text: A deciduous forest is a forest in which broadleaved trees make up the largest share. In Switzerland, pure deciduous forests are found mainly on the **Central Plateau**, in the Jura and on the southern edge of the Alps, often mixed with conifers to form a **mixed forest**. The most important tree species is the **beech**, which thrives on many soils and tolerates a lot of shade. Alongside it grow oaks, sycamores, ashes, limes and hornbeams.

A deciduous forest is built like a house with several **storeys**. At the very bottom lies the moss layer, above it the herb layer with flowers, ferns and grasses. Then comes the shrub layer with hazel bushes, elder and young trees. At the very top spreads the **tree layer** with the crowns of the big trees.

In early spring, before the trees put out their leaves, a lot of sunlight reaches the forest floor. **Early bloomers** such as the wood anemone, wild garlic, the liverwort and the lesser celandine use this short time. They have stored nutrients in bulbs, tubers or thick roots and can therefore grow and flower very quickly. As soon as the leaf canopy closes, many of them withdraw into the ground again.

In summer the crowns form a dense leaf canopy, and it is cool and shady on the ground. In autumn the **chlorophyll** is broken down, yellow pigments become visible, and the forest glows yellow, orange and red. After that the trees drop their leaves so as not to dry out in winter. The leaves form a thick **litter layer** on the ground, which turns into humus.

Deciduous forests offer many animals food and shelter. **Woodpeckers** hammer out holes in old trunks, which later are also lived in by tits, bats or dormice. Squirrels, wild boar and jays eat beechnuts and acorns. In the dead wood of old oaks lives the stag beetle, one of the largest beetles in Europe.

About a third of Switzerland is forested, and at lower altitudes **beech forests** would naturally be found almost everywhere. Many deciduous forests were converted into spruce forests in the past, but today foresters are again promoting broadleaved trees more, because they often cope better with heat and drought. In Ticino there are extensive **chestnut woods**, called selve. Since 2021, beech forests in Ticino have been part of the UNESCO World Natural Heritage site of the ancient beech forests of Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A forest in which broadleaved trees and conifers grow together.
Plants that flower very early in the year, before the trees have leaves.
The storey of the forest with flowers, grasses and ferns.
Dead trees and branches that serve as a habitat for many animals and fungi.

gewusst: In spring, in some deciduous forests you can smell wild garlic long before you see it, because it smells strongly of garlic.
Under a dense beech canopy only a small part of the sunlight reaches the ground in summer.
A great spotted woodpecker can hammer against a trunk up to 20 times a second.

teile.einleitung: The Japanese beetle is a small, shimmering beetle that originally comes from Japan. It eats a great many different plants and counts in Switzerland as a dangerous pest that must be reported.
wichtigste: The scientific name is Popillia japonica.
In Switzerland it was first found in 2017, in Ticino.
It has a green head, copper-brown wing cases and white tufts of hair.
The larvae eat the roots of lawns and meadows.
The beetles eat leaves until only the veins are left.
Finds outside known areas are reported to the cantonal plant protection service.

abschnitte.text: The **Japanese beetle** is called **Popillia japonica** in scientific terms. It is about 1 centimetre long. Its head and thorax shine **metallic green**, and the wing cases are **copper-brown**. Typical are the **white tufts of hair** at the sides and at the end of the abdomen. This is how it is told apart from the similar native **garden chafer**, which lacks these tufts.

The Japanese beetle is not fussy. It eats hundreds of plant species, for example vines, fruit trees, roses and maize. The beetles eat the leaves so that only the **leaf veins** are left. This is called **skeletonising**. The **larvae** live in the soil and eat the **roots of lawns and meadows**. Then the grass turns brown and can be lifted off like a carpet.

At the beginning of the 20th century, the beetle was brought into the **USA**. There it caused great damage. Later it reached Europe. In Switzerland it was first discovered in **2017** in **Ticino**. It counts as a **quarantine organism**. This means that its spread must be prevented by all means.

In infested zones, special rules apply. At times it is forbidden to **water lawns**. The eggs and larvae need **damp soil**, and in dry soil they survive less well. Anyone who finds a Japanese beetle **outside known infested areas** should catch it, photograph it and report it to the **cantonal plant protection service**.

gewusst: A Japanese beetle can travel long distances as a stowaway by car, by train or in deliveries of plants.
The larvae are white, curved grubs that spend the winter in the soil.

teile.einleitung: Ingo Potrykus is a plant biologist from Germany who did research in Switzerland for a long time. He became known for Golden Rice, a genetically modified variety of rice against vitamin A deficiency.
wichtigste: Ingo Potrykus comes from Germany and did research in Switzerland for a long time.
From 1976 he built up a research group at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel.
At ETH Zurich he developed Golden Rice with Peter Beyer.
In 2000 the work was published in the journal “Science”.
Poor farmers were to be allowed to use the rice free of charge under humanitarian licences.
Golden Rice is still controversial today.

abschnitte.titel: From the Basel laboratory to ETH
abschnitte.text: Ingo Potrykus was born in **Germany**. From **1976** he built up a research group for **plant genetic engineering** at the **Friedrich Miescher Institute** in Basel. Later he became professor of plant sciences at **ETH Zurich**. There he worked on how crop plants can be given new characteristics.

In many poor countries, people eat almost nothing but rice. They often lack **vitamin A**, which can lead to eyesight problems and illness. Together with **Peter Beyer** from Freiburg im Breisgau, Potrykus developed a rice that makes **beta-carotene** in the grain. The body turns this into vitamin A. The beta-carotene colours the grains yellowish, hence the name **Golden Rice**. In **2000** they presented their work in the journal “Science”.

Potrykus wanted the rice to help people in need. Poor farmers were to be allowed to grow it **free of charge** under **humanitarian licences**. To promote its spread, he chaired the **Golden Rice Humanitarian Board**. This body works with research institutes in Asia.

There is a long debate about Golden Rice. **Critics** doubt its usefulness and reject genetically modified plants. They propose fighting vitamin A deficiency with a varied diet or vitamin tablets. Potrykus argued, on the other hand, that very **strict regulation** delays help for people with vitamin A deficiency. In Switzerland, the growing of genetically modified plants has been severely restricted by a moratorium since a popular vote in 2005.

gewusst: The colour of Golden Rice comes from the same substance that also makes carrots orange.
Around two decades passed from the first publication to approval in a country.

teile.einleitung: A hydrophyte is an aquatic plant that lives wholly or partly in water. Such plants have special body plans so that they can float, breathe and take up nutrients.
wichtigste: Hydrophytes grow submerged, floating or with floating leaves.
Air-filled cavities, the aerenchyma, provide buoyancy and gas exchange.
In floating leaves, the stomata are on the upper side.
Submerged leaves often have only a thin cuticle.
Many water plants overwinter as winter buds on the bottom.
Canadian waterweed from North America has spread widely in Swiss waters.

abschnitte.text: Many water plants have large, **air-filled cavities** in their stems and leaves. This tissue is called **aerenchyma**. It gives **buoyancy**, so that leaves and stems float. It also carries **oxygen** down to the roots in the muddy ground. There, there is hardly any oxygen otherwise.

With **floating leaves**, such as those of the **water lily**, the underside lies on the water. That is why the **stomata** for gas exchange sit on the **upper side**. Submerged leaves often have only a very thin **cuticle**, that is, a layer of wax. Under water there is no danger of drying out. The plant takes up gases, water and nutrients directly through its whole surface.

The **water crowfoot** forms finely divided leaves under water, which offer little resistance to the current. Above water it has broad, lobed floating leaves. Different leaf shapes on one plant are called **heterophylly**. Many water plants such as the **bladderwort** form compact **winter buds** in autumn, called **turions**. They sink to the bottom and sprout again in spring.

On the shore of a lake, plants follow one another in zones. From deep water towards the land, there is first the **submerged leaf zone**, then the **floating leaf zone** and after that the **reedbed** with reeds. Further towards the land come **sedges** and fen woodland. This sequence also shows how a lake slowly **silts up**. In Switzerland, **Canadian waterweed** from North America has spread widely. As an invasive neophyte, it can form dense stands and push out native species.

gewusst: The giant water lily Victoria amazonica from the Amazon basin has leaves more than two metres across, which can bear great weight thanks to ribs on the underside.
Hydrophyte literally means “water plant”, from the Greek hydor for water and phyton for plant.

teile.einleitung: Burr fruits have tiny hooks and stick everywhere: in the fur of animals, on socks and on trousers. In this way they travel far away from their parent plant. A Swiss inventor took inspiration from them for the hook-and-loop fastener.
wichtigste: Burr fruits hook themselves into the fur of animals with little hooks.
In this way their seeds are carried far.
The burdock has round fruit heads with many hooks.
In a new place the fruit drops off and can germinate.
The hook-and-loop fastener was invented on the model of the burdock.
The inventor was the Swiss engineer George de Mestral.
Cleavers is also called “Klebkraut” in German, meaning sticky herb.

abschnitte.text: Burr fruits have many small **hooks**. With them they stay caught in the **fur** of animals and are carried far. Sooner or later they drop off or are brushed off. In the new place a new plant can then **germinate**. This is how plants spread without being able to walk themselves.

**Dogs** run through meadows and bushes. Afterwards they often have burrs in their fur. Burr fruits also easily stick to **socks and trousers**, because the hooks catch in the fabric. The best-known plant is the **burdock**, with round, prickly **fruit heads**. **Cleavers** is covered all over with fine hooks. Because it sticks to clothes, it is also called **Klebkraut**, sticky herb, in German.

The Swiss engineer **George de Mestral** had an idea after a walk with his dog. He looked closely at the burrs in its fur under the microscope. In doing so he discovered the tiny hooks. He copied them in plastic. This is how the **hook-and-loop fastener** came about. This copying from nature is called **biomimetics**.

A hook-and-loop fastener has two sides. On one sit many small **hooks**, on the other many soft **loops**. If you press them together, they hook into each other. If you pull hard, they come apart with a ripping sound. You find hook-and-loop fasteners on shoes, bags and jackets.

gewusst: George de Mestral came from the canton of Vaud.
The brand name Velcro is made up of the French words velours, meaning velvet, and crochet, meaning hook.

teile.einleitung: IP-Suisse is an association of farmers in Switzerland. Its label with the ladybird stands for food that is produced in an especially environmentally friendly and animal-friendly way.
wichtigste: IP-Suisse is an association of Swiss farmers.
“IP” stands for “integrated production”.
The label shows a ladybird.
The farms must give special support to biodiversity.
For cereals, they do without insecticides and fungicides.
For animals, especially animal-friendly keeping with outdoor access applies.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who sees a **ladybird** on bread, flour, meat or potatoes in a shop has a product from IP-Suisse in front of them. The ladybird fits well: it eats aphids and is a well-known **beneficial insect**. It shows that nature helps to keep the plants healthy. Many of these products can be bought in large Swiss shops.

**Integrated production** means: as little chemistry as necessary. First, preventive measures, robust varieties and beneficial insects are relied on. Unlike in **organic farming**, synthetic sprays may be used in a targeted way, but only if it is really necessary. For cereals such as wheat, IP-Suisse farmers do without **insecticides** against insects and **fungicides** against fungi.

IP-Suisse farms must give special support to **biodiversity**, that is, the variety of plants and animals. To do this they collect points with measures such as hedges, flower meadows, piles of stones or nesting places. That way insects, birds and small mammals find food and shelter in the middle of farmland.

For animals, too, strict rules apply. They are to be kept in an **especially animal-friendly** way, with enough space in the barn and regular **outdoor access**. Cows, pigs and hens can then move around more and show their natural behaviour.

gewusst: The ladybird on the label is a beneficial insect that eats aphids.
Integrated production lies between conventional farming and organic farming.

teile.einleitung: When people think of a desert, many think of hot sand. But there are also **cold deserts**. There it is so cold and dry that almost no plants can grow. The biggest of them is Antarctica.
wichtigste: In a cold desert, the cold prevents almost any plant growth.
If cold deserts are counted, Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.
The McMurdo Dry Valleys are ice-free valleys in Antarctica.
Cold air can hardly take up water vapour, so little precipitation falls.
On the Antarctic continent there are only two native flowering plants.
Frost shattering shapes the landscape.

abschnitte.text: A **desert** is an area where hardly any plants grow. In hot deserts, water is lacking. In **cold deserts**, the **cold** is the main reason. In addition, little precipitation falls here too. Cold deserts exist in **Antarctica**, in parts of the **Arctic** and in very high mountains. If they are counted, Antarctica is the **largest desert on Earth**, even ahead of the Sahara.

**Cold air can hardly take up water vapour**. That is why only a few clouds form over polar regions, and little snow falls. In some parts of Antarctica, less precipitation falls in a year than in the Sahara. The great amount of snow and ice there has built up over a very long time, because it hardly ever melts.

In Antarctica there are also areas without ice. The best known are the **McMurdo Dry Valleys**. Strong, dry katabatic winds stop snow from staying there. It is one of the driest places on Earth. Researchers study the valleys because the conditions there are similar to those on Mars.

Despite the cold, there is life. Some **lichens and algae** live **inside rocks**. They are called **endolithic**. In the stone they are protected from wind and drying out, and a little light gets through. On the Antarctic continent there are only **two native flowering plants**: Antarctic hair grass, a grass, and Antarctic pearlwort. They grow mainly on the Antarctic Peninsula. Mosses and lichens are more common.

In cold deserts, **frost shattering** shapes the landscape. Water gets into cracks in the rock and freezes. Ice needs more room than water, so it breaks the rock apart. Through constant freezing and thawing, stones in the ground are sorted. This creates **patterned ground** with stone circles and polygons. Such ground is also found in the high mountains of the Swiss Alps.

gewusst: The lowest air temperature ever measured on Earth was minus 89.2 °C at Vostok Station in Antarctica.
In the McMurdo Dry Valleys there are areas where no rain has fallen for a very long time.

teile.einleitung: A hypha is a fine fungal thread. What we see in the woods as a mushroom is only a small part. Most of the fungus lives invisibly in the soil or in wood as a network of hyphae.
wichtigste: Fungi consist of microscopically thin threads, the hyphae.
Hyphae grow at their tip.
The mesh of many hyphae is called a mycelium.
In mycorrhiza, fungi and trees exchange substances.
Hyphae digest their food outside the fungus.
A dark honey fungus in Oregon is regarded as one of the largest living things on Earth.

abschnitte.text: Fungi consist of microscopically thin threads, the **hyphae**. Many hyphae together form a mesh, the **mycelium**. It runs through the soil, leaf litter or wood. The mushroom that we pick is only the **fruiting body**. Hyphae grow longer at their **tip**. In this way they can work their way purposefully through soil or wood.

Fungi cannot carry out photosynthesis. They have to take in their food. To do this, the hyphae give off **enzymes**, that is, digestive substances. These break down the food **outside** the fungus. The hyphae then absorb the dissolved building blocks through their surface. In this way many fungi break down dead wood and leaves and help to form humus.

Many fungi live with trees in a **partnership**, the **mycorrhiza**. The hyphae wrap around the fine tree roots. The tree gives the fungus **sugar** that it has made by photosynthesis. The fungus supplies the tree with **water and mineral salts**. Its fine network reaches much further into the soil than the roots do. Because hyphae can connect several trees, people jokingly speak of the **“Wood Wide Web”**.

Some fungi attack living trees and harm them. Such fungi are called **parasites**. They draw nutrients from their host and weaken it. One example is the **honey fungus**, which can kill whole trees. In **Oregon** in the USA, the mycelium of a single **dark honey fungus** stretches over several square kilometres. It is probably several thousand years old.

gewusst: In one gram of forest soil there can be fungal hyphae with a total length of many metres.
Even mould on old bread is made of hyphae.

teile.einleitung: Late blight is one of the most dangerous diseases of the potato. In wet summers it can destroy whole fields in a few days. Tomatoes are also attacked.
wichtigste: The pathogen is called **Phytophthora infestans**.
It looks like a fungus, but belongs to the oomycetes, also called water moulds.
It attacks mainly potatoes and tomatoes.
Damp, mild weather over several days strongly promotes the disease.
Typical are brown spots with a white coating on the underside of the leaf.
Healthy seed potatoes and copper preparations in organic farming help against the disease.

abschnitte.text: The pathogen of the disease is called **Phytophthora infestans**. The name comes from Greek and means roughly “plant destroyer”. For a long time it was thought to be a fungus. Today we know that it belongs to the **oomycetes**, which are also called “egg fungi” in German. They are more closely related to brown algae than to true fungi. Their cell walls consist of cellulose and not of chitin as in fungi.

The pathogen attacks mainly **potatoes** and **tomatoes**. Both belong to the nightshade family. In the tomato it is also called **brown rot**. On the leaves, brown spots appear that spread quickly. On the underside of the leaf, in damp conditions, a fine, whitish coating forms at the edge of the spots. Later the tubers in the soil also turn brown and rot.

The pathogen needs **wet leaves** and high humidity. If it is damp and mild for several days, its spore containers germinate on the leaves. Then the disease can spread explosively. The rain washes the spores from the leaves into the soil, where they infect the tubers. That is why the soil is heaped up well around the plants, so that the tubers are better protected.

Often the pathogen survives in **infected seed potatoes** or on heaps of discarded tubers. In spring these sprout and form new spores. Healthy planting stock is therefore very important. In organic growing, limited amounts of **copper** may be sprayed, which works as a preventive. Because copper builds up in the soil, the permitted amount is restricted. In addition, varieties are bred that are less susceptible. In Switzerland, forecasting services warn farmers when the weather is favourable for the disease.

In the 19th century the disease spread in Europe. In **Ireland**, many people at that time lived almost only on potatoes. When the harvests rotted for several years from 1845, the **Great Famine** came. About a million people died, and even more emigrated, mainly to America.

gewusst: A whole potato field can die off within a few days in wet weather.
The Great Famine in Ireland from 1845 was triggered by this disease.

teile.einleitung: Info Flora is the national data and information centre for the wild plants of Switzerland. It collects observations and shows where which plants occur.
wichtigste: Info Flora collects data on wild plants in Switzerland.
Experts and amateurs can report plant finds.
With the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), Info Flora produces the Red List of vascular plants.
Invasive neophytes are watched especially closely.
For animals there is info fauna, and for birds the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach.
All these centres together form the InfoSpecies network.

abschnitte.text: Info Flora collects **data on wild plants** across the whole of Switzerland. Anyone who finds a plant can report the find with place and date. **Experts and amateurs** may do this, for example through an app. From many reports, **distribution maps** are produced. They show where a species occurs and whether it is becoming more common or rarer.

Together with the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)**, Info Flora produces the **Red List of vascular plants**. Vascular plants are plants with conducting tissues, so for example flowers, grasses, trees and ferns. The list shows which species are threatened. That way nature conservation and the authorities know where help is especially needed.

**Neophytes** are plants that have come to us from other continents since the discovery of America. Some spread strongly and **push out native species**. They are called **invasive**. Examples are Japanese knotweed or goldenrod. Info Flora watches these plants especially closely and gives information on how to control them.

Info Flora is not alone. For wild animals there is **info fauna**, and for birds the **Swiss Ornithological Institute** in Sempach. Further centres look after fungi, mosses or lichens. Together they form the **InfoSpecies** network. This produces an overall picture of biodiversity in Switzerland.

gewusst: Every year thousands of new plant reports come in, many of them from volunteers.
Distribution maps also show how plants are shifting because of global warming.

teile.einleitung: Cork is light, floats on water and can be squeezed together. We know it from bottle stoppers and pinboards. It is obtained from the bark of a special tree, which does not have to be felled for it.
wichtigste: Cork is obtained from the bark of the cork oak.
The cork oak does not have to be felled for this, only the bark is stripped.
The bark can be stripped about every nine years.
Portugal has the most cork oaks.
Cork floats on water and feels light and slightly soft.
Cork is used for bottle stoppers and pinboards.

abschnitte.text: Cork comes from the **cork oak**. It grows in the warm countries around the western **Mediterranean**. Most cork oaks are in **Portugal**, many also in Spain. The cork oak has an especially thick bark. It protects the tree from heat and even from forest fires.

To obtain cork, you **do not have to fell** the tree. Workers carefully strip off the outer **bark** with a hatchet. Afterwards it grows back. The first time, the bark is stripped only when the tree is about 25 years old. After that this can be repeated **about every nine years**. A cork oak can be harvested many times in this way.

Cork consists of tiny, dead **cells** filled with **air**. That is why it is very **light** and **floats** on water. It feels slightly soft and can be squeezed together, but then springs back. Cork lets hardly any water through and insulates well against cold and noise.

Best known are **bottle stoppers** made of cork. Because it can be squeezed together and then expands again, it seals bottles tightly. In classrooms there are often **pinboards** made of cork, in which drawing pins hold well. Cork is also used for floors, coasters, shoe soles and insulation boards.

gewusst: In 1665, the researcher Robert Hooke saw small chambers in cork under the microscope and called them “cells”.
Cork oaks can live to be several hundred years old.

teile.einleitung: A climate diagram is a graph that shows at a glance how warm and how wet it is in a place over the whole year. It reveals whether a place has hot summers, cold winters, rainy seasons or long dry seasons. Anyone who can read climate diagrams understands the climate in Zurich just as well as that in the Sahara.
wichtigste: A climate diagram shows the temperature and precipitation of a place over the whole year.
The temperature is usually drawn as a red line.
The precipitation usually appears as blue columns for each month.
On the horizontal axis are the twelve months from January to December.
The values are averages from many years, usually from 30 years.
From the diagram you can recognise wet and dry seasons.
Climate diagrams help to compare the Earth’s climate zones with one another.

abschnitte.text: A climate diagram is a drawing with two measured quantities in one picture. On the left is a scale for the **temperature** in degrees Celsius, on the right a scale for the **precipitation** in millimetres. One millimetre of precipitation means that one litre of water has fallen on one square metre of ground. At the top of the diagram there are often the name of the place, its height above sea level, as well as the mean annual temperature and the annual total of precipitation.

First you look at which months the red temperature line is highest and lowest. Then you compare the blue columns: tall columns mean a lot of rain or snow. If the temperature curve lies above the precipitation columns, this is called an **arid** period, that is, a dry period. If the precipitation lies above it, the period is **humid**, that is, wet.

A particularly well-known form is the climate diagram after **Walter and Lieth**. The two researchers Heinrich Walter and Helmut Lieth published a large atlas with such diagrams from all over the world in the 1960s. In their way of drawing, 10 degrees Celsius on the temperature axis correspond to 20 millimetres on the precipitation axis. In this way dry months can be read off directly.

The values come from **weather stations**, which measure temperature and precipitation every day. For a climate diagram, averages are calculated over a long time, usually over 30 years, for example from 1991 to 2020. In this way the diagram shows the climate and not the weather of a single year. In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, **MeteoSwiss**, runs a dense measuring network.

A climate diagram of Zurich shows mild summers, cool winters and enough precipitation all year round. In the Valais, the columns are clearly lower, because the Rhone valley is among the **driest regions** of Switzerland. On high mountains such as the Säntis, the temperature line lies below zero degrees for many months. A diagram from Lugano shows warmer temperatures than north of the Alps, but nevertheless heavy rainfall.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water that falls from the air to the ground, for example as rain, snow or hail.
Dry: more water evaporates than falls from the sky.
Wet: more water falls than evaporates.
The average temperature of a place over the whole year.

gewusst: For places in the Southern Hemisphere, the climate diagram often begins in July, so that the summer lies in the middle as it does for us.
In some desert places the precipitation columns are so small that you can hardly see them in the diagram.
A single climate diagram sums up millions of individual measurements from many years.

teile.einleitung: Coltsfoot is a small plant with yellow flowers that blooms as early as the very start of spring. It is one of the first signs of spring and likes to grow on bare ground.
wichtigste: Coltsfoot has bright yellow flowers.
It blooms as early as February or March.
The flowers appear before the leaves.
The leaves have the shape of a horse’s hoof.
It is often mistaken for the dandelion.
Its seeds fly on the wind with tiny little parachutes.

abschnitte.text: **Coltsfoot** blooms as early as the **very start of spring**, often from February or March. Its flowers are **bright yellow**. They are among the first yellow flowers of the year. For **bees** and other insects they are an important early food. In dull weather and in the evening, the flowers close.

With coltsfoot, the **flowers** appear first. The large **leaves** only grow later, when the flowering is over. They are round and remind people of the **hoof of a horse**. That is where the name comes from. The underside of the leaves is white and covered in felty hairs.

The flower looks similar to that of the **dandelion**. But coltsfoot blooms earlier and is smaller. A good feature is the **stem**. It is covered with small, reddish **scale leaves**. The dandelion has a smooth, hollow stem and already has leaves when it flowers.

Coltsfoot likes **open, bare ground**. You find it at the **edges of paths**, on **railway embankments**, in gravel pits and on building sites. It is a **pioneer plant** that quickly settles on new ground. Its **seeds** have fine hairs like little **parachutes**. This lets the wind carry them far away.

gewusst: Coltsfoot used to be used as a cough remedy. Because it can contain harmful substances, people nowadays advise against collecting and eating it yourself.
Its scientific name Tussilago means roughly “to drive away a cough”.

teile.einleitung: Can two species that have exactly the same needs live permanently in the same place? The competitive exclusion principle says no. It is one of the most important rules of ecology, but it also has interesting exceptions.
wichtigste: The principle says that complete competitors cannot exist side by side permanently.
Georgy Gause demonstrated it in 1934 with laboratory experiments on paramecia.
Garrett Hardin summed it up in 1960: “Complete competitors cannot coexist”.
It deals with interspecific competition, that is, between different species.
A precondition is a limited resource that is shared.
The paradox of the plankton seems to contradict the principle.

abschnitte.text: The Russian biologist **Georgy Gause** published experiments with paramecia in **1934**. When he kept two species apart, both grew well. In a shared culture with the same food, **Paramecium aurelia** prevailed, and the other species disappeared. After him the rule is also called the **Gause principle**. The ecologist **Garrett Hardin** summed it up briefly in 1960: “Complete competitors cannot coexist”.

The principle concerns **interspecific competition**, that is, the contest between different species. A precondition is always a **limited resource that is shared**. If one species simply uses the resource faster, this is called exploitation competition. If one species directly hinders the other, for example by defending a **territory**, this is called **interference competition**.

Mathematically, competition can be described with the **Lotka-Volterra competition model**. It shows under what conditions two species can coexist. This works if **each species inhibits itself more strongly than it inhibits the other**. Then each species brakes itself by its own density before it displaces the other. In nature this often happens when the species use slightly different niches.

In the open sea, very many species of **plankton** live side by side, although they need almost the same nutrients and the light. According to the principle, most of them should be displaced. The ecologist George Evelyn Hutchinson called this the **paradox of the plankton** in 1961. One possible explanation: conditions in the water change constantly, so that no species has the advantage for long enough to displace all the others.

gewusst: Gause worked in Moscow and was only about 24 years old when his famous book on the “struggle for existence” appeared.
The principle helps us understand why introduced species can displace native ones.

teile.einleitung: In nature, food, light, water and space are often scarce. When several living things need the same thing, a contest arises. Biologists call it competition.
wichtigste: Competition is the contest for scarce resources.
Competition within a species is often especially strong, because all have the same needs.
Trees in a dense forest compete mainly for light.
Georgy Gause showed displacement through competition with paramecia.
The competitive exclusion principle says: two species with the same niche cannot live together permanently.
Through niche differentiation, species avoid competition.

abschnitte.text: **Competition** means that living things contend for the same scarce **resources**. These can be food, water, light, nesting sites or hiding places. Whoever prevails better has more of it and is more likely to survive. Competition need not be a fight. Often one species simply eats up the food faster than the other.

Competition is often especially strong among animals of the same species, because they have exactly the **same needs**. This is called **intraspecific competition**. Many **songbirds** therefore defend a **territory** in spring. In this way they secure enough food for themselves and their young. With their song they show their neighbours where the boundary is.

Different species can also compete. In a dense forest, trees contend mainly for **light**: whoever grows higher shades the others. A well-known example among animals is the **grey squirrel**. It was brought from North America to Britain and there displaces the native **red squirrel**.

The Russian biologist **Georgy Gause** kept two species of **paramecia** together in one vessel. Both ate the same food. After some time only one species was left. From this came the **competitive exclusion principle**: two species with exactly the same niche cannot live together permanently.

In nature, many similar species nevertheless live side by side. They avoid competition through **niche differentiation**. That means each species uses the environment a little differently. Different species of tit, for example, search for food in different parts of a tree. Other species are active at different times of day or eat prey of different sizes.

gewusst: Plants also compete underground: their roots contend for water and nutrients.
Some plants release substances into the soil that inhibit the growth of other plants.

teile.einleitung: At the **tree line** in the Alps, life becomes hard for trees. Instead of tall trunks, low, bent woody plants grow there. They are called **krummholz**, which means “crooked wood”.
wichtigste: Krummholz means low, crookedly growing woody plants at the tree line.
Heavy snow presses the trunks downwards.
In the Swiss Alps, mountain pine and green alder form most of the krummholz.
The flexible branches of the green alder spring back under avalanches.
The transition from forest to tree line is called the struggle zone.
Krummholz protects steep slopes from sliding.

abschnitte.text: The higher you climb in the mountains, the colder it gets and the shorter the summer is. At some point upright trees can no longer grow. There lies the **tree line**. The transition area between closed forest and the tree line is called the **struggle zone**. The trees stand here singly and are often small and stunted. Above it, **krummholz** still grows.

In winter, there is often **snow** metres deep in the mountains. It is heavy and presses the young trunks and branches to the ground. If the snow cover slowly slides down the slope, the trunks are bent further. So they first grow along the ground and then bend upwards. Under the snow, the plants are protected in winter from icy wind.

In the Swiss Alps, two woody plants above all form the krummholz. The **mountain pine**, in German “Legföhre”, is a form of the mountain pine group. It grows like a lying pine and forms dense thickets, especially on limestone soils. The **green alder** grows on damp, shady slopes. Its branches are very **flexible**. When an avalanche sweeps over it, they lie flat and spring back afterwards. That is why it often survives in avalanche tracks.

The wind also shapes the trees. In winter it carries **ice crystals** with it. These grind down the shoots on the windward side like sandpaper. That is why many trees at the tree line grow almost without branches on the windward side. This is called **flag growth**, because the tree looks like a flag in the wind. The **Swiss stone pine** withstands these conditions well. It has five needles per bundle and often grows right up to the tree line.

Krummholz is very useful. The dense roots hold the soil firm and **protect the ground** on steep slopes from sliding. The thickets can also help so that fewer avalanches start. In addition they offer animals such as the black grouse shelter and food.

gewusst: A Swiss stone pine can live to be several hundred years old.
The green alder can use nitrogen from the air with the help of bacteria on its roots.

teile.einleitung: Lavender is a fragrant plant with purple flowers. It comes from the Mediterranean region and today grows in many gardens, including in Switzerland. Its scent is used in soaps, oils and scented sachets.
wichtigste: Lavender mostly blooms violet to blue.
It comes from the Mediterranean region.
In Provence in southern France there are famous lavender fields.
Lavender needs a sunny, dry spot.
Its leaves are narrow and grey-green.
Lavender oil is obtained from the flowers.
Bees and bumblebees like to fetch nectar from the flowers.

abschnitte.text: Lavender is a small **subshrub**: at the bottom it becomes woody, at the top the shoots stay soft. Its leaves are **narrow and grey-green**. Fine hairs give them a grey shimmer and protect them from heat and drying out. In summer long stalks grow with many small flowers in spikes. The flowers are mostly **violet** to blue, which is why people also speak of the colour lavender.

Lavender comes from the **Mediterranean region**, where the summers are hot and dry. That is why it likes a **sunny place** and a rather dry, well-drained soil. It tolerates wet feet, that is waterlogging, badly. In Switzerland lavender grows well in gardens, on balconies and on warm walls. Lavender belongs to the **mint family**, like sage, thyme and mint.

Especially famous are the lavender fields of **Provence** in southern France. In summer huge areas there bloom violet in rows. Many people travel there specially to see the fields and smell the scent. The lavender is harvested and made into **lavender oil**. The oil is obtained from the fragrant flowers.

The name lavender perhaps comes from the Latin word **“lavare”**, which means to wash. Even in the past people put lavender in the bath water. Today its scent is found in **soaps**, bath additives and scented oils. Dried flowers are put into small sachets. In the wardrobe they keep **moths** away, because these do not like the scent.

The flowers of lavender contain a lot of sweet **nectar**. That is why in summer many **bees and bumblebees** hum around the plant. Butterflies also like to visit it. Anyone who plants lavender therefore helps the insects in the garden. If you cut it back after flowering, it stays nicely bushy.

gewusst: Lavender belongs to the same plant family as sage, thyme and mint.
The fine hairs on the leaves are a protection against the strong sun in the south.

teile.einleitung: Japanese knotweed is a very vigorous plant from East Asia. In Switzerland it counts as an invasive neophyte, because it pushes out native plants and causes damage.
wichtigste: Japanese knotweed comes from East Asia.
In the 19th century it came to Europe as an ornamental and fodder plant.
In one summer it can grow up to about 3 metres tall.
Even small pieces of the rootstock can form new plants.
In Europe almost only female plants grow, so there are hardly any seeds able to sprout.
Plant parts belong in the general waste, not on the compost.

abschnitte.text: Japanese knotweed comes from **East Asia**, for example from Japan and China. In the **19th century** it was brought to Europe as an **ornamental and fodder plant**. At that time nobody guessed how strongly it would spread. Today, in Switzerland it is on the list of **invasive neophytes**, that is, introduced plants that cause problems.

In spring, reddish shoots push out of the ground. Within one summer they grow **up to about 3 metres** tall. The stems are **hollow** and resemble bamboo. The plant forms dense stands in which hardly anything else grows. In autumn the parts above ground die off, but the strong **rootstock** in the soil survives.

In Europe almost only **female plants** occur. That is why they hardly form seeds able to sprout here. Even so, the knotweed multiplies very well: even **small pieces of the rootstock** or of the stems can grow into a new plant. They are spread with soil, water or garden waste.

On **stream banks**, the knotweed pushes out native plants with firm roots. In winter the ground beneath it is **bare**, and the water can wear away the bank more easily. This promotes **erosion**. In built-up areas it grows through **cracks in asphalt and walls** and can damage them.

Because even small pieces sprout, plant parts must **not be composted**. They belong **in the general waste**, where they are burned. Control usually takes many years. The plants have to be pulled out or mown again and again until the rootstock is weakened.

gewusst: The rootstock can reach down about two metres into the soil and spread several metres sideways.
In Switzerland it is forbidden to plant or sell Japanese knotweed.

teile.einleitung: How strongly is an animal or plant species threatened with extinction? For this, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, IUCN, has laid down categories that are used worldwide. They are the basis of the Red Lists.
wichtigste: The IUCN was founded in 1948.
Since 1964 it has published the Red List of Threatened Species.
CR, EN and VU together count as “threatened” in the wider sense.
LC means not threatened, and DD means the data are not sufficient.
NE means that a species has not yet been assessed.
Regional Red Lists such as Switzerland’s also have RE.

abschnitte.titel: The International Union for Conservation of Nature
abschnitte.text: The **IUCN** was founded in **1948**. Its seat is in **Gland** in the canton of Vaud, that is, in Switzerland. States, authorities and nature conservation organisations from all over the world belong to it. Since **1964** it has published the **Red List of Threatened Species**. It states how strongly thousands of species are threatened.

Every species gets an abbreviation. **EX** means extinct, **EW** extinct in the wild. Then follow **CR** (critically endangered), **EN** (endangered) and **VU** (vulnerable). These three together count as “threatened” in the wider sense. **NT** means near threatened, **LC** least concern. **DD** means that the data are not sufficient for a classification, and **NE** that a species has not yet been assessed.

Whether a species counts as CR, EN or VU is decided by five **criteria**. Criterion **A** looks at how fast the population is shrinking. If the causes have not been removed, a species counts as CR if it declines by at least **80 per cent** in 10 years or 3 generations. Other criteria look at a small range or very few animals. Criterion **E** is based on a calculation of how likely the species is to die out.

Switzerland also has its own Red Lists, for example for birds, plants or dragonflies. They apply only to the country itself and use the same categories. In addition there is **RE**: a species is extinct in the region but still lives elsewhere. The lists help the authorities to decide where protection is especially urgent.

gewusst: The headquarters of the IUCN is in Switzerland, in Gland on Lake Geneva.
Even a species with many animals can count as threatened if its population is shrinking very quickly.

teile.einleitung: A climate feedback is an effect that strengthens or weakens an original climate change. It works like a chain reaction: if it gets warmer, something changes on Earth, and this change in turn influences the temperature. Feedbacks are one reason why climate change sometimes proceeds faster than you would first expect.
wichtigste: A climate feedback strengthens or weakens a climate change.
Strengthening effects are called positive feedbacks.
Weakening effects are called negative feedbacks.
The ice-albedo feedback is a well-known example: when ice melts, it gets even warmer.
Water vapour in the air also strengthens the warming.
Thawing permafrost can release additional greenhouse gases.
Feedbacks are important for predicting the future of the climate.

abschnitte.text: In a feedback, a result acts back on its own cause. If the temperature rises, for example, ice surfaces, clouds or plants can change. These changes then influence the temperature again. If the first change thereby becomes larger, this is called a **positive feedback**, and if it becomes smaller, a **negative feedback**.

Light surfaces such as snow and ice throw a lot of sunlight back into space. This reflecting power is called **albedo**. Fresh snow throws back a large part of the light, whereas the dark sea swallows almost all of it. If the sea ice in the Arctic melts, more dark water surface becomes visible, which warms up more strongly and lets even more ice melt.

Warm air can take up more **water vapour** than cold air. Water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas and holds additional heat back in the atmosphere. That is why it strengthens the warming that was triggered, for example, by carbon dioxide. With **clouds** the effect is more complicated, because some clouds cool the Earth and others warm it.

In **permafrost**, that is, permanently frozen ground, huge amounts of plant remains are locked in. When the ground thaws, micro-organisms break this material down and release carbon dioxide and **methane**. These gases strengthen the greenhouse effect further. Forest fires and drying-out forests can also release carbon that was previously stored in the wood.

There are also feedbacks that weaken a warming. The most important is that a warmer body radiates more heat into space, just as a hot stove gives off more heat than a lukewarm one. With more carbon dioxide, plants can in part grow faster and so take up more CO2. These braking effects, however, are not enough to stop today’s **climate change**.

Researchers build feedbacks into **climate models**, that is, into computer programs that calculate the climate of the future. Special attention is paid to so-called **tipping points**, at which a change suddenly can no longer be reversed. Examples are the melting of large ice sheets such as in Greenland. In Switzerland, too, feedbacks play a role, for example when winters with little snow warm the ground earlier.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a surface throws back sunlight. Snow has a high albedo, asphalt a low one.
Ground that has been frozen without a break for at least two years.
A threshold beyond which part of the climate system changes strongly and in a way that can hardly be reversed.
A gas that holds heat in the atmosphere, for example carbon dioxide or methane.

gewusst: The Arctic is warming clearly faster than the average of the Earth, mainly because of the ice-albedo feedback.
A white T-shirt stays cooler in the sun than a black one, because it throws back more light, just like snow.
In the Earth’s permafrost, more carbon is stored than is found today in the whole atmosphere.

teile.einleitung: In autumn the leaves fall from the trees. On the ground they form a layer of old leaves, the **leaf litter**. It looks inconspicuous, but is full of life and very important for the forest.
wichtigste: Leaf litter is a layer of old leaves on the ground.
In autumn leaves turn yellow and red because the green leaf pigment is broken down.
Woodlice, worms and many other animals eat the damp leaves.
With time the leaf litter turns into dark soil, the humus.
The leaf litter keeps the ground warm and damp in winter.
Leaves in the forest give the soil nutrients back.

abschnitte.text: In summer the leaves are green. This is due to the **leaf green**, chlorophyll. In autumn the tree takes valuable substances back from the leaves. In the process the green **chlorophyll is broken down**. Now you can see the yellow pigments that were already in the leaf before. Some trees also make red pigments. After that the leaves fall off and form the **leaf litter** on the ground.

Countless animals live in the leaf litter. The small grey **woodlice** with their armour like to eat damp leaves. **Earthworms**, millipedes and tiny springtails also nibble the leaves. **Snails** like to hide in the damp litter. In addition **fungi** and **bacteria** are at work. Together they break up and decompose the leaves.

With time the leaf litter turns into **dark soil**, the **humus**. This usually takes several years. In the humus there are many **nutrients** that the trees take up again. In this way the cycle closes. That is why the **leaves should stay lying in the forest**. They give the soil back what the tree took from it.

The leaf litter acts like a **blanket**. In winter **it keeps the ground warm and damp**. Beneath it the soil freezes less deeply. Many animals spend the winter in the litter or in heaps of leaves, for example beetles, toads and the **hedgehog**. That is why it is good to leave a heap of leaves lying in the garden as well.

abschnitte.titel: Looking for food in the leaves
abschnitte.text: The leaf litter is also a laid table for birds. The **blackbird** often **tosses leaves about** while looking for food. With its beak it turns the leaves over and searches underneath for worms, snails and insects. If you hear a loud rustling under a bush in autumn, it is often a blackbird.

gewusst: In a handful of forest soil there are more living things than there are people on Earth.
A large deciduous tree loses tens of thousands of leaves in autumn.

teile.einleitung: Climate zones are regions of the Earth with a similar, typical climate. They stretch like broad belts around the Earth, from the hot equator to the icy poles. In each climate zone, typical plants grow and typical animals live.
wichtigste: Climate zones are large regions of the Earth with a similar climate.
Usually people distinguish tropics, subtropics, temperate zone, subpolar zone and polar zone.
The most important reason for the climate zones is the angle at which the sun’s rays strike the Earth.
At the equator it is warm all year, at the poles cold all year.
Switzerland lies in the temperate zone.
Mountains, seas and winds also influence the climate of a place.
A well-known division of the climate zones comes from Wladimir Köppen.

abschnitte.text: Climate zones group together regions in which temperature, precipitation and seasons are similar. They run roughly parallel to the **equator** and repeat on the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Between the zones there are no sharp borders, but gradual transitions. With **climate diagrams** you can compare the zones well with one another.

The Earth is a sphere, so the sun’s rays do not strike at the same steepness everywhere. At the equator the sun shines almost vertically and warms the ground strongly. The closer you get to the poles, the shallower the rays fall and the more they spread over a larger area. Because the **Earth’s axis** is tilted, the seasons also arise.

The **tropics** lie around the equator between the two tropics lines, and there it is always warm and often very damp. In the **subtropics** lie many large deserts such as the Sahara, but also the countries around the Mediterranean. The temperate zone has clear seasons with warm summers and cool winters. The subpolar and the polar zones are cold, with tundra, ice and very long winters.

Each climate zone has its own typical landscapes, which are called **vegetation zones**. In the damp tropics, rainforests grow with countless animal and plant species. In the temperate zone, deciduous and mixed forests are widespread, and further north huge coniferous forests called the **taiga**. In the tundra only mosses, lichens and low shrubs still grow.

The climate researcher **Wladimir Köppen** developed a precise division of the Earth’s climates around 1900. Later it was developed further by Rudolf Geiger and is therefore often called the **Köppen-Geiger classification**. In it each climate gets an abbreviation made of letters, for example A for tropical and E for polar climates. This division is still used today in school books and in research.

Switzerland belongs to the **temperate zone** with four clear seasons. Because of the Alps, however, there are big differences in a small space. The higher you climb, the colder it gets, roughly half a degree per 100 metres of height, so on high summits you find an almost polar climate. In Ticino, by contrast, even palms grow, because the Alps hold off cold north winds.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line that divides the Earth exactly into a northern and a southern half.
The circles of latitude over which the sun stands exactly overhead at noon once a year.
Treeless, cold landscape with mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.
A huge belt of coniferous forest in the north of Europe, Asia and North America.

gewusst: If you climb from Locarno to a high Alpine summit, in a few hours you pass through almost as many climate zones as on a journey from the Mediterranean to the Arctic.
There are glaciers even in the tropics, for example on Kilimanjaro in Africa.
The largest desert in the world is actually Antarctica, because extremely little precipitation falls there.

teile.einleitung: Nodule bacteria are tiny living things that live in small swellings on the roots of legumes such as peas, beans or clover. They convert nitrogen from the air into a form that the plant can use. In this way they fertilise their host plant quite naturally.
wichtigste: Nodule bacteria live in nodules on the roots of legumes.
They convert nitrogen from the air into a form usable by the plant.
In return they receive sugar from the plant as food.
Such a partnership for mutual benefit is called a symbiosis.
Host plants include peas, beans, lentils, clover, lupins and soya.
Farmers therefore use legumes as a natural fertiliser.
The scientific name for many of these bacteria is rhizobia.

abschnitte.text: Nodule bacteria are bacteria that live in the soil and can enter the roots of certain plants. Experts call them **rhizobia**, after the Greek word for root. They are so small that you can see them only under a microscope. The nodules in which they live, by contrast, can be seen with the naked eye, and they are about as big as a pinhead up to a small pea.

The plant sends chemical signal substances into the soil through its roots. Suitable bacteria recognise these signals and enter through the fine **root hairs**. The plant then forms small growths around the bacteria, the **root nodules**. If you cut open an active nodule, it is pink to reddish inside.

Plants need **nitrogen** to make proteins and the green chlorophyll. Air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen, but plants cannot use this gas directly. Nodule bacteria have a special tool, the enzyme **nitrogenase**, which converts the nitrogen from the air into ammonium. This process is called nitrogen fixation.

The cooperation between plant and bacteria is a **symbiosis**, and both gain from it. The bacteria supply nitrogen, and the plant gives them sugar from photosynthesis and a protected home in return. So that the delicate enzyme works, the plant makes a red pigment, **leghaemoglobin**, which regulates the oxygen in the nodule. This pigment is responsible for the pink colour.

Because legumes get their nitrogen themselves, they hardly need fertiliser. After the harvest, nitrogen-rich roots stay behind in the soil, and the next crop benefits from this. That is why farmers like to sow clover, peas or vetches as **green manure** or grow them in a **crop rotation**. Especially in organic farming, in which no chemical-synthetic nitrogen fertiliser is allowed, they are very important.

begriffe.erklaerung: Living together of two different living things, in which both gain an advantage.
Plants whose seeds grow in a pod, for example peas, beans and lentils.
The conversion of nitrogen from the air into a form that living things can use.
Plants that are grown to improve the soil and are then worked into it.

gewusst: To turn nitrogen from the air into fertiliser artificially, industry needs high temperatures and enormous pressure, whereas the bacteria manage it at room temperature.
The black alder also has root nodules, though with different bacteria, which is why it grows well on nutrient-poor soils.
A clover field can bring as much nitrogen into the soil per year as a strong dose of fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: Common ragwort is a wild plant with yellow flowers that grows at the edges of paths and in pastures. It is pretty, but poisonous to horses and cattle.
wichtigste: Common ragwort blooms from about the end of July, around St James’s Day.
Its flowers are bright yellow.
It contains poisons called pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
These poisons damage mainly the liver.
In hay it is especially dangerous, because the bitter taste is missing.
The seeds have white hairs and fly on the wind.

abschnitte.text: The plant blooms from about **St James’s Day** on 25 July, which is where the first part of its German name, “Jakobs-Greiskraut”, comes from. It grows up to about a metre tall and bears many **yellow** flower heads. After flowering, seeds with **white hairs** form. These are reminiscent of the hair of old people, **“Greisenhaar”**. That is why it is called “Greiskraut” in German.

Common ragwort contains **pyrrolizidine alkaloids**. These poisons damage mainly the **liver**. If an animal eats small amounts again and again, the damage builds up. In the pasture, horses and cattle usually avoid the plant because it tastes **bitter**. In **hay** or silage, however, the bitter taste has gone, but the poison has not. That is why the animals then eat it along with the rest.

For the **caterpillar of the cinnabar moth**, the plant is a feast. The caterpillar is conspicuously **ringed in black and yellow**. It takes up the poison and as a result becomes inedible even to birds. The colours warn its enemies. The adult moth has black wings with red spots.

A single plant can produce a great many seeds. These fly off **on the wind** with their hairs. They sprout easily in pastures with gaps in the grass. That is why farmers pull the plants out by the root before the seeds ripen. It is best to wear gloves when doing so.

gewusst: Common ragwort is a native plant and not an introduced neophyte.
The poison can also get into food through honey, if bees collect a lot from the plant.

teile.einleitung: Humus is the dark, fertile part of the soil. It forms from dead plants and animals and is very important for plant growth.
wichtigste: Humus is dark brown to black.
It lies mainly in the topmost layer of soil.
Humus stores water like a sponge.
It contains many nutrients for plants.
Worms, fungi and bacteria turn fallen leaves into humus.
The word “humus” comes from Latin and means earth.

abschnitte.text: **Humus** is an important part of the soil. It makes the earth **fertile** and **loose**. Humus is very dark, **dark brown to black**. The more humus a soil has, the darker it is. The word comes from **Latin** and means earth or ground.

In autumn, leaves fall to the ground, and plants die. **Earthworms**, **woodlice** and other small animals break up the remains. After that, **fungi** and **bacteria** break them down further. In this way humus forms little by little. Because the remains come from above, the **topmost layer of soil** is richest in humus. A thick layer forms only **very slowly**, over many years.

Humus soaks up **water** like a **sponge**. That way plants have water for longer even in dry spells. Humus substances also bind with clay particles and glue soil particles together into small **crumbs**. A crumbly soil is loose and well **aerated**. Roots can grow easily in it.

In humus there are many **nutrients** from rotted plants. The roots of new plants take them up slowly. In this way a **cycle** closes: what once grew becomes food again. That is why gardeners make **compost**. From garden waste and kitchen peelings, humus-rich soil is made.

gewusst: In a handful of good garden soil, there are more living things than there are people on Earth.
Earthworms pull leaves into their burrows and so help to mix the soil.

teile.einleitung: Liverworts are small, simple land plants. Some look like flat green lobes, others like tiny leafy mosses. They grow in damp places, for example on walls, stream banks or in flowerpots.
wichtigste: Liverworts get their name from the liver-like shape of some species.
People distinguish thalloid and leafy liverworts.
A thallus is a flat body without stem and leaves.
The common liverwort often grows on damp walls and in nurseries.
Liverworts never have stomata.
Elaters help to fling the spores out of the capsule.

abschnitte.text: Among the liverworts, two forms are distinguished. **Thalloid liverworts** consist of a flat body, the **thallus**. It is not divided into stem and leaves. In algae too people speak of a thallus. **Leafy liverworts** have small stems with little leaves and look similar to true mosses. Because some species look lobed like a **liver**, people in the past believed they helped against liver complaints.

A well-known example is the **common liverwort**, called “Brunnenlebermoos” in German. It forms flat, green lobes on damp ground, for example on walls, fountains and path edges. In nurseries it often grows on the soil of **flowerpots**. On its surface sit small **gemma cups**. In them lie tiny gemmae. Raindrops splash them out, and new little plants grow from them. In addition, little **umbrellas** grow upwards on stalks, which likewise serve for reproduction.

Like all mosses, liverworts also spread with **spores**. These form in a small capsule. In it lie cells thickened in a spiral, the **elaters**. When the moisture changes, they twist back and forth. In this way they loosen the spores and fling them out of the capsule. The wind then carries the spores further.

Most land plants regulate gas exchange with **stomata** in the skin. Liverworts never have such stomata. Some have simple **air pores** instead, which are always open. Liverworts also have no true roots, but fine anchoring threads. That is why they need damp, shady places.

gewusst: Liverworts probably belong to the oldest groups of land plants.
A single raindrop can fling the gemmae out of the cup of the common liverwort.

teile.einleitung: The **onion** is one of the most important vegetables in the world. Almost every kitchen needs it. In Bern there is even a market of its own in its honour, the Zibelemärit.
wichtigste: When cut, the onion gives off a substance that irritates the eyes.
The dry skin of most onions is golden brown.
Cooked slowly for a long time, the onion tastes sweetish and mild.
Chives, leek and garlic are related to the onion.
Onion sets are small onions that you put into the garden in spring.
The Bernese Zibelemärit takes place on the fourth Monday in November.

abschnitte.text: The onion that we eat is a **storage organ** of the plant. It consists of fleshy leaves that lie tightly one over another. In them the plant stores water and nutrients. On the outside sits a **dry skin**, which in most onions is **golden brown**. There are also red and white onions. If an onion lies in the kitchen for a long time, **green shoots** grow from it, because it wants to become a new plant.

When cutting, the cells of the onion are damaged. In the process, new compounds are formed from substances containing sulphur. One of them rises as a gas and **irritates the eyes**. The eyes then make tears to wash the substance away. A sharp knife and a chilled onion help, because then fewer cells are crushed.

Raw, the onion tastes sharp. If it is **cooked gently in the pan for a long time**, it becomes **sweetish and mild**. It also turns golden brown. Onions give soups, sauces and Rösti a lot of flavour. Related to the onion are **chives**, leek and garlic. They all belong to the genus Allium.

In the garden you can grow onions from seed. It is easier with **onion sets**. These are small onions that you put into the soil in spring. By summer they grow into large onions.
