When the foliage turns yellow and bends over, they are ripe. You then leave them to dry, so that they keep for a long time.

In **Bern**, every year on the **fourth Monday in November**, the **Zibelemärit** takes place. “Zibele” means onion in Bernese German. Farmers from the surrounding area bring tonnes of onions into the old town. Especially popular are the artfully plaited **onion braids**. There is onion tart and onion soup. Children and adults also throw confetti and hit each other with plastic hammers.

gewusst: The Zibelemärit begins early in the morning, while it is still dark.
Onions were already grown thousands of years ago in ancient Egypt.

teile.einleitung: Canadian waterweed is a plant that grows entirely under water. It comes from North America and spread so quickly in Europe that it got its strange German name, which means “water plague”. Today it is also known as a popular plant in aquariums.
wichtigste: Waterweed grows entirely under water.
It originally comes from North America.
It got the German name “Pest”, meaning plague, because it quickly overgrew waters.
Its dark green little leaves usually stand in threes around the stem.
In sunlight it gives off oxygen in small bubbles.
In Europe it multiplies mainly from broken pieces of stem.
It is a popular aquarium plant.

abschnitte.text: Waterweed is an **underwater plant**. Its long stems grow entirely in the water of ponds, lakes, ditches and slow streams. Stems and little leaves are **dark green**. The small leaves usually stand **in threes** in a circle around the stem. This arrangement is called a **whorl**.

As its name says, Canadian waterweed comes from **North America**. In the 19th century it was accidentally brought to Europe. There it grew so strongly that it choked ponds and canals. This got in the way of boats and fishing. That is why it was given the German name **“Wasserpest”**, water plague. Later its spread weakened again in many places.

In Europe waterweed multiplies mainly from **broken pieces of stem**. A torn-off piece drifts on in the water, forms new roots and grows into a new plant. Boats, waterbirds and currents can carry such pieces far away. In this way it can settle new waters.

When waterweed stands in sunlight, it makes food with the help of the light. This is called **photosynthesis**. In doing so it gives off **oxygen**, which rises as small bubbles. That is why it is often used in school experiments. Because it grows easily and quickly, it is also a popular plant in the **aquarium**.

gewusst: The brighter the light, the more bubbles rise from waterweed. In this way you can almost count photosynthesis.
Today, in many Swiss lakes the related Nuttall’s waterweed is spreading more strongly than the Canadian one.

teile.einleitung: Coral reefs are among the most colourful habitats on Earth. If the sea becomes too warm, corals lose their colour and turn white. This coral bleaching is one of the great dangers of climate change for the seas.
wichtigste: In coral bleaching, corals expel their symbiotic algae.
Corals belong to the animal phylum of the cnidarians.
The NOAA measures heat stress with “Degree Heating Weeks”.
In April 2024 the NOAA declared the fourth global coral bleaching event.
At 2 °C of warming, according to the IPCC, more than 99 per cent of tropical reefs are lost.
Ocean acidification also harms the corals.

abschnitte.text: Corals are not plants but animals. They belong to the **cnidarians**, like jellyfish. In their tissue live tiny **algae**. The algae carry out photosynthesis and supply the coral with food. In return they get protection and nutrients. Such a living together for mutual benefit is called a **symbiosis**. The algae also give the corals their colour.

If the water is too warm for a longer time, the symbiosis falls out of balance. The corals **expel their algae**. What is left is the white limestone skeleton, which shimmers through the transparent tissue. The coral looks **bleached**. Without its algae it starves. If the water stays warm for too long, it dies.

The American weather and ocean agency **NOAA** watches sea temperatures with satellites. It describes the accumulated heat stress with the **Degree Heating Weeks**. This number shows how strongly and for how long the water was warmer than normal. In April 2024 the NOAA declared the **fourth global coral bleaching event**. The **Great Barrier Reef** off Australia has also suffered several mass bleachings in quick succession since 2016.

According to a special report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the **IPCC**, of 2018, at **2 °C** of warming more than **99 per cent** of tropical coral reefs are expected to be lost. On top of this comes **ocean acidification**: the sea takes up CO2 and becomes more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons. But there is also hope: if the water cools in time, corals can **take their algae back** and recover.

gewusst: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system on Earth and can even be seen from space.
Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the sea floor but are home to a large part of all marine species.

teile.einleitung: The potato is one of the most important foods in the world. It comes from the Andes in South America and reached Europe in the 16th century. In Switzerland it comes to the table as Rösti, Gschwellti or mashed potato.
wichtigste: In many Swiss dialects the potato is called “Härdöpfel”.
Spanish sailors brought it to Europe in the 16th century.
The green berries of the potato plant are poisonous.
Its flowers are white, pink or violet.
Potatoes are stored cool and dark.
Gschwellti are potatoes boiled in their skins.
With raclette, potatoes are traditionally eaten.

abschnitte.text: What we eat is the **tuber** of the potato plant. It grows underground on runners and stores a lot of **starch**. In summer the plant flowers, **white, pink or violet** depending on the variety. After flowering, small green **berries** form. They contain poison and must not be eaten. Green patches and sprouts on the tuber are also cut off.

The potato comes from the **Andes** in South America. People there have grown it for thousands of years. The Andean peoples made potatoes keep: they let the tubers freeze at night, dried them in the day and pressed them out. This produced **chuño**, which keeps for years and was an important store in the Inca Empire.

**Spanish sailors** brought the potato to Europe in the second half of the **16th century**. At first it was seen in many places as a strange plant for botanical gardens. Only later did it become an important food, because it gives a large yield on a small area. So that it does not sprout too quickly, it is stored **cool and dark**, for example in the cellar.

In many Swiss dialects the potato is called **Härdöpfel**, which means earth apple. **Gschwellti** are potatoes that are boiled in their skins and happily eaten with cheese. Such potatoes belong with **raclette**, along with pickled gherkins and silverskin onions. Mashed potatoes with milk and butter are called **Kartoffelstock**. And **Rösti** is known all over Switzerland.

For **chips** (French fries), potatoes are cut into strips and fried in hot oil. Besides that there are crisps, gratin and potato salad. There are floury varieties that fall apart when cooked, and waxy varieties that keep their shape. Depending on the dish, you choose the suitable variety.

gewusst: The potato and the tomato are closely related. Both belong to the nightshade family.
In the middle of the 19th century, a plant disease destroyed large parts of the potato harvest in Ireland and triggered a severe famine.

teile.einleitung: After the arrival of Christopher Columbus in America in 1492, a huge exchange of plants, animals and, sadly, diseases began between America and the rest of the world. It is called the Columbian exchange.
wichtigste: The historian Alfred W. Crosby coined the term “Columbian Exchange” in 1972.
Tomato, potato, maize, pepper and cocoa came from America to the rest of the world.
Horses, cattle and pigs came from Europe to America.
Imported diseases such as smallpox sharply reduced the number of Indigenous people.
Sugar cane growing in the Caribbean drove the transatlantic slave trade.
Cassava from America became a staple food in Africa.

abschnitte.text: Before 1492, America and the so-called Old World of Europe, Africa and Asia had long had separate plants and animals. With the ships of the Europeans they suddenly crossed the Atlantic. The American historian **Alfred W. Crosby** called this process “**Columbian Exchange**” in 1972. In German it is called **Kolumbianischer Austausch**.

From America came many plants that are eaten everywhere today: **tomato**, **potato**, **maize**, beans and **peppers**. The pepper, paprika, today shapes Hungarian cooking, for example. The **cocoa plant** comes from Central and South America. **Cassava** became a staple food in Africa. The **turkey** also came from America to Europe.

abschnitte.titel: From the Old World to America
abschnitte.text: In the other direction travelled wheat, rice, coffee and **sugar cane**. The Europeans also brought **horses**, cattle, pigs and sheep. The horse changed the life of many peoples of the North American **prairie**: they could now hunt much more easily and cover long distances. Cattle and sheep turned large landscapes into pasture.

The Europeans also brought in diseases, such as **smallpox** and measles. The people of America, by contrast, had no defences against them. That is why a large part of the Indigenous population died. For the **sugar cane plantations** in the Caribbean, the colonial rulers needed many workers. They carried off millions of people from Africa as slaves. This **transatlantic slave trade** is a dark chapter of history.

gewusst: Before the Columbian exchange there were no tomatoes in Italy and no potatoes in Switzerland.
Chilli, today typical of the cooking of India and Thailand, originally comes from America.

teile.einleitung: In the high mountains, plants have to survive icy nights and long winters. With many tricks they become resistant to frost. This ability is called **cold hardiness**.
wichtigste: Shorter days and falling temperatures trigger frost hardening in autumn.
In many frost-tolerant plants, ice forms outside the cells.
Sugar in the cells lowers the freezing point.
Some tissues cool below 0 °C without freezing: this is supercooling.
In cushion plants it is warmer and windless.
Red pigments such as anthocyanins protect against strong radiation.

abschnitte.text: In summer, even a light frost would harm many alpine plants. In autumn they prepare for winter. This is called **frost hardening**. It is triggered by **shorter days** and **falling temperatures**. In the process the plants change their cells and become more resistant step by step. In spring they lose this hardening again.

If ice forms inside a cell, the crystals tear the cell apart and it dies. Many frost-tolerant plants therefore let the ice form **outside the cells**, in the spaces between them. This draws water out of the cells. In addition, the plants build up **sugar** in their cells. Sugar **lowers the freezing point**, rather like salt on the road. Some tissues use **supercooling**: the water cools below 0 °C without ice forming.

The **alpine snowbell** is a small member of the primrose family with violet, fringed little bells. In spring it often pushes its flowers up **through the melting snow cover**. Under the snow it has already formed its buds. The snow protects it in winter like a blanket from great cold and wind. That way it can make good use of the short time in the mountain summer.

**Cushion plants** such as **moss campion** grow densely and in a half-round shape. **Inside the cushion it is warmer and windless**. The sun warms it up, and it stores moisture. The **creeping azalea** is an evergreen dwarf shrub that presses itself flat to the ground. It settles on wind-swept ridges, which in winter are often **free of snow**. It is among the frost-hardiest plants of the Alps.

In the high mountains, the **radiation** of the sun is very strong, especially the UV light. Many high-mountain plants therefore make red pigments such as **anthocyanins** in their leaves. These act like sun cream and protect the inside of the leaf. That is why some alpine plants are reddish in colour.

gewusst: Under a thick cover of snow, the ground often stays only a little below 0 °C even in the hardest winter.
Some cushion plants grow only a few centimetres tall but live for many decades.

teile.einleitung: Leaf fall is the name for the dropping of the leaves that you can watch on deciduous trees here every autumn. The trees do this to save water in winter and to avoid frost damage. Before the leaves fall, the tree takes valuable nutrients back from them, and in the process the colourful autumn colours arise.
wichtigste: Leaf fall is the dropping of leaves, mostly in autumn.
Trees drop their leaves to save water in winter and to avoid frost damage.
A lot of water evaporates through the leaves, which the tree could not replace from the frozen soil.
Before dropping them, the tree takes nutrients back from the leaves.
At the base of the leaf stalk, a separation layer forms.
Shorter days and cooler temperatures trigger leaf fall.
The fallen leaves turn into nutrient-rich humus in the soil.

abschnitte.text: Leaf fall is the name for the dropping of the leaves of trees and shrubs. In central Europe this happens mainly in October and November. Trees that lose their leaves every year are called **deciduous**, literally “summer-green”. Trees such as spruce, fir or holly that keep their leaves or needles in winter are called **evergreen**.

Through the many small openings in the leaves, water constantly evaporates, which is called **transpiration**. In winter the ground is often frozen, and the roots can hardly take up any water. If the tree still had leaves, it would therefore dry out. In addition, frost and heavy **snow** could damage the tender leaves and branches.

Before the leaves fall, the tree breaks down the green **chlorophyll** and stores valuable substances such as nitrogen in branches and roots. Now yellow and orange pigments become visible, the **carotenoids**, which were previously covered by the green. Some trees such as certain maples also make red pigments in autumn. In the end brown remains are left, as you see in oaks and beeches.

Leaf fall is triggered mainly by the shorter days and the falling temperatures in autumn. Plant hormones make sure that a **separation layer** forms at the base of the leaf stalk. This layer of cells releases the leaf from the twig as if at a predetermined breaking point. At the same time, a layer of cork seals the wound so that no pathogens get in.

The fallen leaves are an important part of the forest floor and are called **leaf litter**. Earthworms, woodlice, fungi and bacteria break the leaves down and make nutrient-rich **humus** from them. In this way the nutrients return to the soil and are available again to the trees the next year. Hedgehogs, toads and many insects use heaps of leaves in gardens as winter quarters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The evaporation of water through the leaves of a plant.
A layer of cells at the leaf stalk where the leaf comes away from the twig.
The layer of fallen leaves on the ground.
The name for plants that carry leaves only in summer.

gewusst: A large old beech can carry several hundred thousand leaves, which it drops every autumn.
Young beeches and oaks often keep their brown, dry leaves until spring.
There are also trees in the tropics that drop their leaves, but they do so in the dry season instead of in winter.

teile.einleitung: Cacti are plants that are adapted to dry regions. They store water in their thick stems and protect themselves with spines. Almost all cacti come from the Americas.
wichtigste: Many cacti grow in dry deserts.
The spines protect the cactus from animals.
The saguaro is a giant columnar cactus from Mexico and the USA.
Many cacti bloom only for a short time, but brightly.
The prickly pear is the edible fruit of the prickly pear cactus.
Flat, widely branching roots quickly soak up water after rain.

abschnitte.text: Cacti grow especially often in **dry deserts** and semi-deserts, mainly in the Americas. There it rarely rains. Their thick, green stem stores a lot of **water**. It also does the work of the leaves and makes sugar with sunlight. A thick skin with wax stops the water from evaporating.

Many cacti have **flat, widely branching roots** close beneath the surface. When it does rain, they **quickly soak up water** before it seeps away or evaporates. The cactus can visibly swell as it does so. After that it can manage a long time without rain again.

The **spines** are modified leaves. They serve **as protection against animals** that would otherwise eat the juicy stem. They also give a little shade and slow the wind. This way the cactus loses less water. The ball-shaped **golden barrel cactus** from Mexico is covered with golden-yellow spines.

The **saguaro** is a giant **columnar cactus** from the deserts of **Mexico and the USA**. It can grow over ten metres tall and grows very slowly. Many cacti show **bright flowers** only for a short time, some for just a single night. The **prickly pear cactus** produces edible fruits, the **prickly pears**.

Many people keep cacti on the **windowsill**. They need a lot of light and **only rarely water**. Too much watering harms them, because then the roots rot. In winter, many species like it cool and almost dry. In the Succulent Collection in Zurich, you can see very many cacti from around the world.

gewusst: After heavy rain, a large saguaro can store several hundred litres of water.
Almost all species of cactus originally come from the Americas.

teile.einleitung: The corn poppy glows bright red in summer at the edges of fields and in meadows. Its delicate flowers last only briefly, but the plant forms countless seeds. It is one of the best-known wild flowers.
wichtigste: The corn poppy has bright red petals.
At the bottom of the petals there is often a black spot.
A flower has four petals.
A single flower lasts only a few days.
The seeds are in a capsule and fall out as if from a salt shaker.
Bees collect pollen from it, because it has no nectar.
The corn poppy is slightly poisonous.

abschnitte.text: The corn poppy has **four** large, **bright red** petals. Two are a little larger than the other two. At the bottom of each petal there is often a dark, almost **black spot**. In the bud the petals are tightly folded. That is why at first they look **crumpled like tissue paper**.

A single flower loses its petals after only **a few days**. In return, new buds keep opening. The corn poppy offers no **nectar**. Bees and bumblebees, however, collect a lot of **pollen** there. You often see it at the edges of fields, on fallow land and in cornfields.

abschnitte.titel: A salt shaker full of seeds
abschnitte.text: After flowering, the corn poppy forms a **capsule**. Inside are very many tiny **seeds**. At the top of the capsule there are small holes. When the wind shakes the plant, the seeds fall out like salt from a **salt shaker**. This form is called a **pore capsule**.

The corn poppy contains a **milky sap**. In it are substances that are **slightly poisonous**. That is why it is not eaten. The poppy whose seeds you find in rolls and cakes is a different species, the **opium poppy**.

gewusst: The seeds of the corn poppy can survive in the soil for many years and germinate as soon as the soil is dug over.
In Britain the poppy is a sign of remembrance of the dead of the First World War.

t1y6gono.t: Larch and Swiss stone pine forest

teile.einleitung: The larch and Swiss stone pine forest is a light mountain forest high up in the Alps. It grows right up to the tree line and is typical of the Engadine and the Valais.
wichtigste: Larch and Swiss stone pine forests are found mainly in the Engadine and the Valais.
The Aletsch Forest near Riederalp is an old larch and Swiss stone pine forest.
The larch settles open ground first, the Swiss stone pine follows later.
The Swiss stone pine grows very slowly.
In winter the larch loses its needles and so hardly any water.
The larch budmoth sometimes eats whole forests brown.

abschnitte.titel: Forest of the inner Alpine valleys
abschnitte.text: Larch and Swiss stone pine forests love the dry climate of the **inner Alpine valleys** with cold winters and a lot of sun. In Switzerland they are especially widespread in the **Engadine** and the **Valais**. The spruce copes less well there. A famous example is the **Aletsch Forest** above the Great Aletsch Glacier near Riederalp. It belongs to the UNESCO World Heritage site **Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch**.

The **larch** needs a lot of light and grows fast when young. As a **pioneer tree** it conquers open areas such as avalanche tracks or glacier forelands first. It is the only native conifer that drops its needles in autumn. In this way it loses hardly any water in winter, when the ground is frozen. Larches usually grow 30 to 40 metres tall, but at the tree line they often stay much smaller.

The **Swiss stone pine** moves in later and grows **very slowly**. At altitude the growing season is short, so it adds only a little wood each year. Its wood therefore has very narrow **tree rings**. It smells pleasant and is gladly used for furniture.

Larches have a loose crown with fine needles. A lot of light reaches the ground. That is why grass and herbs grow under them, and livestock can graze there. In this way **larch meadows** arise in the mountains, a mixture of forest and pasture.

In the Engadine, the **larch budmoth** eats whole larch forests brown at regular intervals. The caterpillars of this small moth multiply in huge numbers about every eight to ten years and eat the needles. The larches usually do not die of it. They sprout again afterwards.

gewusst: The nutcracker hides Swiss stone pine nuts as a store and so makes sure that new Swiss stone pines grow.
Swiss stone pines can live to be several hundred years old at the tree line.

teile.einleitung: If you turn a mushroom over, you often see many thin little plates under the cap. These are the **gills**. On them tiny spores form, from which new mushrooms can grow.
wichtigste: Gills are thin little plates under the cap of a mushroom.
They are arranged in a radiating pattern from the stalk.
Spores form on the gills.
From the spores, new mushrooms can grow.
The wind carries the tiny spores far away.
With a spore print on paper you can see the colour of the spores.

abschnitte.text: A mushroom as we see it in the woods usually consists of a **stalk** and a **cap**. **Under the cap**, many mushrooms have thin little plates. They are called **gills**. They are arranged **in a radiating pattern from the stalk**, like the spokes of a wheel. The fly agaric and the button mushroom have gills. The porcini, by contrast, has fine tubes under the cap that look like a sponge.

On the gills, **spores** form. They are so tiny that you **cannot see** a single spore **with the naked eye**. A single mushroom makes millions of them. The spores serve so that **new mushrooms grow**. They have a similar job to the seeds of a plant.

When the spores are ripe, they fall out of the gills. The **wind** carries them far away. If a spore lands in a good place, it germinates. Fine threads grow in the soil or in the wood. This network is called the **mycelium**. From the mycelium, new mushrooms later grow out, which we see and collect.

You can make the colour of the spores visible. To do this you cut off the stalk and **lay the cap gills down on a sheet of paper**. It is best to cover it with a bowl. After a few hours the spores fall out and form a beautiful pattern. The spores can be white, pink, brown or black. Experts use this to identify mushroom species.

Many mushrooms with gills are poisonous, some even deadly. That is why you should never eat mushrooms you have collected yourself without having them checked. In Switzerland, many municipalities have a **mushroom inspection service**. There trained experts look at every mushroom and say whether you may eat it.

gewusst: A single mushroom can form billions of spores.
The mycelium of a mushroom in the soil can be much larger than the mushroom that we see.

teile.einleitung: The carrot is one of the most popular vegetables in Switzerland. Here it is mostly called “Rüebli”. You eat its orange root raw, cooked or even in cake.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the carrot is mostly called “Rüebli”.
The canton of Aargau is often called “Rüebliland”.
The Rüeblitorte is a well-known Swiss cake.
The pigment carotene colours the carrot orange.
From carotene the body makes vitamin A, which the eyes need.
In the past, many carrots were purple or yellow.
The carrot is biennial and flowers only in its second year.

abschnitte.text: What we eat of the carrot is its thick **root**. It sits in the ground. Above the soil you see only the green **foliage** with finely feathered leaves. Most carrots in the shop are **orange**. But there are also yellow, white and purple varieties.

The pigment **carotene** colours the carrot orange. Its name even comes from the word carrot. The body can make **vitamin A** from carotene. The eyes need this vitamin, especially for **seeing in the dark**. The first carrots were often **purple** or yellow. Orange varieties were only bred later.

abschnitte.titel: Only in its second year does it flower
abschnitte.text: The carrot is **biennial**. In the first year the root grows and stores nutrients. If you leave it in the ground, it flowers in the second year. Then it forms a tall stem with white **umbels**, that is, umbrella-shaped flower clusters, and finally seeds. That is why carrots are harvested in the first year.

In many Swiss dialects the carrot is called **Rüebli**. In the canton of **Aargau**, many carrots have been grown for a long time. That is why it is also called **Rüebliland**. A well-known cake is the **Rüeblitorte**, with finely grated carrots in the batter. It is often decorated with small marzipan Rüebli. In Aarau, the **Rüeblimärt** takes place every autumn.

gewusst: The wild carrot, the ancestor of the carrot, grows here on meadows and at the edges of paths.
In the middle of the white umbel of the wild carrot there is often a single dark flower.

teile.einleitung: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids in plant cells. Plastids are small cell parts with their own jobs, like the green chloroplasts. Leucoplasts serve mainly as stores, for example for starch.
wichtigste: Leucoplasts are colourless; the name comes from the Greek word for white.
Amyloplasts make and store starch grains.
Elaioplasts store oils and fats.
Proteinoplasts store proteins.
Leucoplasts are found mainly in roots and storage organs.
In light, the leucoplasts of potatoes become chloroplasts.

abschnitte.text: Plant cells contain various **plastids**. The green **chloroplasts** carry out photosynthesis. Coloured chromoplasts colour flowers and fruits, for example. **Leucoplasts**, by contrast, contain no pigments, they are **colourless**. Their name comes from the Greek word leukos for white. They are found mainly in **non-green** tissues far from light, such as in roots, tubers and seeds.

Leucoplasts are distinguished by what they store. **Amyloplasts** build **starch** and keep it as grains. The name comes from the Greek amylon for starch flour. **Elaioplasts** store **oils and fats** in the form of droplets. **Proteinoplasts**, also called aleuroplasts, store **proteins**, for example in some seeds.

In the **root cap** at the root tip lie especially heavy amyloplasts. They always sink downwards in the cells. They are therefore called **statoliths**, that is position stones. In this way the root recognises where **down** is, and grows into the earth. This growing according to gravity is called **gravitropism**.

abschnitte.titel: Green potatoes and the starch test
abschnitte.text: If **potato tubers** lie in the light, they turn green. Their leucoplasts then develop into **chloroplasts** with chlorophyll. At the same time the tuber often makes more poisonous **solanine**, which is why green parts are not eaten. Starch grains can be detected with **iodine-potassium iodide solution**, also called Lugol’s solution. It stains starch **blue-violet to black**.

gewusst: A drop of Lugol’s solution on a slice of potato stains it dark at once.
Plastids can change into one another, for example from a store to a green chloroplast.

teile.einleitung: Many leaves shine, and raindrops roll off them in beads. This is due to the **cuticle**, a thin, waxy protective layer. It covers the surface of leaves and young stems.
wichtigste: The cuticle is a waxy layer on the epidermis of a leaf.
Its most important job is protection from drying out.
It is formed by the epidermal cells.
It consists mainly of cutin and waxes.
It is transparent, so it does not hinder photosynthesis.
Plants of dry sites usually have an especially thick cuticle.

abschnitte.text: The outermost layer of cells of a leaf is called the **epidermis**. The **epidermal cells** release a layer on their outer side. This is the **cuticle**. It consists mainly of **cutin**, a fat-like substance, and **waxes**. The cuticle is usually very thin, often thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre. Even so, it is vital for the plant.

The most important job of the cuticle is **protection from drying out**. It lets hardly any water through. Without it, a leaf would quickly dry up on a sunny day. So that the plant can still exchange air, there are small openings in the epidermis, the **stomata**. They can be opened and closed. The cuticle also protects against fungi, bacteria and dirt.

The cuticle is **transparent**. Sunlight can therefore enter the leaf unhindered. There the green cells carry out **photosynthesis** and make sugar with the help of the light. In this way the cuticle protects the leaf without taking its light away.

How thick the cuticle is depends on the habitat. **Plants of dry sites** such as cacti or plants by the Mediterranean usually have an **especially thick cuticle**. Evergreen plants such as **ivy** and **holly** also have a thick cuticle. That is why their leaves **shine**. Water plants, by contrast, often have only a very thin cuticle.

On some leaves, water simply rolls off and takes dirt with it. This is called the **lotus effect**, after the lotus flower. The surface has tiny wax knobs. A drop rests only on the tips, rolls off and collects dust on the way. This trick has been copied for facade paints and other products that clean themselves.

gewusst: Insects also have a cuticle, which in them forms the hard armour.
The lotus effect was discovered by botanists and copied in paints and coatings.

teile.einleitung: Dragonflies are fast, shimmering insects that you see by ponds and streams in summer. They are skilful hunters in the air. They spend their childhood, however, under water.
wichtigste: Dragonflies lay their eggs in the water or in plants beside the water.
A larva that lives in the water hatches from the egg.
Dragonflies catch small insects such as midges in flight.
Their eyes are very large and consist of many thousands of single eyes.
Dragonflies have no sting and are harmless.
After hatching, the empty larval skin stays behind on the stalk.

abschnitte.text: Dragonflies lay their **eggs** in the water or in plants beside the water. A **larva** hatches from the egg. It looks quite different from the finished dragonfly. The larva lives **in the water**, often for several months or even years. It is a predator and catches small water animals with a kind of grasping arm, the **mask**. As it grows, it moults several times.

When the larva has finished growing, it **climbs up a stalk** out of the water. Then its skin splits open, and the **dragonfly emerges**. At first its wings are soft and crumpled. It pumps them up and lets them dry. The **empty larval skin** stays hanging on the stalk. You can often find it by the pond.

The **eyes** of a dragonfly are **very large**. They take up almost the whole head and consist of many thousands of **single eyes**. In this way the dragonfly sees almost all around. Dragonflies are **hunters**: they catch small insects such as **midges** in flight. They can move their four wings independently of one another. That is why they fly very skilfully and can even hover in the air.

Dragonflies have **no sting**. For people they are completely **harmless**. Many species need clean waters with plants on the bank. That is why every nature-friendly pond helps dragonflies. In Switzerland dozens of species of dragonfly live, from the delicate **damselflies** to the large **dragonflies**.

gewusst: Even about 300 million years ago, giant dragonfly-like insects with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres flew.
A dragonfly larva often lives in the water much longer than the finished dragonfly in the air.

teile.einleitung: Seed leaves, or cotyledons, are the very first leaves of a young plant. They are already inside the seed and appear first when it germinates. By the number of seed leaves, flowering plants are divided into two large groups.
wichtigste: The first leaves from the seed are called seed leaves.
The bean and the sunflower have two seed leaves.
Maize, wheat and rice have only one seed leaf.
Seed leaves often look quite different from the later leaves.
After the seed leaves, the foliage leaves grow.
Later the seed leaves wilt and fall off.
In the light, seed leaves turn green.

abschnitte.text: When a seed germinates, the **seed leaves** appear first. They are already formed in the seed. Often they are simpler and **rounder** in shape than the later leaves. In some plants, for example the bean, they are thick, because they store **nutrients** for the young plant.

The **bean** and the **sunflower** have two seed leaves. If you let sunflower seeds germinate, two large seed leaves come out of the husk. Such plants are called **dicotyledons**. **Maize**, wheat and rice belong to the grasses and have only one seed leaf. They are called **monocotyledons**. Tulips and palms also belong to them.

After the seed leaves, the plant forms its true leaves. They are called **foliage leaves**. They have the typical shape of the plant. When enough foliage leaves have grown, the plant no longer needs the seed leaves. They **wilt** and fall off.

In the light, the seed leaves form the green pigment **chlorophyll**. With it they can make food like normal leaves. You can see this well with **cress**: its little leaves, which you sprinkle on bread, are seed leaves. Cress is easy to grow on damp cotton wool on the windowsill.

gewusst: In pines and other conifers, a seedling can have many seed leaves at once, sometimes more than ten.
In monocotyledons the leaf veins usually run parallel, in dicotyledons they are often net-like.

teile.einleitung: The **leek** is a long vegetable, white at the bottom and green at the top. It is related to the onion and can even stand the winter in the garden.
wichtigste: A leek stalk is white at the bottom and green at the top.
Leek is also called porree in German.
It is related to the onion.
Leeks tolerate cold and can be harvested in winter.
If you earth up soil, the white part becomes longer.
The Vaud dish papet vaudois is cooked with leeks and potatoes.

abschnitte.text: The **leek**, in German also called **Porree**, consists of many leaves that fit tightly inside one another. Together they form a thick shaft. A leek stalk is **white at the bottom and green at the top**. The white part tastes especially mild and tender. The leek is **related to the onion**. Garlic and chives also belong to the same genus. That is why it smells similar when cut.

Leeks are planted in spring or summer. To make the white part longer, you **earth up soil** around the plants. Where no light gets in, the leek stays white. Leeks are hardy. They **tolerate cold** and can therefore stay in the garden **in winter** and be harvested. In Switzerland a lot of leek is grown, for example in the Seeland.

When earthing up, soil gets into the leek. It often sits **between the leaves**, especially where the white turns into green. That is why you cut the leek open lengthways and **wash it out well**. After that you can cut it into rings or strips. Leek goes well in soups, tarts, gratins and stews.

In the canton of **Vaud** there is a well-known dish with leeks: the **papet vaudois**. For it, leeks and **potatoes** are cooked slowly together until a creamy mash forms. Traditionally it is eaten with a Vaud sausage, the saucisse aux choux. The dish is especially popular in autumn and winter.

The leek is an emblem of **Wales**, a part of Great Britain. On 1 March, the day of the national saint, Saint David, some people there wear a leek or a daffodil on their clothes. According to a legend, Welsh warriors once wore leeks on their helmets so that they could recognise one another.

gewusst: Leeks were already grown in ancient Egypt.
The daffodil is also an emblem of Wales, and its Welsh name sounds similar to the word for leek.

teile.einleitung: Many flowering plants need insects so that their pollen reaches other flowers. This is called insect pollination. Bees, bumblebees, butterflies and flies are important helpers.
wichtigste: Many flowers reward insects with sweet nectar.
For bees, pollen is a protein-rich food for the larvae.
Honey bees carry pollen in baskets on their back legs.
Around 600 species of wild bee live in Switzerland.
Red clover is pollinated mainly by bumblebees with a long tongue.
Honey bees show with a dance where good flowers are.

abschnitte.text: In **pollination**, pollen passes from one flower to the stigma of another. Only then can seeds and fruits form. Many plants attract insects with colours, scent and **nectar**, a liquid containing sugar. While the insect drinks, pollen sticks to its body. At the next flower it brushes it off again.

Bees also collect **pollen**. It is rich in protein and serves as food for the **larvae**. The **honey bee** carries it home in little “baskets” on its back legs. In Switzerland there are also **around 600 species of wild bee**, which include the bumblebees. In **red clover**, the nectar lies deep in the flower. Only bumblebees with a long tongue can reach it well.

When a honey bee has found a rich source of flowers, she returns to the hive and **dances**. In the so-called waggle dance, the direction of the dance shows where the others should fly. Its length tells how far it is. The researcher Karl von Frisch decoded this bee language.

It is not only bees that pollinate. **Honeysuckle** smells strongly in the evening and is visited mainly by **moths**. Their long tongues reach the nectar in the narrow flower tubes. Some flowers smell of rotting meat and so attract **flies**. They are called **carrion flowers**.

Without insects there would be far fewer apples, cherries, berries and many vegetable seeds. That is why it is important to preserve flower meadows, hedges and nesting places. Every flowering corner of the garden helps the pollinators.

gewusst: In 1973, Karl von Frisch received the Nobel Prize for his research on the language of bees.
Some flowers have patterns that only insects can see, because they perceive ultraviolet light.

teile.einleitung: The carbon cycle describes how the element carbon constantly travels back and forth between air, plants, animals, soils, seas and rocks. Carbon is in every living thing, in wood, in limestone and in the carbon dioxide of the air. Because humans are changing this cycle strongly, it is especially important for understanding climate change.
wichtigste: Carbon travels constantly between atmosphere, living things, soils, ocean and rock.
Photosynthesis removes the most CO2 from the atmosphere on land.
The ocean holds more carbon than the atmosphere, soils and vegetation together.
By far the largest part of the carbon is stored in the long term in carbonate rocks such as limestone.
Bogs are important carbon stores, because dead plants are hardly broken down for lack of oxygen.
In the annual mean for 2024, the CO2 concentration of the atmosphere was about 420 ppm.
If the sea takes up additional CO2, the pH of seawater falls.

abschnitte.text: Carbon is a chemical element and the most important building block of all living things. It occurs in many forms: as the gas **carbon dioxide** in the air, as sugar and wood in plants, as lime in shells and as coal or oil deep in the ground. Places where carbon is stored are called **carbon stores** or sinks. The exchange between these stores is called the carbon cycle.

In **photosynthesis**, plants take up CO2 from the air and build sugar, wood and leaves from it. On land, no other process removes as much CO2 from the atmosphere. Animals eat plants, and in breathing, animals and plants give off CO2 again. When a living thing dies, fungi and bacteria break down the remains, and the carbon gets back into the air or into the **humus** of the soil.

The seas are a huge store and hold more carbon than the atmosphere, soils and vegetation together. At the water surface, CO2 dissolves from the air, and tiny **plankton** use it for photosynthesis. When the tiny organisms die, their remains sink into the depths. If the sea takes up additional CO2, the pH falls and the water becomes more acidic, which is called **ocean acidification** and harms corals and shellfish.

Over millions of years, sea animals build shells of lime, which settle on the sea floor as **limestone**. In such carbonate rocks, by far the largest part of the Earth’s carbon is stored. **Coal, oil and natural gas** also formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and tiny organisms. Through weathering and volcanic eruptions, a small part of this carbon gets very slowly back into the atmosphere.

Since industrialisation, people have been burning, in a short time, carbon that was stored over millions of years. In burning, each carbon atom combines with two oxygen atoms, which is why 3 tonnes of carbon produce 11 tonnes of CO2. As a result, the CO2 concentration of the air rose from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to about 420 ppm in the annual mean for 2024. Clearing forests and draining **bogs** also releases a lot of CO2.

Swiss forests store large amounts of carbon in the wood and in the forest soil. Switzerland’s **raised bogs** are especially valuable, because over thousands of years peat has built up there from hardly decomposed plants. The limestone mountains of the **Jura** and many limestone rocks in the Alps also consist of ancient stored carbon. Anyone who uses wood for building holds the carbon fast in the building for decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place that takes up more carbon than it gives off, for example a growing forest or a bog.
Rock made of lime that contains a lot of carbon, for example limestone.
Seawater becomes more acidic because it takes up additional CO2 from the air.
Soft, dark soil made of hardly decomposed plant remains in a bog.

gewusst: A carbon atom in your body may once, long ago, have been part of a dinosaur or a tree.
The white chalk cliffs on some sea coasts consist of the limy shells of billions of tiny sea creatures.
Bogs cover only a small part of the Earth’s land area but store a great deal of carbon.

teile.einleitung: **Laterite** is a red, hard soil of the tropics. It forms when rock weathers over a very long time in a hot, damp climate. It is found in Africa, South America, India and South-East Asia.
wichtigste: Laterite contains mainly iron and aluminium oxides.
It forms through ferrallitisation.
The name comes from the Latin word for brick.
The red colour comes from iron oxides such as haematite.
If exposed laterite dries out repeatedly, it turns into a hard crust.
Bauxite forms in a similar way and is the most important aluminium ore.

abschnitte.text: Laterites form mainly **in the hot, damp tropics**. There it is warm all year round, and it rains a lot. Under these conditions rock **weathers** very deeply and very strongly. This process often takes hundreds of thousands or millions of years. In the end only a remainder of substances is left that hardly dissolve.

In weathering, rainwater washes out many substances, including **silicic acid**. What is left is mainly **iron** and **aluminium** in the form of **oxides**. This soil-forming process is called **ferrallitisation**. The word is made up of ferrum, the Latin word for iron, and aluminium. In addition a lot of **kaolinite** forms. This clay mineral can bind **nutrients** only poorly. That is why strongly weathered tropical soils are often poor in nutrients.

Many laterites are bright **red** or reddish brown. The colour comes from **iron oxides** such as **haematite**. Iron oxide is also known as rust. If more goethite is present, the soil looks more yellow-brown. Red earth roads in Africa or India often consist of lateritic material.

The name **laterite** comes from the Latin word **later**, which means **brick**. Damp laterite can be cut. If it is exposed and **dries out repeatedly**, it **hardens** into a hard crust. That is why it was used as a building stone in India and South-East Asia. For farming this hardening is a problem, because hardly any plants grow on the hard crust.

**Bauxite** forms in a similar way to laterite. It is especially rich in aluminium and is the most important **aluminium ore**. From bauxite, the aluminium for cans, window frames and aeroplanes is obtained. The name bauxite comes from the French place Les Baux, where the rock was described in the 19th century.

gewusst: In some old temples in South-East Asia, laterite was used as a building material.
Laterite can become many metres thick.

teile.einleitung: A compost heap of your own in the garden turns waste into valuable soil. To work well and not stink, it needs the right place, air and the right moisture.
wichtigste: It is best to put a compost heap in partial shade.
It should stand on bare soil, so that worms can get in.
Coarse twigs go right at the bottom.
A compost heap should be as damp as a wrung-out sponge.
Turning it lets air in.
A well-working heap feels warm inside.

abschnitte.text: A compost heap is best placed in **partial shade**, for example under a bush. In full sun it dries out, and in deep shade it stays too wet. It is important that it stands on **bare soil** and not on concrete. In this way earthworms and other soil animals can move in from below, and surplus water can drain away.

Right at the bottom you lay a layer of **coarse twigs**. It makes sure that air gets in from below and water can run off. On top of it you layer damp and dry waste in turn. Large branches are **chopped up** beforehand, because they rot faster that way. Small pieces give the bacteria more surface to work on.

When a compost heap is working well, it feels **warm** inside. The warmth arises because countless bacteria are breaking down the waste. For this they need **moisture**: the heap should feel like a **wrung-out sponge**. But they also need **air**. That is why you turn the heap over now and then, that is, you pile it up anew with a fork.

If a compost heap is too wet, the air is lacking and it begins to **stink**. Then it helps to mix in **dry leaves** or chopped twigs and to loosen the heap. A compost heap is also a habitat. The **hedgehog** likes to seek shelter there and finds worms and beetles. That is why you should be careful when turning it.

gewusst: Inside a large compost heap it can get so warm that steam rises in winter.
A compost bin with a lid is also suitable for small gardens.

teile.einleitung: Humification is the name for the process in which stable humic substances form in the soil from dead plants and animals. It makes the soil dark and fertile and stores a lot of carbon.
wichtigste: In humification, new, stable humic substances form from organic remains.
The opposite process is mineralisation, complete breakdown.
Mull is an active, well-mixed form of humus.
Under acidic conifer forests, raw humus often forms.
Straw has a wide C/N ratio and breaks down slowly.
Soils store more carbon than the atmosphere and plants together.

abschnitte.titel: Building up instead of breaking down
abschnitte.text: When leaves fall or animals die, they are broken down in the soil by living things. One part is broken down completely into **carbon dioxide**, water and mineral salts. This is called **mineralisation**. In the process, nutrients are released again for plants. Another part is converted into new, stable substances, the **humic substances**. This building up is called **humification**.

Humic substances colour the soil **dark** and last a long time. They are classified by their solubility. **Fulvic acids** are relatively small and stay dissolved in acids and alkalis, and they are especially mobile. **Humic acids** dissolve in alkalis but precipitate out in acid. **Humins** are insoluble. An important starting material is **lignin** from wood, which fungi break down only slowly.

Depending on the site, different **forms of humus** arise. **Mull** is very active biologically. Earthworms quickly work the litter in and mix it with the mineral soil. Mull is typical of fertile deciduous woodland and meadow soils. Under acidic **conifer forests**, earthworms are largely absent. Fungi break down the litter slowly, and a thick layer of **raw humus** forms.

How quickly material is broken down depends on the **C/N ratio**, that is, the ratio of carbon to nitrogen. **Cereal straw** contains a lot of carbon and little nitrogen. The microorganisms then lack nitrogen and break it down only slowly. People also distinguish **nutrient humus**, which is broken down quickly and quickly supplies nutrients, from **stable humus**, which lasts for decades to centuries and improves the soil structure.

abschnitte.titel: The soil as a carbon store
abschnitte.text: Worldwide, more **carbon** is bound in the humus of soils than in the **atmosphere** and in all **plants** together. That is why soils play a big part in the climate. When humus is built up, carbon dioxide is taken from the air. When it is broken down, for example when bogs are drained or the soil is worked intensively, carbon dioxide goes into the air.

gewusst: The dark colour of fertile arable soils comes largely from humic substances.
Some humic substances in the soil are hundreds to thousands of years old.

teile.einleitung: What we flush down the toilet, shower and basin does not end up directly in the stream. First it flows into a sewage treatment plant, which cleans the waste water in several stages.
wichtigste: In Switzerland a sewage treatment plant is called an ARA, which stands for “Abwasserreinigungsanlage”.
The screen holds back coarse material such as paper and rags.
In the grit chamber, sand and small stones settle out.
In the aeration tank, bacteria break down the dirt and need oxygen to do so.
Phosphate is precipitated with iron salts.
In the digester tower, biogas is produced from sewage sludge.
Since 2006, sewage sludge in Switzerland has been burned.

abschnitte.text: First the waste water flows through a **screen**. It holds back coarse things, such as wet wipes, paper or plastic. Then comes the **grit chamber**: there the water flows more slowly, and heavy particles such as sand and small stones sink to the bottom. In the primary settling tank, further suspended matter settles out. This stage therefore cleans the water purely mechanically, without chemicals and without living things.

In the **aeration tank**, countless **bacteria** are at work. They eat the dissolved dirt and convert it. So that they work well, air is blown into the tank, because the bacteria need **oxygen**. Then the water flows into the secondary settling tank. There the flocs of bacteria sink to the bottom and are separated off as sludge.

Phosphate from detergents and human waste would greatly promote the growth of algae in lakes. That is why **iron salts** are added to the water. They bind the phosphate into flocs that settle. This process is called **precipitation**. Many Swiss sewage plants also have an additional stage against **micropollutants** such as drug residues. They work with **ozone** or **activated carbon**.

The separated **sewage sludge** goes into the **digester tower**. There bacteria break it down without air, and **biogas** is produced. With it the plant generates electricity and heat for its own operation. In the past, sewage sludge was spread on fields as fertiliser. But because it can contain pollutants, this has been forbidden in Switzerland since 2006, and the sludge is burned.

A sewage plant cannot filter everything out. Wet wipes, cotton buds and food scraps therefore belong in the bin, not in the toilet. Old medicines are taken back to the pharmacy, paints and oils to the collection point. Almost all households in Switzerland are connected to a sewage plant. Thanks to it, today you can swim again in many Swiss lakes and rivers.

gewusst: In the 1960s, swimming in some Swiss lakes was forbidden because of polluted water.
In Switzerland, people want in future to recover phosphorus from sewage sludge ash, because it is an important fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: The jet stream is a strong band of wind high in the atmosphere. It blows at a height of about 8 to 12 kilometres like an invisible river of air around the Earth. It affects our weather and even how long a flight takes.
wichtigste: The jet stream is a strong band of wind high in the atmosphere.
It usually blows at a height of 8 to 12 kilometres.
The winds often reach more than 200 kilometres per hour.
The jet stream blows around the Earth from west to east.
It arises where warm and cold air masses meet.
It steers high and low pressure areas and thus our weather.
Aeroplanes use it as a tailwind to save fuel.

abschnitte.text: A jet stream is a narrow but very fast **band of strong wind**. It is a few hundred kilometres wide but only a few kilometres thick. It lies just below the **tropopause**, the boundary between the lowest layer of air and the next. You cannot see it, but sometimes long streaks of thin cloud show where it runs.

At the equator the air is warm, at the poles it is cold. Where these air masses meet, a large **temperature difference** arises. This difference and the rotation of the Earth drive the wind at great height towards the east. In this way a **polar front jet stream** forms in each hemisphere, and closer to the equator a subtropical jet stream.

The jet stream does not run dead straight but in large waves and loops around the Earth. These waves are called **Rossby waves**. Sometimes the loops stay in the same place for a long time. Then it can be hot and dry in Europe for weeks, or wet for weeks. In winter the jet stream is usually stronger than in summer, because the temperature differences are greater.

The jet stream steers the **low pressure areas** that move from the Atlantic to Europe. When it lies over central Europe, lows bring wind, cloud and rain to Switzerland. If it shifts northwards, a stable high with sunshine can hold over us. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss therefore watch the jet stream closely.

Many airliners fly at exactly the height at which the jet stream blows. A flight from North America to Europe is often clearly shorter with a **tailwind** than the return flight. Pilots plan their route so that they use the jet stream or avoid it. At the edge of the jet stream, however, it can get bumpy, which is called turbulence.

As early as the 1920s, the Japanese researcher Wasaburo Oishi measured very strong winds at great height with weather balloons. But the jet stream only became well known in the Second World War. At that time American bombers flew so high that they were suddenly slowed down by a huge **headwind**. Today, weather satellites and aeroplanes measure the jet stream every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: The envelope of air that surrounds the Earth.
The boundary between the lowest layer of air, in which the weather happens, and the layer above it.
An area of low air pressure that often brings cloud, wind and rain.
Unsettled, swirling air that can shake an aeroplane.

gewusst: In the core of the jet stream, the wind can reach more than 400 kilometres per hour, faster than a high-speed train.
Because of the jet stream, a flight from New York to Zurich usually takes about an hour less than the flight in the opposite direction.
In 1999, the Swiss Bertrand Piccard and the Briton Brian Jones were the first to fly around the world non-stop in a balloon, carried by jet streams.

teile.einleitung: A habitat is a place where particular plants and animals find everything they need to live, that is food, water, shelter and room for their young. Forests, bogs, lakes, hedgerows, deserts and alpine pastures are examples of very different habitats. Every living thing is especially adapted to its habitat.
wichtigste: A habitat offers living things food, protection and room for their young.
Experts also speak of a biotope or a habitat.
Every species of plant and animal is adapted to its habitat; the cactus, for example, stores water in its thick stem.
A raised bog is supplied with water by rain alone.
In 1987 the Swiss electorate accepted the Rothenthurm Initiative to protect bogs.
Above the tree line in the Alps lies the alpine zone with alpine pastures and dwarf shrubs.
Hedgerows offer animals food, nesting places and hiding places.

abschnitte.text: A habitat is an area with particular conditions such as temperature, light, water and soil. The technical words for it are **biotope**, which in Greek means roughly “place of life”, and **habitat**. A habitat and the plants and animals living there together form an **ecosystem**. A habitat can be huge like an ocean or tiny like a puddle or a tree stump.

In the course of evolution, living things have developed special features that suit their habitat. The **cactus** stores water in its thick stem and has spines instead of leaves, so that it loses little water in the desert. The polar bear has dense fur and a thick layer of fat against the cold of the Arctic. Fish breathe with **gills** so that they can use the oxygen from the water.

A **raised bog** is supplied with water by rain alone and is therefore very poor in nutrients. Mainly peat mosses grow here, and specialists such as the sundew, which catches small insects. A fen, by contrast, also receives groundwater or spring water. Because the greater part of the bogs in Switzerland have been drained since 1800, the electorate in 1987 accepted the **Rothenthurm Initiative**, which places bogs under strict protection.

In the Alps, habitats change with height, which is called **altitudinal zones**. At the bottom lie deciduous and mixed forests, higher up coniferous forests with spruces, larches and Swiss stone pines. Above the tree line, which mostly lies between about 1,800 and 2,300 metres, the **alpine zone** begins, with alpine pastures and dwarf shrubs such as the alpenrose. Marmots, ibexes and ptarmigans live here.

Landscapes shaped by people also offer valuable habitats. **Hedgerows** between fields give birds, hedgehogs, weasels and insects food, nesting places and hiding places. They also connect different habitats like a green network, so that animals can move about. Dry-stone walls, flower meadows, orchards and ponds are also small but important habitats.

Many habitats are becoming smaller or are being cut up by building, roads, intensive farming and climate change. As a result animals and plants lose their place to live, and **biodiversity** declines. In Switzerland, bogs, floodplains, dry meadows and waters are especially at risk. Protected areas such as the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine, restored streams and new hedgerows help to preserve habitats.

begriffe.erklaerung: A habitat with particular conditions, in which typical plants and animals live.
A habitat together with all the living things that live in it and affect one another.
The height in the mountains above which no closed forest grows any more.
The variety of living things, habitats and genes.

gewusst: A single old tree can be a habitat for hundreds of different insects, fungi and birds.
The Rothenthurm Initiative is named after a raised bog in the canton of Schwyz, where a military training ground was to be built.
Even in hot springs and in eternal ice there are living things that are adapted exactly to these extreme habitats.

teile.einleitung: Diatoms are tiny algae that live in a shell of glass. They are found in seas, lakes, streams and even on damp stones. Although you can see them only under a microscope, they are very important for life on Earth.
wichtigste: Diatoms have a shell of silicon dioxide, the frustule.
The shell consists of two halves like a box with a lid.
With many divisions, some of the cells get smaller and smaller.
An auxospore restores the original size.
Fucoxanthin gives them their golden-brown colour.
They store oil and chrysolaminarin instead of starch.
From fossil shells, diatomaceous earth forms.

abschnitte.text: Diatoms build their cell wall from **silicon dioxide**, the substance of which glass is also made. This casing is called the **frustule**. It consists of a larger upper shell, the **epitheca**, and a slightly smaller lower shell, the **hypotheca**. The two fit into each other like a **box with a lid**. Fine pores and patterns on the shell help to identify the species.

In cell division, each daughter cell forms a new, smaller **lower shell** inside the old half of the shell. As a result, some of the cells get smaller with every division. When a critical minimum size is reached, an **auxospore** forms. It grows without a rigid shell and afterwards forms a large cell again.

Traditionally, diatoms are divided by the **symmetry** of their shell. **Centric** forms are radially symmetrical and often round like a tin. **Pennate** forms are elongated and bilaterally symmetrical. Many pennate diatoms have a lengthwise slit in the shell, the **raphe**. By releasing mucus, they glide slowly over surfaces with it.

Diatoms carry out **photosynthesis**. Their golden-brown colour comes from the pigment **fucoxanthin**. It covers the green of the chlorophyll and helps to catch light in the blue-green range. Instead of starch, diatoms store **oil droplets** and the soluble carbohydrate **chrysolaminarin**. They are an important food for many small water animals.

When diatoms die, their shells sink to the bottom. Over a long time, **diatomaceous earth**, also called **diatomite**, forms from them. This is a fine, porous rock. **Alfred Nobel** used it to soak up nitroglycerin, and in this way invented **dynamite**. Today diatomaceous earth is used, for example, as a filter material.

gewusst: Diatoms produce a large part of the oxygen on Earth, and estimates speak of about a fifth.
In Switzerland, the water quality of streams and rivers is assessed with the help of diatoms.

teile.einleitung: Wood is a valuable raw material that can be used several times in a row. In cascade use, wood is first used as a material and burned only at the very end. This spares the forest and helps the climate.
wichtigste: In cascade use, wood is used as a material for as long as possible.
Only at the very end is it burned.
A typical sequence is: roof beam, chipboard, heating plant.
As long as wood is in use, the carbon stays stored in it.
One cubic metre of timber used in building binds about one tonne of CO2.
If wood replaces concrete, steel or heating oil, emissions are saved as well.
Contaminated waste wood belongs in special plants.

abschnitte.text: A **cascade** is a waterfall in several steps. In **cascade use**, the wood flows, so to speak, down step by step. First it is put to high-value use, for example as **construction timber** or for furniture. After that it is reused or recycled into materials. Only at the end is the energy in the wood used, by burning it.

A **roof beam** stands in a house for many decades. If the house is pulled down, the waste wood can be turned into chips and made into **chipboard**. For chipboard, small pieces of wood are enough, so waste wood and sawdust are suitable. **Glued laminated timber** and solid wood, by contrast, need fresh sawn timber. If the chipboard is no longer usable either, it is burned in a **heating plant**.

As trees grow, they take **CO2** from the air and store the **carbon** in the wood. One cubic metre of softwood contains about a quarter of a tonne of carbon. That corresponds to around **one tonne of CO2**. As long as the wood is used as a product, the carbon stays bound. Repeated use lengthens this storage time.

Wood can replace materials or fuels that cause a lot of CO2, such as **concrete**, **steel** or **heating oil**. This effect is called **substitution**, which means replacement. It comes on top of the storage effect in the wood. If wood is burned too early, on the other hand, it is lost as a material. That is why burning should come only when no sensible use as a material is possible any more.

abschnitte.titel: Take care with contaminated waste wood
abschnitte.text: Some waste wood has been treated with **paints** or **wood preservatives**. These can contain poisonous substances. If you burn such wood in an ordinary stove, **pollutants** are released. That is why contaminated waste wood belongs in special plants with **flue gas cleaning**. In Switzerland, burning waste in your own stove is forbidden.

gewusst: About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest.
Paper can also be a step in the cascade: waste paper is often recycled several times before the fibres become too short.

teile.einleitung: In hybrid breeding, two different, true-breeding parent lines of a plant are crossed. The first daughter generation, the F1, is often stronger and higher-yielding than both parents.
wichtigste: For hybrids, true-breeding inbred lines are crossed.
The special performance of the F1 is called heterosis.
If you sow seeds from F1 plants, the characteristics split up.
That is why hybrid seed has to be bought again every year.
Hybrid maize greatly raised yields in the USA.
On seed packets, hybrid seed is marked “F1”.

abschnitte.text: First, **inbred lines** are bred. These are plants that have been pollinated only with themselves over several generations and are therefore largely **true-breeding**. If two different inbred lines are crossed, the **F1** results, the first daughter generation. As described by Gregor Mendel’s **law of uniformity**, the F1 plants are very **uniform**. The abbreviation **F1** is also printed on seed packets in the shops.

Often the F1 surpasses both parents in growth and yield. This effect is called **heterosis**. But it is lost in the next generation. If you sow seeds from F1 plants, the characteristics **split up** according to Mendel. The plants become uneven, and the special performance disappears. That is why farmers and gardeners buy **hybrid seed** again every year.

Around **1908**, the researcher **George Harrison Shull** showed with **maize** that inbreeding weakens the plants. Crossing two inbred lines, however, gave strong plants. This laid the foundation for hybrid breeding. In the **USA**, **hybrid maize** took hold from the 1930s. Yields per hectare then rose sharply.

In seed production, the mother line may receive only pollen from the father line. With maize, the **male flower tassels** at the top of the mother plants are removed for this. This is called **detasselling**. It can be done without hand labour using **cytoplasmic male sterility**: such plants do not produce functioning pollen and are therefore only cross-pollinated.

The father of **hybrid rice** is considered to be the Chinese agricultural scientist **Yuan Longping**. In the **1970s** he developed the first high-yielding hybrid rice varieties. As a result, significantly more people could be fed in China from the same area. Today there are also hybrid varieties of vegetables such as tomatoes, cucumbers and cabbage.

gewusst: A large part of the maize grown in Europe and North America today comes from hybrid seed.
If you keep and sow seeds from an F1 tomato, you usually get plants that all look quite different.

teile.einleitung: Seasons are the parts of a year with typical weather, light and temperatures. In Switzerland there are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. They arise because the Earth’s axis is tilted relative to the Sun.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there are four seasons.
Winter is followed by spring, and spring by summer.
In autumn, many nuts and apples are ripe.
In winter many plants rest, and it can snow.
Seasons arise because the Earth’s axis is tilted relative to the Sun.
In the Southern Hemisphere the seasons are exactly the other way round.
In the tropics, people distinguish rather between a rainy season and a dry season.

abschnitte.text: The Earth goes around the Sun once in a year. Its **axis** is tilted at an angle of about 23 degrees. In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun stands high and shines for a long time, and then it is summer here. In December, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, the days are short, and it is winter.

In **spring**, the days get longer and warmer, trees put out leaves and many flowers bloom. Migratory birds return, and many animals have young. In summer the days are longest, fields ripen and the grain is harvested. In Switzerland it is then the time for swimming, hiking and the summer on the alpine pastures.

In **autumn**, many fruits ripen, for example apples, pears, grapes and nuts. The deciduous trees turn their leaves colourful and drop them. In winter many plants rest, some animals hibernate, and it can snow. In the Swiss mountains, the winter sports season then begins.

Astronomically, spring begins around 20 March, when day and night are equally long. Summer begins around 21 June with the longest day, the **solstice**. Autumn starts around 22 or 23 September and winter on 21 December with the shortest day. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss calculate more simply and let the seasons begin on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December.

In the **Southern Hemisphere**, for example in Australia or Argentina, it is exactly the other way round. When it is winter here, it is summer there, and at Christmas people go swimming. Close to the equator it is warm all year round, and people distinguish a rainy season and a dry season. In the polar regions there is the midnight sun in summer and the polar night lasting months in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole around which the Earth turns.
The day with the longest or the shortest daylight of the year.
A day in spring or autumn on which day and night are about equally long.
The half of the Earth south of the equator.

gewusst: In January the Earth is actually a little closer to the Sun than in July, so the seasons do not depend on distance.
In Zurich, the longest day of the year is over seven hours longer than the shortest.

teile.einleitung: Climate describes what the weather is normally like in a place over many years. Weather is short-term and can change every hour, whereas climate is the long-term average. Whether it is mostly hot, cold, dry or wet somewhere depends on the climate.
wichtigste: Weather is short-term, climate is the long-term average of the weather.
Experts usually calculate the climate from measurements over 30 years.
The Earth is divided into climate zones, from the tropics to the polar regions.
Climate depends on the sun’s radiation, altitude, the sea and the winds.
Switzerland lies in the temperate climate zone with four seasons.
In the mountains it is colder, and per 100 metres of height the temperature falls by about half a degree.
Through greenhouse gases, humans are changing the Earth’s climate.

abschnitte.text: The **weather** describes what it is like outside right now: sunny, rainy, warm or windy. The **climate**, by contrast, is the typical weather of a place over many years. For this, experts add up measurements such as temperature, precipitation and hours of sunshine, usually over 30 years. A cold summer day therefore says nothing about the climate, but an average over decades does.

Because the sun shines steeply on the Earth at the equator and at a shallow angle at the poles, it is not equally warm everywhere. That is why the Earth is divided into **climate zones**: tropics, subtropics, temperate zone and polar regions. In the tropics it is warm all year round, and in the rainforest also very damp. In the subtropics lie many large deserts such as the Sahara. In the polar regions it stays icy cold almost all year.

Besides the position on the Earth, mountains, seas and winds also influence the climate. By the sea, summer and winter are milder, because water stores heat well. Inland, the differences are greater, which is called a **continental climate**. The higher a place lies, the colder it is, which is why there is snow even in summer on high mountains. Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream bring Europe extra warmth.

Switzerland lies in the temperate zone and has four clear seasons. Westerly winds often bring damp air from the Atlantic, which is why it rains regularly here. The Alps divide the country into climate regions: in Ticino, south of the Alps, it is milder and sunnier than on the Central Plateau. Inner-Alpine valleys such as the Valais are especially dry. A typical wind is the **foehn**, a warm, dry downslope wind.

Since industrialisation, people have been burning a lot of coal, oil and natural gas. This produces **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas that holds heat back in the atmosphere. That is why the Earth is getting warmer. In Switzerland, the temperature has risen about twice as strongly as the world average since measurements began in 1864. The consequences are melting glaciers, hotter summers and less snow at low altitudes.

In the **Paris Agreement** of 2015, almost all countries committed themselves to keeping warming well below 2 degrees. Switzerland, too, wants to emit no more greenhouse gases by 2050 than are removed from the air again. Everyone can help, for example with cycling, trains, saving energy and less waste. Researchers at MeteoSwiss and universities measure and study the climate closely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large region of the Earth with a similar climate, for example the tropics.
Water that falls from the sky, that is, rain, snow or hail.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that holds heat in the Earth’s envelope of air.
A warm, dry wind that blows from the mountains into the valley.

gewusst: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be about minus 18 degrees on average.
From air bubbles in the ancient ice of Antarctica, researchers can read off the climate of hundreds of thousands of years ago.
In Switzerland, palms grow in Ticino, while on the Jungfraujoch there is ice all year round.

teile.einleitung: The coloured leaves of a flower are called **petals**. They make a flower beautiful and eye-catching. Their most important job is to attract insects.
wichtigste: Petals are the coloured leaves of a flower.
All the petals together are called the corolla.
Their colours attract pollinators such as bees.
A rape flower has 4 petals, an apple blossom 5.
After pollination the petals wilt and fall off.
Rose oil is obtained from rose petals.

abschnitte.text: A typical flower consists of several parts. On the outside there are usually green **sepals**. They protect the bud. Then come the coloured **petals**. All the petals together form the **corolla**. In the middle stand the stamens with the pollen and the pistil.

Petals are conspicuously coloured to attract **pollinators**. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies fly to the flowers and fetch nectar. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower. Bees also see **ultraviolet light**. Many flowers have patterns that are visible only in UV light. They show the insects the way to the nectar. After pollination the plant no longer needs the petals. They **wilt** and fall off.

The number of petals helps in identifying plants. **Crucifers** such as rape have **4** petals. The corn poppy also has four. Rose-family plants such as the **apple blossom** and the wild **dog rose** have **5** petals. Garden roses often have many more, because they were bred that way.

The **corn poppy** has bright red, thin petals that look almost like tissue paper. The **cornflower** blooms bright blue. Both often grew in cornfields in the past. In Switzerland they are now sown again in flower strips at the edge of fields. There they offer insects food.

From the petals of some flowers, **fragrant oils** are obtained. Especially well known is **rose oil**. The flowers are picked early in the morning and boiled out with steam. For a little oil you need huge amounts of flowers. Rose oil is used for perfume and cosmetics.

gewusst: For one kilogram of rose oil you need several tonnes of rose petals.
On flowers, bees see patterns made of UV light that are invisible to humans.

teile.einleitung: The hook-and-loop fastener holds shoes, jackets and bags together and can still be opened with a tug. It was invented by a Swiss man who looked closely when plant fruits stuck to his dog’s fur.
wichtigste: The hook-and-loop fastener was invented by the Swiss engineer George de Mestral.
The model was the fruits of the burdock, which stick in fur with tiny hooks.
A hook-and-loop fastener consists of one tape with hooks and one tape with loops.
Today the tapes are mostly made of plastic such as nylon.
Copying ideas from nature is called biomimetics.
In the doctor’s surgery, a hook-and-loop strap closes the cuff for measuring blood pressure.

abschnitte.text: George de Mestral came from western Switzerland. After an outing with his dog, he noticed that burrs were hanging everywhere in its fur and on his clothes. Curious, he looked at the fruits under the microscope. There he saw many small, elastic hooks. These catch in hairs and fabric fibres. This gave him the idea for a new kind of fastener.

A hook-and-loop fastener has two sides. On one side sit thousands of tiny **hooks**, on the other many small **loops**. If you press the two sides together, the hooks grip into the loops. If you pull hard, the hooks bend open and come free again. Because the plastic is flexible, the fastener can be opened and closed very many times.

When people copy inventions from plants and animals, this is called **biomimetics**. In German the word, “Bionik”, is made up of biology and technology. The hook-and-loop fastener is one of the best-known examples. The burdock itself uses its hooks so that animals carry its fruits far away. In this way the plant can spread to new places.

You find hook-and-loop fasteners on children’s shoes, jackets, rucksacks and sports kit. They are practical, because you do not have to tie shoelaces. In the doctor’s surgery, the **blood pressure cuff** is closed around the upper arm with one, so it fits every arm. Hook-and-loop tape has also been used in space travel, so that objects do not float away in weightlessness.

gewusst: The brand name Velcro is made up of the French words “velours” (velvet) and “crochet” (hook).
