Until the fastener worked well, de Mestral tinkered with suitable materials for several years.

teile.einleitung: When forests are cleared, bogs are drained or meadows are built over, plants and animals lose their habitat. Worldwide, this habitat loss is regarded as one of the most important causes of the decline in biodiversity. In Switzerland too it is a big issue.
wichtigste: Habitat loss is a main cause of species decline.
Soil sealing means that soil is covered with asphalt or concrete.
Alpine pastures that are no longer used become overgrown with scrub and then forest.
Old trees with holes are living space for woodpeckers and owls.
In South-East Asia, rainforest is cleared for oil palm plantations.
Bogs are home to specialised species and store a lot of carbon.

abschnitte.text: For houses, roads and car parks, soil is covered with **asphalt or concrete**. This is called **soil sealing**. Sealed soil can no longer take up water. Plants and soil animals no longer find room there. Roads and settlements also **cut up** habitats. For animals such as hedgehogs, toads or deer they become dangerous borders.

Worldwide, large areas of forest are disappearing. In Indonesia and Malaysia a lot of **rainforest** is cleared for **oil palm plantations** to obtain palm oil. In the process orangutans and many other species lose their home. Here at home too, every old tree counts. **Hollow trees** and dead wood offer woodpeckers, owls, bats and beetles living space. Young trees have such holes only after decades.

In the past many **bogs** were drained to gain fields or to cut peat. Bogs are home to specialised plants such as the **sundew** and many rare insects. They also store a lot of **carbon**. In Switzerland a large part of the former bogs has disappeared. Since the **Rothenthurm Initiative** was accepted in 1987, bogs have been protected in the Federal Constitution.

Less use can also destroy habitat. If remote **alpine pastures** are no longer grazed or mown, they become **overgrown with scrub** and later turn into forest. Light-loving flowers and their insects then disappear. **Global warming** has an effect as well: species that love the cold move upwards. Higher up, however, there is less area, and at the summit it is the end of the line.

Protected areas, hedgerows, flower meadows and nature-friendly gardens create new habitats. **Networking** is important so that animals can get from one area to the next. For this, people build, for example, **wildlife bridges** over motorways. Small things help too, such as a pile of branches or a pond in the garden.

gewusst: The sundew from the bog catches small insects with sticky droplets.
For mountain plants a summit is a dead end: they cannot move any higher.

teile.einleitung: Honey is a sweet food that bees make from nectar or honeydew. For the bees it is the store for the winter, and for us humans it is a popular spread for bread.
wichtigste: Bees make honey mainly from the nectar of flowers.
Dark forest honey is made from honeydew.
The bees store the honey in the cells of the honeycomb.
Honey is the bees’ winter supply.
The beekeeper gets the honey out of the combs with a honey extractor.
Honey consists mostly of sugar and often turns solid with time.

abschnitte.text: Bees suck **nectar** out of flowers with their tongue. This is a sweet juice. In the hive they pass it on to other bees. These add substances from their bodies and let water evaporate. This makes the juice thicker and it becomes **honey**. Then the bees fill it into the cells of the **honeycomb** and seal them with **wax**.

Honey made from nectar is called **blossom honey**. But there is also **forest honey**. It is darker and stronger in taste. Forest honey is made from **honeydew**. This is a sweet juice that aphids give off on trees such as firs and spruces. The bees collect it in the same way as nectar.

In winter there are no flowers. The bees then stay in the hive and eat their **honey store**. This is how the bee colony survives the cold season. When the beekeeper harvests honey, he has to leave the bees enough food or give them sugar water. Otherwise they would starve in winter.

A person who keeps bees is called a **beekeeper**. He takes the full combs out of the beehive and opens the wax caps. Then he puts the combs into the **honey extractor**. It spins quickly, and the honey sprays out. After that it is strained and filled into jars. Runny honey often turns **solid** with time, because the sugar forms **crystals**. This is quite normal.

gewusst: Honey hardly ever goes off, because it contains very little water and a great deal of sugar.
Honey should not be given to small children under one year old.

teile.einleitung: Jasmonic acid is a plant hormone. It helps plants to defend themselves against enemies that eat them, such as caterpillars. It gets its name from jasmine.
wichtigste: Jasmonic acid is made from the fatty acid alpha-linolenic acid.
Its methyl ester was first found in the fragrant oil of jasmine.
The truly active signal form is jasmonoyl-isoleucine.
Methyl jasmonate is volatile and can warn neighbouring plants.
Wounded tomatoes make proteinase inhibitors via the signal.
Salicylic acid often acts as an opponent of jasmonic acid.

abschnitte.titel: A hormone with a fragrant name
abschnitte.text: **Jasmonic acid** is a **plant hormone**, that is, a messenger substance that passes on signals inside the plant. Its name comes from **jasmine**: in the fragrant oil of this plant, its **methyl ester**, **methyl jasmonate**, was found. Jasmonic acid is made from the fatty acid **alpha-linolenic acid**, which occurs in the cell membranes of plants. The related substances are together called **jasmonates**.

When a caterpillar feeds on a tomato leaf, a small protein is released: **systemin**. In **1991** it was described as the first **peptide hormone** of plants. Systemin triggers the jasmonate defence. The truly active signal form is **jasmonoyl-isoleucine**, a compound of jasmonic acid and a protein building block.

Via the jasmonate signal, the wounded tomato makes **proteinase inhibitors**. These disturb the digestion of the caterpillars, so that they grow worse. The **tobacco plant** makes more **nicotine** after feeding damage, which is poisonous to many insects. In this way the plant protects itself, even though it cannot run away.

**Methyl jasmonate** is **volatile**, so it evaporates into the air. Neighbouring plants can take it up and prepare their defences before an enemy reaches them. Against some disease organisms, by contrast, **salicylic acid** mainly acts. It controls the defence against **biotrophic** pathogens, which live on living tissue. Salicylic acid and jasmonic acid often act as **opponents**.

gewusst: Jasmonic acid occurs in very many plants, not only in jasmine.
Plants can even use volatile substances to attract beneficial insects that eat their enemies.

teile.einleitung: Josias Braun-Blanquet was a botanist from the Grisons. He is regarded as one of the founders of phytosociology, the study of plant communities. His method is still used all over the world today.
wichtigste: Josias Braun-Blanquet was born in Chur in 1884.
In Montpellier he studied under the botanist Charles Flahault.
In 1928 his textbook “Pflanzensoziologie” appeared.
With Eduard Rübel he wrote the “Flora von Graubünden”.
In 1930 he founded the research station SIGMA in Montpellier.
He took the second part of his name, Blanquet, from his wife.

abschnitte.text: Josias Braun was born in **1884** in **Chur**. Even when young he was interested in the plants of the Grisons mountains. In **Montpellier** in southern France he studied under the botanist **Charles Flahault**. He married Gabrielle Blanquet and afterwards called himself **Braun-Blanquet**. So the second part of his name comes from his **wife’s family name**.

Braun-Blanquet noticed that certain plants keep occurring together. Such groups are called **plant communities**. In 1928 his textbook **“Pflanzensoziologie”** appeared. Species that are typical of a community are called **characteristic species**. He arranged the communities into a system. Names of **associations** end in “-etum”, names of **alliances** in “-ion”.

For his method, a **sample plot** is chosen, for example a piece of meadow. All the plant species growing there are written down. For each species, you **estimate** how much area it covers. This **vegetation survey** can be compared with others. That way you can see which communities exist and how they differ.

Together with **Eduard Rübel**, Braun-Blanquet wrote the **“Flora von Graubünden”**. In **1930** he founded the research station **SIGMA** in Montpellier. Experts from many countries worked there. His way of working is also called the Zurich-Montpellier school. He died in 1980 in Montpellier.

gewusst: Braun-Blanquet’s method is still used today in nature conservation and research around the world.
Josias Braun-Blanquet lived to be over 95.

teile.einleitung: High up on mountain meadows blooms a small orchid that looks almost black and smells of vanilla: the black vanilla orchid, called “Kohlröschen” or “Männertreu” in German. If you find it, you may admire it, but not pick it.
wichtigste: The black vanilla orchid is also called “Männertreu” in German.
Its flowers are very dark red, almost black.
It smells of vanilla.
It is an orchid and grows about 10 to 20 centimetres tall.
It grows on mountain meadows and alpine pastures and is protected in many places.

abschnitte.text: The **black vanilla orchid** is a small plant about 10 to 20 centimetres tall. Its many tiny flowers sit tightly together in a small **head**. The colour is a **very dark red** that looks almost black from a distance. That is where the German name “Kohlröschen” comes from, which recalls coal, “Kohle”. Especially on warm days it gives off a strong scent of **vanilla**.

The black vanilla orchid grows on sunny **mountain meadows** and **alpine pastures** in the Alps. It needs poor soils that are not heavily fertilised. If meadows are fertilised too much or are no longer mown and grazed, it disappears. With its scent it attracts butterflies, which pollinate its flowers.

The black vanilla orchid belongs to the **orchid** family. Like many orchids, it is sensitive and grows only slowly. In Switzerland and in many other countries, orchids are under **protection**. That is why you should not pick or dig up the black vanilla orchid. A photo is the best souvenir.

gewusst: Orchid seeds are as fine as dust and can germinate only with the help of certain fungi in the soil.

teile.einleitung: Stone piles are heaps of stones that farmers have gathered from their fields. For many animals they are a valuable habitat. Today such piles are also deliberately built anew in nature conservation.
wichtigste: The stones were picked off arable fields and meadows.
Stone piles are among the small structures.
Weasels hide in them from enemies.
The smooth snake loves sunny stone piles.
New piles should lie partly in the ground, so that animals can overwinter free of frost.
Around them an unmown herb margin is left standing.

abschnitte.text: When ploughing, **stones** keep coming up to the surface in fields. The farmers collected them, in German they “read” them off, which is where the word **Lesesteine** comes from. Then they piled the stones up at the edge of the field. In this way **stone piles** arose. If the stones were stacked along field boundaries, long, narrow banks arose. Such **stone ridges** shape some landscapes to this day.

In the gaps between the stones, animals find **hiding places**, sunning spots and winter quarters. **Lizards** warm themselves on the sunny stones. The harmless **smooth snake** hunts there, mainly lizards. It gets its name from its smooth scales. Small predators such as the **stoat** and the **least weasel** are protected in stone piles from birds of prey and foxes.

For a new stone pile you use mainly **larger stones**. Between them many **hollows** stay open, which serve as hiding places. The pile should be partly **sunk into the ground**. In the ground, it freezes less deep than at the surface. In this way animals deep in the pile find a **frost-free winter shelter**. A sunny spot is best.

Stone piles, piles of branches, hedgerows or pools are called **small structures** in nature conservation. They are small, but very important for many species. Around the stone pile an **unmown herb margin** is left standing. It offers cover and food. In this way animals can move unseen between the pile and the surroundings. In Switzerland, conservation organisations and farmers promote such structures.

gewusst: In winter a stoat wears a white coat, and only the tip of its tail stays black.
The smooth snake is harmless to people and has no poison fangs.

teile.einleitung: Invasive species are introduced plants or animals that spread strongly in a new area and push out native species. Many came to us with trade, as garden plants or as stowaways. In Switzerland, some of them are deliberately controlled.
wichtigste: Invasive species are introduced species that push out native ones.
Plants introduced after 1492 are called neophytes.
In the new area, invasive species often lack their natural enemies.
Common ragweed must be controlled in Switzerland because of its allergenic pollen.
The sap of giant hogweed causes severe skin burns in sunlight.
Since 1 September 2024, cherry laurel may no longer be sold in Switzerland.
Not every introduced species is invasive, and many do no harm.

abschnitte.text: Species that humans have brought into a new area are called **non-native**. Most of them hardly attract attention. But when such a species spreads strongly and causes damage, it counts as **invasive**. It can push out native plants, spread diseases or damage buildings.

In botany, the year 1492, when Columbus reached America, separates old and new arrivals. Plants that came to us before then, such as many arable weeds, are called **archaeophytes**. Plants that were only introduced afterwards are called **neophytes**. From 1492 on, trade and seafaring brought especially many new species across the oceans.

**Himalayan balsam** flings its seeds several metres and forms dense stands on stream banks. Japanese knotweed forms deep rootstocks that can damage bank reinforcements and road surfaces. Giant hogweed grows up to three metres tall, and its sap, together with sunlight, causes severe skin burns. Common ragweed has strongly allergenic pollen and must be reported and controlled in Switzerland.

One important explanation is the **enemy release hypothesis**. It says that in the new area the natural enemies are missing, that is, insects, fungi or diseases that keep the species in check in its home region. In addition, many invasive species grow very quickly and produce many seeds. Climate change also helps some warmth-loving species.

The specialist body Info Flora keeps lists of invasive neophytes in Switzerland. Since 1 September 2024, for example, **cherry laurel**, butterfly bush and tree of heaven may no longer be sold. Municipalities and volunteers pull out invasive plants before they produce seeds. Animals such as the Asian tiger mosquito, the Asian hornet or the quagga mussel in Swiss lakes are also regarded as invasive.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant that was brought into a new area by humans after 1492.
A plant that was introduced by humans before 1492.
A species that already lives naturally in an area.
Animals, fungi or diseases that naturally keep a species in check.

gewusst: Many invasive plants were originally planted in gardens as beautiful ornamental plants.
Parts of invasive neophytes do not belong on the garden compost heap but in the general waste, so that they do not spread further.

teile.einleitung: The **crocus** is one of the first heralds of spring. Often it blooms while snow still lies nearby. One special species of crocus supplies the expensive spice saffron.
wichtigste: A crocus grows from a corm in the ground.
Many crocuses bloom violet, others white or yellow.
Its leaves are narrow like grass.
In rain and in the evening, the flowers close.
From the red threads of the saffron crocus, the spice saffron is made.
In the Valais village of Mund, saffron is grown.

abschnitte.text: In the garden, most crocuses bloom in **early spring**, often as early as February or March. The crocus grows from a **corm**. In it it has stored nutrients. In this way it can sprout very early, when it is still cold. Its leaves are **narrow like grass** and often have a pale stripe in the middle. The crocus belongs to the iris family.

Many crocuses bloom **violet**. But there are also white, yellow and striped varieties. The flower has the shape of a goblet. In sun it opens wide. In the **evening** and in **rain** it closes. In this way it protects its flower parts from wet and cold. Early in the year, crocuses are an important food for bees and bumblebees.

In Switzerland **wild crocuses** also grow. In spring they turn many **mountain meadows** into a sea of flowers dotted white and violet. They often bloom right at the edge of melting snowfields. In the mountains their flowering season begins later than in the lowlands, depending on height only in May or June.

The spice **saffron** comes from the **saffron crocus**. It blooms not in spring but in autumn. As a spice, only the **red threads** in the middle of the flower are used. These are the stigmas, and each flower has only three of them. They are picked by hand. For one kilogram of saffron you need over a hundred thousand flowers. That is why saffron is one of the most expensive spices in the world.

In the Valais village of **Mund**, saffron has been grown for centuries. The small fields lie on the sunny slopes above Brig. In October the violet saffron flowers bloom there. Saffron from Mund is a speciality and has a protected designation of origin (AOP).

gewusst: For one kilogram of saffron you need over a hundred thousand crocus flowers.
The saffron crocus blooms in autumn and not in spring like most other crocuses.

teile.einleitung: Pitcher plants are carnivorous plants with astonishing traps. Their leaves have turned into pitchers into which insects slide. Most species grow in the warm rainforests of South-East Asia.
wichtigste: Pitcher plants catch insects in pitcher-shaped traps.
The pitcher is a modified leaf.
Sweet nectar on the rim lures the insects.
The walls are smooth, so the animals slide in.
At the bottom of the pitcher there is a digestive juice.
Most species grow in South-East Asia, for example on Borneo.
Some large pitchers serve as toilets for tree shrews.

abschnitte.text: The pitcher is a **modified leaf**. It often hangs from a kind of **tendril** at the end of the leaf. Many pitchers have a **lid** on top. Some pitcher plants climb up trees with their tendrils. The pitchers can be green, red or spotted.

On the rim and the lid of the pitcher there is sweet **nectar**. Insects want to nibble and so get into danger. The rim and the inner walls are so **smooth and slippery** that the animals find no grip. They slide in and cannot get out again. This kind of trap is called a **pitfall trap**.

At the bottom of the pitcher there is a liquid with **digestive juice**. In it the trapped animals are slowly broken down. The plant takes up the nutrients, above all **nitrogen**. The largest pitchers hold more than a litre of liquid. Small **rats** have been found in them, but that is very rare.

Most pitcher plants grow in damp, warm regions of **South-East Asia**, for example on **Borneo**. On Borneo, **tree shrews** sit on the rim of some large pitchers and lick nectar. In doing so, their droppings fall into the pitcher. They serve the plant as **fertiliser**. In this way animal and plant help each other.

gewusst: In the liquid of some pitchers live mosquito larvae and other small animals, without being digested.
The lid of the pitcher helps to stop too much rainwater from falling in and diluting the digestive juice.

teile.einleitung: In nature everything is connected: plants are eaten, and whoever eats is often eaten in turn. Ecology therefore sorts living things by their role in the food chain. Whoever eats other living things is a consumer.
wichtigste: Consumers feed on other living things.
Animals are consumers because they cannot carry out photosynthesis.
Plant eaters are first-order consumers.
Whoever eats plant eaters is a second-order consumer.
The Latin word “consumere” means to use up.
Consumers that mainly eat other animals are called carnivores.

abschnitte.text: Plants make their food themselves with sunlight, through **photosynthesis**. That is why they are called **producers**, that is, makers. Animals cannot do this. They have to eat other living things and are therefore **consumers**. The word comes from the Latin “**consumere**” and means **to use up**. Fungi and bacteria that break down dead remains are called **decomposers**.

Animals that eat plants directly are **first-order consumers**, for example mice, caterpillars or roe deer. Whoever eats them is a **second-order consumer**. If a **great tit** eats caterpillars that nibble oak leaves, the great tit is a second-order consumer. So is the **fox** that eats a mouse that has eaten grain.

In the lake, the chain begins with the **algae**, the producers. **Water fleas** eat algae and are first-order consumers. The **perch** eats water fleas and is a second-order consumer. The **pike** eats perch and is therefore a **third-order consumer**. At each step a large part of the energy is lost, which is why there are far fewer pike than water fleas.

Consumers that eat mainly plants are called **herbivores**. Whoever feeds mainly on other animals is a **carnivore**, such as the lynx. **Omnivores** such as the wild boar or the badger eat both. Depending on the meal, they can belong to different orders. That is why in nature people often speak of a **food web** instead of a simple chain.

gewusst: Humans too are consumers, of the first or a higher order depending on the meal.
Carnivorous plants such as the sundew carry out photosynthesis and get only additional nutrients from the insects they catch.

teile.einleitung: The mountain pine, in German “Legföhre”, is a low, dense conifer of the Alps. It grows with trunks lying on the ground on steep slopes. In this way it protects villages and roads from avalanches and erosion.
wichtigste: The mountain pine is a form of the mountain pine group and belongs to the pines.
Föhre is the Swiss word for pine.
In Austria and southern Germany it is called Latsche.
It carries two needles per short shoot.
Its trunks lie on the ground and grow in an arc upwards.
The upright form of the mountain pine is called the hooked pine.

abschnitte.titel: A pine that lies on the ground
abschnitte.text: The mountain pine is a form of the **mountain pine group** and belongs to the genus of the **pines**. In Switzerland pines are mostly called **Föhren**. In Austria and southern Germany the plant is called **Latsche**. Its trunks lie on the ground and grow **in an arc upwards**. This produces a dense thicket, often as tall as a man. Like other pines it carries its needles in bundles, and in its case there are **two needles** per short shoot.

In the mountains there is a lot of snow in winter. The branches of the mountain pine are **flexible** and lie flat. Under the load of snow they bend instead of breaking. **Avalanches** slide over the flat thicket. In spring the branches straighten up again. The mountain pine grows very slowly and can nevertheless become many decades old.

Dense stands of mountain pine hold the **snow on the slope**. In this way fewer avalanches break away. The roots also hold the soil together so that it is not washed away. For villages, railways and roads in the valley this is very important. In Switzerland such forests are called **protection forest**.

In the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine, mountain pines shape wide areas, for example around the **Ofenpass**. There both lying mountain pines and upright trees grow. The upright form is called the **hooked pine**. It gets its name from the hooked scales on its cones. The National Park was founded in 1914 and is the oldest in the Alps.

gewusst: From the needles of the Latsche, a fragrant oil is obtained for ointments and bath additives.
The mountain pine can grow in places where upright trees would be crushed by snow.

teile.einleitung: The higher you climb in the mountains, the cooler it gets, and the plant life changes. Experts therefore divide the land into altitude zones. The lowest is the colline zone, the warm hill country.
wichtigste: “Colline” means belonging to the hill country.
On the north side of the Alps, the colline zone reaches up to about 600 metres.
Naturally, mainly deciduous forests grow here, often with oaks.
On sunny slopes the grapevine grows.
The lowest point in Switzerland lies on Lake Maggiore.
The colline zone is followed by the submontane zone as a transition to the montane.

abschnitte.text: The word **colline** comes from the Latin “collis”, which means hill. The colline zone is the lowest altitude zone. Above it follow the **montane**, the **subalpine**, the **alpine** and the **nival** zones. Between the colline and the montane zones lies the **submontane zone** as a transition. On the north side of the Alps the colline zone reaches up to about **600 metres**, and on the warmer south side of the Alps the boundary lies higher.

Naturally, **deciduous trees** shape the forests of the colline zone. In dry, warm places **oaks** are typical. Common is the **oak-hornbeam forest**. The hornbeam has a very hard, pale wood that was formerly used for tools. In these forests many flowers grow in spring, before the leaf canopy closes.

Because of the mild climate, warmth-loving crops thrive here. Typical of the sunny slopes is the **grapevine**. Well-known wine-growing regions of Switzerland lie, for example, on Lake Geneva, on Lake Neuchâtel, in the Valais and in Ticino. Fruit trees and many kinds of vegetables also grow well at this height.

Because it is warm and rather flat here, especially many people live in the colline zone. Towns, villages, roads and fields have replaced a large part of the original forests. That is why little of the natural vegetation is left today. The **lowest point in Switzerland** lies on **Lake Maggiore** in Ticino, at just under 200 metres above sea level.

gewusst: On Lake Maggiore, thanks to the mild climate, even palms and camellias grow in gardens.
The highest point in Switzerland, the Dufourspitze, lies more than 4,400 metres higher than the lowest.

teile.einleitung: A seedling is a very young plant that is just growing out of the seed. It is small and delicate, but astonishingly strong. Some seedlings are even eaten as sprouts.
wichtigste: A plant straight after germinating is called a seedling.
Usually the root comes out of the seed first.
The stem grows upwards towards the light.
At the beginning the seedling lives on the store in the seed.
The bean seedling pushes through the soil with a bent stem.
A bean germinates in damp soil in a few days.
Edible seedlings are called sprouts.

abschnitte.text: To germinate, a seed needs above all **water**, **warmth** and **air**. First it soaks up water and swells. Then the husk bursts open. Usually the **radicle**, the first root, pushes out first. In this way the young plant can soon take up water from the soil. In damp, warm soil a bean usually needs **a few days** up to about a week to germinate.

The root grows downwards into the soil. The stem grows **upwards**, because up there it finds light. To do so the seedling has to **break through the soil**. The bean seedling pushes through the ground with a stem **bent like a hook**. In this way it protects its delicate tip. Out in the light it straightens up.

In the seed a **food store** is kept, for example starch or oil. The seedling lives on this at the beginning. As soon as its leaves are green and get light, it can make food itself. This is called **photosynthesis**. Only then does it no longer depend on the store.

Young seedlings that are eaten are called **sprouts**. Well known are the sprouts of the **mung bean**. They are eaten in salad or in Asian dishes. You can also let cress, lentils or radishes sprout. It is important to keep them clean and to change the water often.

gewusst: Seedlings that grow in the dark become long, thin and pale, because they are desperately searching for light.
The root of a seedling always grows downwards, even if you put the seed into the soil the wrong way up.

teile.einleitung: The Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe is an alpine garden in the Valais. It lies in the mountain village of Champex-Lac and shows plants from mountains all over the world.
wichtigste: The garden lies in Champex-Lac in the canton of Valais.
Champex-Lac belongs to the municipality of Orsières.
It lies at around 1,500 m above sea level on Lac de Champex.
It goes back to a garden by Jean-Marcel Aubert.
The plants come from mountains all over the world.

abschnitte.text: The **Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe** lies in the Valais mountain village of **Champex-Lac**. The village belongs to the municipality of **Orsières** and lies on **Lac de Champex**, at **around 1,500 m above sea level**. People speak **French** here, because the garden is in western Switzerland. “Jardin alpin” means alpine garden. In the cool mountain climate, mountain plants thrive much better than in the lowlands.

The garden from which Flore-Alpe grew was laid out by **Jean-Marcel Aubert**. The plants are shown mainly in **rock gardens** with **rocks and streams**. That way they find conditions similar to those in their home regions, with stony ground and plenty of light. Between the rocks grow small cushion plants, gentians and many other mountain flowers.

abschnitte.titel: Mountain plants from all over the world
abschnitte.text: In the Jardin alpin, it is not only plants from the Alps that grow. They come from **mountains all over the world**, for example from Asia or America. Visitors can thus compare how plants in different mountain regions have adapted to cold, wind and short summers. The garden also serves research and education about the plant life of the mountains.

gewusst: Champex-Lac lies above Orsières, not far from Martigny.
In winter, the snow cover protects alpine plants from frost like a warm blanket.

teile.einleitung: The **royal fern** is a particularly large and magnificent fern. Its scientific name is Osmunda regalis. It grows in wet places and is rare in Switzerland.
wichtigste: “Regalis” means royal.
The royal fern is among the largest ferns in Europe.
Its spores form on brown leaflets at the tip of the fronds.
It grows on wet, acidic, low-lime soils.
Its spores contain chlorophyll and germinate very quickly.
Its fronds are twice pinnate.

abschnitte.text: The royal fern is called **Osmunda regalis** in scientific terms. The Latin word **regalis** means **royal**. It is among the **largest ferns in Europe**. In good places its fronds grow up to two metres tall, sometimes even more. The large leaves of a fern are called **fronds**.

The fronds of the royal fern are **twice pinnate**. That means: on the stalk sit leaflets, and these are divided again into **elongated little leaflets**. The little leaflets are fairly broad and recall a little the leaves of a tree. In autumn the fronds turn yellow to brown before they die. In spring new, rolled-up fronds sprout.

Like all ferns, the royal fern forms no flowers but **spores**. These form on special **brown leaflets at the tip of the fronds**. They have almost no chlorophyll and look like a brown flower head. That is why in English it is also called the **“flowering fern”**. Its spores are special: they **contain chlorophyll** and **germinate very quickly**. In return they stay able to germinate only briefly.

The royal fern likes **wet, acidic and low-lime soils**. It is found in swamp woods, bogs and on banks. In Switzerland it is rare and occurs in only a few places, especially on the south side of the Alps. Many of its habitats have disappeared through drainage. It therefore counts as **endangered** and is protected.

Plants of the royal fern family have existed for a very long time. In **2014**, researchers reported an astonishing find from **Sweden**. In a fossilised member of the royal fern family about **180 million years** old, **cell nuclei with chromosomes** were preserved. The comparison showed that the genetic material of these ferns has hardly changed since the time of the dinosaurs.

gewusst: A fossilised relative of the royal fern still showed chromosomes after 180 million years.
The spores of the royal fern are green because of their chlorophyll and not brown as in many other ferns.

teile.einleitung: Cherries are among the first fruits of summer. There are sweet and sour varieties, which are eaten fresh or made into cakes and jam. Even their stones and the wood of the tree are used.
wichtigste: Here, cherries are ripe in June and July.
They belong to the stone fruits.
Often they hang in pairs on long stalks.
Ripe sweet cherries are mostly dark red.
Sour cherries are often used in cakes.
In a lot of rain, ripe cherries often burst open.
A small bag of cherry stones stays warm for a long time.

abschnitte.text: Fruits with a single hard **stone** in the middle are called **stone fruit**. Besides the cherry, these include plum, peach and apricot. Cherries have **long stalks**. Often **two or more** cherries hang together. Ripe sweet cherries are mostly **dark red**, but there are also paler varieties.

Here, cherries ripen around **June and July**. **Sweet cherries** are gladly eaten fresh from the tree. **Sour cherries** are less sweet. That is why they are gladly baked or cooked, for example for cake, compote or jam. After picking, cherries keep for only a few days.

In rain, ripe cherries take up **water**. Then their skin becomes too tight, and the cherries **burst**. Such fruits rot quickly. That is why some fruit growers protect their trees with **plastic sheets** or roofs. Nets against birds are also common.

Cherry stones store warmth well. A **small bag of cherry stones** is warmed in the oven. The stones give off the warmth for a long time, for example for tummy ache. The **wood** of the cherry tree is also popular. It is reddish and beautifully grained. Joiners gladly make **furniture** from it.

gewusst: For some years now, the spotted wing drosophila from Asia has been causing trouble for cherry growers in Switzerland. It lays its eggs in ripe fruit.
You should not bite open cherry stones, because the kernel contains substances that are poisonous in large amounts.

teile.einleitung: Capsule fruits are dry fruits that open when ripe and release their seeds. You find them on many well-known plants, from the poppy and the tulip to cotton. Some foods also come from capsules.
wichtigste: A ripe capsule fruit opens and releases its seeds.
Capsules develop from several fused carpels.
In the poppy, small pores open, which is a pore capsule.
The spiny husk of the horse chestnut is a capsule.
The tulip, flax and cotton also form capsules.
The vanilla pod is botanically a capsule.
Brazil nuts are seeds from a woody capsule.

abschnitte.text: Capsule fruits belong to the **dehiscent fruits**: they dry out when ripe and scatter their seeds. A capsule develops from at least two **carpels** fused together. That is why it often has several **chambers**. Other fruits such as cherries or hazelnuts, by contrast, stay closed.

Capsules open in different ways: through slits, lids or holes. In the **poppy**, small holes open at the top under the stigma disc. This form is called a **pore capsule**. The **tulip** grows an upright capsule with three chambers, which opens with slits. The spiny green husk of the **horse chestnut** splits open into three parts. The glossy brown conkers inside are the seeds.

In **cotton**, the capsule bursts open when ripe, and white **seed hairs** billow out. Fabrics are made from these hairs. **Flax**, also called linseed, forms small round capsules with glossy **linseeds**. From its stems, linen fibres are obtained.

The so-called **vanilla pod** is not really a pod at all. The fruit of the vanilla orchid is a long **capsule**. **Brazil nuts** are not true nuts either. On the Brazil nut tree grows a large, very hard, woody capsule. Inside lie many tightly packed seeds, which are sold as Brazil nuts.

gewusst: The capsule of the Brazil nut tree is so hard that mainly agoutis, which are rodents, can gnaw it open.
The capsules of touch-me-not burst open at a touch and fling the seeds several metres away.

teile.einleitung: If you cut through a tree trunk, the inside is often darker than the outer part. This inner wood is called heartwood. It is no longer alive, but is often especially hard and resistant.
wichtigste: Heartwood is the inner, dead part of the wood.
The outer, living wood is called sapwood.
In heartwood formation, cells die and heartwood substances are deposited.
Heartwood substances inhibit fungi and insects.
Heartwood no longer conducts water, but supports the trunk.
Robinia, larch and walnut have durable heartwood.
Spruce and beech are ripewood trees without a dark coloured core.

abschnitte.text: The outer part of the wood is called **sapwood**. It is alive and conducts water from the roots upwards. Further inside, in many trees, lies the **heartwood**. It is dead and **physiologically inactive**, so it no longer conducts water. Even so, it is important, because it goes on **supporting** the trunk mechanically.

In the change from sapwood to heartwood, the last living cells die. Before that they form **heartwood substances** such as **tannins**, **resins** and phenols. These are deposited in the wood and often colour it darker. This process is called **heartwood formation**. Heartwood substances inhibit **fungi and insects** that destroy the wood. In addition, nutrients are lacking, and the conducting channels are often blocked.

Trees with a dark coloured core are called **heartwood trees**. One example is the **walnut** with pale sapwood and a dark brown heart. In **ripewood trees** such as **spruce** or beech, the inside is drier but hardly differently coloured. Maple, birch and lime are pale woods without a coloured core. The **beech** can form a reddish-brown **red heart** in old age. This false heartwood does not occur in every tree and often lowers the price of the timber.

The heartwood of **robinia** is among the most durable woods in Europe. That is why it is gladly used for posts and outdoor playgrounds. In Switzerland, **larch heartwood** is often used untreated for facades and **shingles**. It is rich in resin and weather-resistant. With time it turns a silvery grey. Beech, spruce and poplar, by contrast, do not last long in contact with the ground.

gewusst: In oak, small cell bubbles block the conducting channels in the heartwood. That is why oak wood is well suited to watertight wine barrels.
A tree can go on living for a long time even with a hollow trunk, because the living parts lie on the outside.

teile.einleitung: A forest has several storeys like a house. The **herb layer** is the storey close to the ground. Here grow grasses, herbs, ferns and many spring flowers.
wichtigste: The herb layer consists of grasses, herbs and ferns.
Below it lies the moss layer with soft cushions of moss.
Many woodland flowers bloom in spring, because then a lot of light falls on the ground.
The wood anemone often covers the ground in beech forest in spring.
Lily of the valley is pretty, but poisonous.
The stinging nettle burns on the skin when you touch it.

abschnitte.text: A forest is built in **layers**. Right at the top is the tree layer with the crowns of the large trees. Below it follows the shrub layer with bushes and young trees. Then comes the **herb layer** with grasses, herbs and ferns. Right at the bottom lies the **moss layer**. There mosses form soft, green cushions that store a lot of water.

In spring the deciduous trees still have no leaves. Then a lot of **light** falls on the forest floor. The **spring bloomers** use this time. The white **wood anemone** often covers whole areas in beech forest. The violet **violet** smells delicate. When the trees have put out their leaves in May, it becomes shady on the ground. Many spring bloomers then withdraw and store nutrients in their underground parts.

The **fern** has no flowers. It has large, feathered leaves and multiplies with tiny spores that sit on the underside of the leaf. The **wood sorrel** has leaves that look like clover leaves. They taste sour. In strong light or at night it folds its leaflets together.

The **lily of the valley** has small, white bells and smells strongly. But all parts of the plant are **poisonous**. The **stinging nettle** has fine stinging hairs. If you touch them, the tips break off and release a substance into the skin that burns and itches. For many butterfly caterpillars, however, the nettle is an important food plant.

On low little shrubs on the forest floor grow the blue **bilberries**. They like acidic soils and in Switzerland often occur in coniferous forests. The berries ripen in summer. They are a popular food for people, birds and other woodland animals.

gewusst: The nettle is food for the caterpillars of the peacock butterfly and the small tortoiseshell.
The wood sorrel folds its leaflets together at night like an umbrella.

teile.einleitung: A comet is a celestial body of ice and dust that gets a glowing tail when it flies near the sun. Thousands of years ago, people already marvelled at these light phenomena in the sky. Today we know that comets are leftovers from the time when our solar system formed.
wichtigste: A comet is a celestial body of ice and dust with a tail.
The solid nucleus of a comet is usually only a few kilometres across.
Near the sun, ice evaporates and forms a shell and tails.
The tail always points away from the sun.
Many comets come from the Kuiper belt or the far distant Oort cloud.
Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years.
The Rosetta space probe studied a comet from close up, with the help of the University of Bern.

abschnitte.text: A comet is a small celestial body that orbits the sun on a mostly elongated path. Its **nucleus** consists of frozen water, frozen gases, dust and rock, which is why it is also called a dirty snowball. The name comes from the Greek word for “long-haired star”, because the tail looks like long hair. Comets, like asteroids, belong to the **small bodies** of the solar system.

Far out in space, a comet is just a dark, icy lump. When it approaches the sun, the ice evaporates, and a glowing envelope of gas forms, the **coma**. The solar wind and sunlight blow gas and dust away, so two **tails** form, a dust tail and a bluish gas tail. These tails can become many millions of kilometres long and always point away from the sun.

Many comets with short orbital periods come from the **Kuiper belt** beyond the orbit of Neptune. Comets with very long orbital periods probably come from the **Oort cloud**, a huge cloud of icy bodies at the outermost edge of the solar system. Now and then such a body is disturbed from its path and flies towards the sun. Some comets need only a few years for one orbit, others many thousands of years.

The best known is **Halley’s Comet**, which returns about every 76 years. It was last seen in 1986 and is expected again in 2061. In 1997 the comet **Hale-Bopp** shone so brightly for months that it could be seen with the naked eye. In the summer of 2020, Comet Neowise could also be observed well in the evening sky in Switzerland.

The European space probe **Rosetta** accompanied Comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko on its way around the sun from 2014. In November 2014, the small lander **Philae** even landed on the comet. On board Rosetta was the measuring instrument ROSINA, which was built under the leadership of the University of Bern. It studied the gases around the comet and found many different chemical compounds.

In the past, many people thought comets were bringers of misfortune, announcing war or disease. On the famous **Bayeux Tapestry** from the Middle Ages, Halley’s Comet of the year 1066 is shown. The English astronomer Edmond Halley calculated around 1700, as the first, that the same comet returns regularly. Today researchers know that comets may have brought part of the water to the young Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The solid part of the comet made of ice, dust and rock.
The glowing envelope of gas that forms around the nucleus when it approaches the sun.
A huge cloud of icy bodies far out at the edge of the solar system.
The time a celestial body needs for one full orbit around the sun.

gewusst: Meteor showers such as the Perseids in August arise when the Earth flies through the dust trail of a comet.
The nucleus of Halley’s Comet is only about 15 kilometres long, but its tail can reach millions of kilometres.
Comet nuclei are among the darkest objects in the solar system, blacker than coal.

teile.einleitung: Trees take carbon dioxide from the air and build the carbon into their wood. A forest that in this way takes up more carbon dioxide than it gives off is called a carbon sink. Such sinks are important in the fight against climate change.
wichtigste: Trees take up carbon dioxide from the air for photosynthesis.
A carbon sink takes up more carbon dioxide than it gives off.
Dry wood consists of about half carbon.
If 12 kg of carbon are burned completely, 44 kg of carbon dioxide are produced.
The forest soil also stores a great deal of carbon.
If many trees die and rot, a forest can become a source of carbon.

abschnitte.text: In **photosynthesis**, leaves take up **carbon dioxide** (CO2) from the air. With water and sunlight, the plants make sugar from it and give off oxygen. From the sugar the tree builds wood, leaves and roots. Dry wood consists of about **half carbon**. In this way the carbon stays stored in the tree for as long as it lives.

A carbon atom weighs 12 units, an oxygen atom 16. A CO2 particle consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, so it weighs 12 + 16 + 16 = 44 units. If **12 kg of carbon** are burned completely, **44 kg of carbon dioxide** are therefore produced. This shows: in a tree trunk there is much more CO2 than you would think.

A forest is a **carbon sink** if it takes up more CO2 than it gives off. If wood rots or burns, the CO2 is released again. If many trees die through drought, storms or bark beetles, a forest can therefore become a **carbon source**. An old forest stores more carbon overall on the same area than a young one, even though young trees grow faster.

Carbon is not only in the trees. A great deal of it is also stored in the **forest soil**, in humus, roots and dead plant remains. If wood is felled and used for **houses and furniture**, the carbon often stays in it for decades. If the wood is burned instead, it quickly returns to the air. That is why building with wood is seen as good for the climate.

gewusst: The largest carbon sink on Earth is the sea, which takes up a large part of the CO2 released by humans.
Bogs store especially much carbon in peat on a small area.

teile.einleitung: Tree rings are the light and dark rings that you see on a sawn-through tree trunk. Every year a tree grows a new ring. That is why tree rings show the age of the tree and reveal a lot about its life story.
wichtigste: Tree rings show the age of a tree.
Every year a tree forms a new ring.
A tree ring consists of light earlywood and dark latewood.
Wide rings mean good growing years, narrow rings bad ones.
With tree rings, the age of wood can be determined exactly.
In the tropics, many trees have no clear tree rings.

abschnitte.text: Under the bark lies a thin growth layer, the **cambium**. Every year it forms new wood inwards. In spring the tree grows quickly and forms light, loose **earlywood**. In summer growth becomes slower and dark, dense **latewood** forms, and in winter growth rests.

One light and one dark stripe together make a tree ring. If you count all the rings from the centre to the bark, you know how old the tree is. With living trees, a thin borer is used to take out a stick of wood, and the rings on it are counted. That way the tree does not have to be felled.

The width of a ring reveals how the tree was doing in that year. In warm, damp years the rings are wide, in dry or cold years narrow. Scars in the rings show forest fires, lightning strikes or injuries. This is how we learn what the **climate** was like long ago, long before there were weather records.

The science that analyses tree rings is called **dendrochronology**. Because all the trees of an area form wide or narrow rings in the same years, a typical pattern arises. By lining up the patterns of old and young woods, long calendars covering many thousands of years have been made. With them, the year a timber beam was felled can often be determined to the exact year.

In Switzerland, tree rings have been used to date the wooden piles of the **pile dwellings** on lake shores, which have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011. This tells us in which years the villages were built thousands of years ago. The beams of old farmhouses, churches and the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne can also be dated this way. In Birmensdorf near Zurich, the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research WSL studies tree rings.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thin growth layer under the bark of a tree.
The light, loose wood that grows in spring.
The dark, dense wood that grows in summer.
Determining the age of wood with the help of tree rings.

gewusst: Some bristlecone pines in California are almost 5,000 years old and are among the oldest trees in the world.
Sometimes a tree forms two rings in one year, for example after a frost or a drought in the middle of summer.

teile.einleitung: The **Kunming-Montreal Agreement** is a worldwide plan to protect nature. Almost all the countries of the world agreed it in Montreal in December 2022. It is meant to slow the disappearance of animal and plant species.
wichtigste: The agreement was adopted in Montreal in December 2022.
Its official name is the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
It contains 23 global targets for the year 2030.
The best-known target is called “30 by 30”: protect 30 per cent of land and sea areas.
At least 30 per cent of damaged ecosystems are to be restored.
The vision for 2050 is: living in harmony with nature.

abschnitte.text: The variety of living things on Earth is called **biodiversity**. It has been shrinking for decades. Many countries have therefore signed the United Nations **Convention on Biological Diversity**, Switzerland too. The countries meet regularly at conferences. At the 15th conference in **December 2022** in **Montreal** (Canada), the new plan was adopted. China held the chair, which is why it also carries the name of the Chinese city of **Kunming**.

The best-known target is called **“30 by 30”**. By 2030, **30 per cent of the Earth’s land and sea areas** are to be effectively protected. The rights of Indigenous peoples are also to be respected. In addition, by 2030 **at least 30 per cent** of damaged ecosystems are to be **restored**, for example drained bogs or destroyed forests.

In all, the plan contains **23 targets** for the year 2030. Some examples: the overall risk from **pesticides** is to fall by at least **half**. The introduction and establishment of **invasive alien species** is to fall by **at least 50 per cent**. These are animals and plants that were brought in from other parts of the world and displace native species. Environmentally harmful **subsidies**, that is, government money, are to be reduced by **at least 500 billion US dollars** per year by 2030.

Besides the targets for 2030, there is a long-term **vision for 2050**. It reads: **living in harmony with nature**. By then, ecosystems are to be healthy again and the extinction of species is to be strongly slowed. Nature is to be used in such a way that future generations can live from it too.

The agreement is **not legally binding**. Each country must decide for itself how it carries out the targets and must present its own plans. Switzerland, too, has to show how it makes its contribution. Supporters see in the plan an important step for nature conservation. Critics complain that earlier targets were often not reached and that monitoring is weak.

gewusst: The earlier worldwide conservation targets were called the Aichi Targets, after a prefecture in Japan.
Around 190 states agreed to the plan in Montreal.

teile.einleitung: The cherry tree is full of white blossom in spring and full of sweet fruit in summer. In Switzerland it has a long tradition, especially in the Zug region. In Swiss German it is called “Chriesibaum”.
wichtigste: Cherry trees usually bloom white.
In every cherry there is a hard stone.
In Swiss German the cherry is called “Chriesi”.
The Zuger Kirschtorte is a well-known Swiss pastry.
The wild cherry tree is called the wild cherry.
Starlings eat ripe cherries in flocks.
In Japan the cherry blossom is celebrated with the festival of Hanami.

abschnitte.text: In spring the cherry tree is full of **white blossom**. Bees and other insects visit it and carry pollen from flower to flower. From the pollinated flowers, the **cherries** later grow. The cherry is a **stone fruit**. In its flesh there is a hard kernel, the cherry stone.

The wild cherry tree is called the **wild cherry**. It grows at the edges of woods and in woods. Its small cherries are gladly eaten by birds, which then spread the stones. The shiny **bark** splits across the trunk and peels off in **horizontal bands**. This is how you easily recognise the cherry tree.

**Starlings** fly in large flocks and love sweet fruit. A flock can quickly strip a tree bare. That is why farmers sometimes hang **nets** over the cherry trees. Blackbirds also like to nibble at the ripe cherries.

In Swiss German the cherry is called **Chriesi**, which is why there are words like **Chriesibaum**. The **Zug** region has long been known for its cherries. The **Zuger Kirschtorte** is a well-known pastry from Switzerland. In Basel-Landschaft and in central Switzerland, too, there are many cherry trees. Kirsch is also distilled from cherries, a spirit for adults.

In **Japan** the cherry blossom is very important. At the festival of **Hanami**, people picnic under flowering ornamental cherries. The weather service even tracks when the blossom begins in which part of the country. The Japanese ornamental cherries mostly bear pink flowers and hardly any edible fruit.

gewusst: In Zug there is a race with ladders, the “Chriesisturm”. In the past, people ran with them to the trees when the harvest was released.
Cherry trees, like the apple, pear and rose, belong to the rose family.

teile.einleitung: How does water get from the roots to the crown of a tree a hundred metres tall, without any pump? The cohesion theory explains it: the water is pulled from above, as if through a very thin drinking straw.
wichtigste: Henry Dixon and John Joly put forward the cohesion theory in 1894.
Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules together, which is called cohesion.
The sticking of the water to the walls of the conducting channels is called adhesion.
The water rises in the xylem as a continuous column.
The water column is under tension, that is, under negative pressure.
If the column breaks and gas bubbles form, this is called cavitation.

abschnitte.text: At the leaves, water is constantly evaporating through tiny pores. This process is called **transpiration**. When a water molecule evaporates at the top, it pulls the next one after it. In this way a suction arises that reaches through the whole plant down to the roots. The Irishmen **Henry Dixon** and **John Joly** described this mechanism in **1894**.

Water molecules attract each other. **Hydrogen bonds** are responsible for this. This holding together is called **cohesion** and makes sure that the water column does not simply fall apart. In addition, the water sticks to the walls of the conducting channels, which is **adhesion**. Together they hold an unbroken thread of water from the root to the leaf.

The water rises in the **xylem**, the wood part of the vascular bundles. It consists of very fine, dead tubes. Because the column is pulled from above, it is under **tension**, that is, under negative pressure. If it breaks at one point, gas bubbles form. This breaking is called **cavitation**. The tube affected can then no longer conduct water, which becomes dangerous in great drought.

abschnitte.titel: Why other explanations are not enough
abschnitte.text: **Air pressure** can hold up a column of water only about **10 metres** high. A tree 30 metres tall could not be supplied that way. **Capillarity** is not enough either: in a tube with a radius of 10 micrometres, water rises only about **1.5 metres**. Only the pull from evaporation together with cohesion explains how water reaches very great heights.

gewusst: The tallest known living tree is a coast redwood called “Hyperion”, about 116 metres tall.
On a hot summer day, a large deciduous tree can evaporate several hundred litres of water.

teile.einleitung: Lichens are a partnership of a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium. The **crustose lichens** grow so tightly on stone, bark or soil that they look like a crust. You cannot detach them without destroying them.
wichtigste: People distinguish crustose, foliose and fruticose lichens.
Crustose lichens are firmly fused with their base and have no lower cortex.
Their body is often divided into small fields, the areoles.
Some grow almost entirely inside the rock and are called endolithic lichens.
The map lichen often grows less than a millimetre a year.
The fruiting bodies often look like small discs or little bowls.

abschnitte.text: Lichens are divided by their shape into three main groups: **crustose lichens**, **foliose lichens** and **fruticose lichens**. Foliose lichens look like small leaves and can often be lifted off. Fruticose lichens grow like tiny bushes. Crustose lichens, by contrast, are completely **fused** with their base. They lack the **lower cortex** that many foliose lichens have. The fungal threads grow directly into the stone or the bark.

The body of many crustose lichens is divided into small fields by fine cracks. These fields are called **areoles**. In the yellow-green **map lichen**, you see black lines between neighbouring lichens. They consist of a dark **prothallus**, formed only of fungal threads without algae. In this way a pattern arises that recalls a map with borders.

Some crustose lichens grow mostly **inside rock**. They are called **endolithic lichens**, which means “living in stone”. From outside you often see only a discolouration and the fruiting bodies. Crustose lichens also grow in places where hardly anything else lives, for example on rocks in the high mountains of the Alps.

Crustose lichens grow very slowly. The map lichen often grows **less than a millimetre a year**. Because it grows so evenly, you can estimate from its size how long a stone has been exposed. In this way you can determine, for example, when a glacier left behind a moraine. The **fruiting bodies** of the fungal partner look in many species like small **discs or little bowls** on the lichen body. In them the fungus forms its spores.

Many lichens react sensitively to **air pollution**. In the past the air in cities was heavily polluted with **sulphur dioxide**. There often only the crustose lichen **Lecanora conizaeoides** survived. Since the air has become cleaner, many other lichens are returning to the cities. Lichens therefore serve as **bioindicators** of air quality.

gewusst: Some map lichens in the mountains are probably several thousand years old.
Lichens have survived experiments in space on the outside of space stations.

teile.einleitung: The International Space Station, or ISS for short, is an inhabited research laboratory in Earth orbit. Since the year 2000, astronauts have lived and worked there all the time. The ISS is the largest structure humans have ever put into space.
wichtigste: The ISS is an inhabited research laboratory in Earth orbit.
It circles the Earth at a height of about 400 kilometres.
One trip around the Earth takes only about an hour and a half.
Since November 2000, the station has been inhabited continuously.
Several space agencies run the ISS together.
You can sometimes see the ISS in the sky with the naked eye.

abschnitte.text: The ISS is a **space station**, that is, a house and laboratory in space. It consists of many modules that were put together like building blocks. With its large solar wings, it is about as wide as a football pitch is long. Electricity is supplied by the **solar cells**, which use sunlight.

The first module was put into space in 1998, and after that the station was extended piece by piece over many years. It is run by the space agencies of the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. Europe contributed the laboratory module **Columbus**, and Switzerland is a member of the European Space Agency, ESA. Astronauts travel to the station in spacecraft such as Soyuz or Crew Dragon.

The ISS flies at a height of about 400 kilometres at around 28,000 kilometres per hour. It needs only about 90 minutes for one lap of the Earth. That is why the people on board experience about 16 sunrises every day. Because the station is constantly falling around the Earth, there is **weightlessness** on board.

Usually six or seven people live on board for a few months. They research, for example, how plants grow without gravity and how muscles and bones change in space. Such experiments help to prepare future trips to the Moon or to Mars. Every day the astronauts train for about two hours so that their bodies stay fit.

Food comes in pouches and tins, and water is recovered from urine and breath. People sleep in sleeping bags fixed to the wall. In the evening or morning sky, you can see the ISS as a bright, fast-moving point with no blinking light. According to current plans, the station is to be brought down in a controlled way around the year 2030 over a remote part of the **Pacific Ocean**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path of an object around a heavenly body.
A single building block of the space station.
A state in which you float because you are constantly falling along with everything else.
The European Space Agency, to which Switzerland also belongs.

gewusst: The ISS is so bright that you can often spot it before most of the stars in the evening sky.
There is no shower on the ISS: the astronauts wash with damp cloths and with shampoo that does not need to be rinsed out.

teile.einleitung: Members of the cactus family, cacti for short, are plants that are perfectly adapted to dry and hot regions. Instead of large leaves they have spines to save water, and in their thick stems they store water for long dry periods. Some are tiny like a button, others grow taller than a house.
wichtigste: Cacti are plants that can survive in dry regions.
Their spines are modified leaves and help to save water.
Cacti store water in their thick, fleshy stems.
Almost all cacti originally come from the Americas.
There are about 1,800 different species of cactus.
Many cacti have large, brightly coloured flowers.
Some cacti, like the prickly pear, have edible fruits.

abschnitte.text: Cacti usually have a thick, green stem, which can be round, columnar or flat like a paddle. The **spines** grow from small, felty cushions, the **areoles**. Only cacti have such areoles, and that is how you recognise them. The green stem does the work of the leaves and makes food with sunlight.

Large leaves would let a lot of water evaporate, but spines hardly any. Cacti are **succulents**, which means that they store water in their tissue. Many have ribs so that the stem can expand like an accordion after rain. They open their pores only in the cool night, to take in carbon dioxide. The spines also give a little shade and protect against hungry animals.

Cacti occur almost only in North and South America, from Canada to Patagonia. Many live in **deserts** such as the Sonoran Desert in Mexico and the USA. Others grow high in the Andes or even on trees in the rainforest. Only a single species also occurs naturally in Africa and Asia.

Many cacti bloom only briefly, often only for a day or a night. The flowers are often large and shine white, yellow, pink or red. They are pollinated by bees, hummingbirds or bats. The flowers turn into fruits with many seeds, for example the sweet **prickly pear** of the opuntia.

The best-known giant cactus is the **saguaro** from the Sonoran Desert. It can grow over 12 metres tall and live more than 150 years. It only gets its typical arms after many decades. Other cacti stay tiny and, fully grown, are only a few centimetres tall.

Here, cacti are mainly popular **houseplants**, such as the Christmas cactus, which flowers in winter. They need a lot of light and, in winter, only very little water. On warm, dry rocky slopes in the Valais and in Ticino, even feral opuntias grow outdoors. There they can push out the native plant life and are therefore regarded as a problem.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small, felty cushion on a cactus from which spines, flowers and new shoots grow.
A plant that stores water in its stem, leaves or roots.
A genus of cactus with flat, paddle-shaped segments, also called prickly pear cactus.
When water turns to vapour and escapes into the air.

gewusst: After heavy rain, a large saguaro can store several hundred litres of water.
The red dye carmine is obtained from tiny insects that live on opuntias.
Woodpeckers and small owls nest in the holes in the saguaro.

teile.einleitung: Canadian goldenrod glows yellow on many embankments in late summer. It comes from North America and was brought to Europe as a garden plant. Today it counts in Switzerland as an invasive plant that pushes out rare native plants.
wichtigste: Canadian goldenrod belongs to the daisy family.
It comes from North America.
It blooms from about July to October.
Its seeds fly far away on the wind.
With underground runners it forms dense stands.
In Switzerland it threatens fen meadows and nutrient-poor meadows in particular.
It is controlled by mowing several times a year before flowering.

abschnitte.text: Canadian goldenrod often grows as tall as a person. At the top it bears many tiny yellow **flower heads**. These are typical composite heads, so, like the sunflower and the dandelion, it belongs to the **daisy family**. It blooms from about **July to October**. Then whole embankments, railway banks and patches of wasteland glow yellow.

abschnitte.titel: From the garden into the wild
abschnitte.text: A long time ago the plant came from **North America** to Europe. People planted it as an ornamental plant and as **bee forage**. When many other plants have finished flowering, it still supplies a lot of nectar and pollen. That is why beekeepers valued it. Soon, however, it also kept growing outside gardens.

One plant produces a great many tiny fruits. Each carries a crown of hairs, the **pappus**, and flies far through the air with it like a parachute. In addition, goldenrod grows with underground runners, the **rhizomes**. This produces ever new shoots and dense stands in which other plants hardly find room.

In Switzerland, Canadian goldenrod counts as an **invasive neophyte**. That is a non-native plant that does harm. Especially at risk are **fen meadows** and **nutrient-poor meadows**, where many rare plants live. The **late goldenrod** from North America is also invasive here. The **common goldenrod**, by contrast, is native.

abschnitte.titel: What can be done about it
abschnitte.text: Larger stands are mown **several times a year before flowering**. This weakens the rhizomes and stops seeds from forming. Smaller stands can be pulled out, best of all with their roots. The plant parts do not belong on your own compost, so that they do not spread further.

gewusst: A whole stand of goldenrod can have grown from a single plant that kept spreading underground.
Common goldenrod, which is native here, grows much more loosely and hardly pushes out other plants.

teile.einleitung: The **cabbage family**, or crucifers, is a large plant family with many well-known vegetables and spices. Cabbage, rape, mustard and radishes belong to it. They get their German name, “Kreuzblütler”, cross-flowerers, from the shape of their flowers.
wichtigste: Crucifers have four petals that stand like a cross.
In spring, rape colours whole fields yellow.
Cauliflower, broccoli and kohlrabi all descend from the wild cabbage.
Typical fruits are siliques.
Mustard oils make mustard, horseradish and radishes hot.
Thale cress is an important model plant of research.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of the crucifers almost always have **four petals**. They stand opposite each other and so form a **cross**. That is where the name of the family comes from. The old scientific name is Cruciferae, which means “cross-bearers”. Worldwide there are several thousand species. Many bloom yellow or white.

Astonishingly many vegetables descend from the **wild cabbage** (Brassica oleracea). Through breeding, **cauliflower**, **broccoli**, **kohlrabi**, Brussels sprouts, white cabbage and savoy cabbage arose from it. In each variety a different plant part was bred especially large. In kohlrabi it is the stem, in cauliflower the flower head. **Rocket** is also a crucifer.

**Rape** blooms bright yellow in spring. In Switzerland too, you see many yellow rape fields in April and May. From its seeds **rapeseed oil** is pressed. **Shepherd’s purse** grows at the edges of paths. Its small fruits are triangular to heart-shaped and recall an old shepherd’s bag.

Crucifers form the typical fruit of the family, the **silique**. If it is short and broad, it is called a silicle. Many species contain **mustard oils**. When the plant is damaged, for example by chewing, these sharp substances are produced. They protect the plant from those that would eat it. That is why **mustard**, **horseradish** and **radishes** taste hot.

The small **thale cress** (Arabidopsis thaliana) is inconspicuous. For research, however, it is enormously important. It grows fast, is small and has a small genome. Its genome was in 2000 the first of a plant to be fully decoded. Researchers all over the world use it to study how plants grow and work.

gewusst: Cauliflower, broccoli and kohlrabi belong biologically to the same species.
Thale cress was the first plant whose genome was fully decoded.

teile.einleitung: From potato peelings, leaves and grass clippings, fertile soil can be made again. This happens on the compost heap, where tiny living things slowly break down the waste.
wichtigste: On the compost heap, new soil is made from garden and kitchen waste.
Potato peelings, leaves and coffee grounds may go on the compost.
Plastic never goes on the compost.
Cooked meat scraps attract rats.
Bacteria and fungi break down the waste.
Finished compost smells like forest soil and is a good fertiliser.

abschnitte.text: On the **compost heap**, plant remains turn into dark, crumbly soil. This is a natural cycle: what has grown in the garden gives its nutrients back to the soil. Tiny helpers such as **bacteria** and **fungi** make this happen. Earthworms, woodlice and millipedes also eat their share and loosen everything up.

Raw kitchen waste belongs on the compost, such as **potato peelings**, vegetable scraps and fruit peel. **Coffee grounds** and tea leaves also rot well. From the garden come leaves, grass clippings, wilted flowers and small twigs. The more varied the mixture, the better the helpers work.

abschnitte.titel: What does not belong on it?
abschnitte.text: **Plastic**, glass and metal do not rot and belong in the bin or in recycling. Cooked food scraps and **meat** should not go on the garden compost, because they attract **rats**. Cat litter, barbecue ash and diseased plants are also better left off. In many Swiss municipalities there is in addition a **green waste collection**, which picks up garden waste.

Until compost is finished, it takes **a few months to a year**. Good compost is dark, crumbly and smells like **forest soil**. It is mixed into the beds as **fertiliser**, so that vegetables and flowers grow better. Anyone who composts needs less artificial fertiliser and produces less waste.

gewusst: In a handful of good compost soil there are more tiny living things than there are people on Earth.
Many towns in Switzerland make compost and biogas from green waste in large plants.

teile.einleitung: A soil must be able to hold on to nutrients so that plants can take them up. The cation exchange capacity, CEC for short, describes how well a soil can do this. It depends above all on humus and clay minerals.
wichtigste: The CEC states how many cations a soil can bind in an exchangeable way.
Cations are positively charged ions such as calcium, magnesium and potassium.
The CEC is often given in cmol(+) per kg of soil.
Humus and clay minerals contribute most to the CEC.
Sandy soils have a small CEC, and nutrients are easily washed out.
Base saturation is the share of Ca, Mg, K and Na in the CEC.
Montmorillonite has a particularly high CEC.

abschnitte.text: Many plant nutrients are present in the soil as **cations**, that is, as positively charged ions. Examples are Ca2+, Mg2+ and K+. The **cation exchange capacity** states how many of them the soil can hold on its surfaces and release again. It is a measure of its **capacity to store nutrients**. It is often given in **cmol(+) per kg of soil**, which corresponds to milliequivalents per 100 grams.

**Humus** and **clay minerals** contribute most to the CEC. They have very large, **negatively charged** surfaces. Clay minerals get these charges because in the crystal lattice some atoms are replaced by others. The cations attach themselves to these. Sand and gravel, by contrast, consist mainly of **quartz** with a small surface and bind hardly any nutrients.

abschnitte.titel: Not every clay is the same
abschnitte.text: **Montmorillonite** is a swelling three-layer clay mineral with a large inner surface. Its CEC is particularly high. **Kaolinite** is a two-layer mineral and has a much smaller CEC. **Quartz** and **calcite** are not clay minerals. In **humus**, the CEC also depends on the pH: if the pH falls, many charge sites are occupied by hydrogen, and the CEC decreases.

The **base saturation** states in per cent how many exchange sites are occupied by calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium. If it is low, many sites are occupied by **H+** and **aluminium**. The soil is then acidic. Acidic soils can be improved by **liming**.

A **sandy soil** can hold on to only a few cations. Nutrients are therefore easily washed out with the **seepage water**. There, fertiliser should be spread in small doses. Loamy and humus-rich soils store nutrients better and release them little by little to the plants.

gewusst: Plant roots release hydrogen ions and swap them for nutrient ions from the soil.
Montmorillonite can take up so much water that it visibly swells.

teile.einleitung: The Jurapark Aargau is a regional nature park in the Jura. It lies between the Aare and the Rhine and is known for its cherries, its dinosaur finds and its landscape of limestone.
wichtigste: The Jurapark Aargau lies in the Jura between the Aare and the Rhine.
It spreads over the cantons of Aargau and Solothurn.
In the park there are the Table Jura and the Folded Jura.
The limestone formed from deposits in a sea.
In the clay pit at Frick, many Plateosaurus were found.
The Fricktal is known for its cherries.

abschnitte.text: The **Jurapark Aargau** is a **regional nature park** of national importance. It lies in the **Jura**, between the **Aare** and the **Rhine**. Most of it belongs to the canton of **Aargau**, and some municipalities lie in the canton of **Solothurn**. In a nature park, nature, landscape and the life of the people in the region are meant to be strengthened together.

The **limestone** in the Jurapark formed in a **sea**. Many millions of years ago, shells, lime mud and remains of sea creatures were deposited there. Over time, rock was made from them. That is why many **fossils** can be found in the Jura, for example ammonites. In the park there are two kinds of Jura: in the **Table Jura** the layers lie almost flat. In the **Folded Jura** they were pushed up into folds.

In the **clay pit at Frick**, especially many skeletons of **Plateosaurus** were found. This plant-eater lived in the **Triassic**, so even before the Jurassic. It often walked on two legs and had a long neck. In the dinosaur museum in Frick, finds from the region can be viewed.

The **Fricktal** is known for its **cherries**. In spring the blossoming trees turn the slopes into a white sea. In **Herznach**, **iron ore** used to be mined from the mountain. Today a museum recalls the mine. Hiking trails lead through meadows, woods and old villages.

gewusst: The dinosaur finds at Frick are among the most important in the whole of Europe.
The Jura mountains gave the geological period Jurassic its name.

teile.einleitung: The hedgehog is a small mammal with spines. In Switzerland it lives in gardens, hedges and at the edge of woods. It is out and about mainly at night.
wichtigste: An adult hedgehog has about 7,000 spines on its back.
When in danger, it rolls itself into a spiky ball.
It is out and about mainly at night.
It eats mainly beetles, worms and other small animals.
It often sleeps through the winter in a nest of leaves.
Hedges give it shelter and food.

abschnitte.text: On its back the hedgehog carries about **7,000 spines**. They are made of the same material as our hair and fingernails. Its belly and face, by contrast, are covered with soft fur. When danger threatens, the hedgehog rolls itself into a **ball**. Then all the spines point outwards, and many enemies leave it alone.

By day the hedgehog sleeps well hidden. At **dusk and at night** it goes looking for food. In doing so it often walks long distances through several gardens. It has a very good nose and good ears. You often hear it before you see it, because it snuffles and rustles in the leaves.

The hedgehog is an **insect eater**. It eats mainly **beetles**, caterpillars and **earthworms**, but also slugs and millipedes. Milk is unhealthy for hedgehogs, and you should never give it to them. A shallow dish of water, on the other hand, helps them on hot days.

In autumn the hedgehog eats itself a layer of fat. When it gets cold and there is hardly any food left, it goes into **hibernation**. For this it builds a **nest of leaves**, often under a hedge or a pile of branches. Its heart then beats much more slowly, and it needs only a little energy. Only in spring does it wake up again.

A **hedge** is ideal for the hedgehog: it finds **shelter** in it and many insects as food. Leaf piles, wild corners and holes in the garden fence help it too. Roads, robotic lawnmowers and garden poisons are dangerous. Anyone who makes their garden close to nature does the hedgehog a great deal of good.

gewusst: In one night a hedgehog can cover several hundred metres up to a few kilometres.
