Young hedgehogs have soft, white spines at first, which only become hard after a while.

teile.einleitung: Evergreen plants bear green leaves or needles all year round. Even in winter you can see them shining green in the woods and in the garden.
wichtigste: Evergreen means that the plant has green leaves all year round.
Evergreen plants also keep losing single old leaves or needles.
A layer of wax protects needles from drying out in winter.
Yew, holly, ivy and box are well-known evergreen plants.
The Swiss stone pine carries its needles in tufts of five, the Scots pine in twos.
The yew is very poisonous in almost all its parts.

abschnitte.text: Many broadleaved trees drop their leaves in autumn. **Evergreen** plants, by contrast, keep them all year round. Even so, their leaves do not last for ever: a **spruce** keeps losing single old needles, which fall off after a few years. Because new ones are constantly growing, the tree stays green. The larch, by the way, is a conifer that drops all its needles in autumn.

In winter the ground is often frozen, and the plant can hardly take up water. That is why needles and hard leaves are well protected. A **layer of wax** on the surface stops them from **drying out**. The narrow shape of the needles also helps to lose little water. In spring, evergreen plants can start making sugar again at once.

With the pines, you can often recognise the species by the tufts of needles. The **Scots pine** has **two** needles together. The **Swiss stone pine**, a tree of the Alps, carries its needles in tufts of **five**. The **yew** has soft, flat needles and red fruits. Its needles and seeds, however, are **very poisonous**, to people and to many animals.

The **holly** has glossy, prickly leaves and red berries. **Ivy** climbs up trees and walls and stays green in winter too. Its berries are winter food for birds, but poisonous for people. The **box** is often clipped into balls or hedges in gardens. Today it suffers in many places from the box tree moth, a moth whose caterpillars eat the leaves.

gewusst: The needles of a spruce often stay on the tree for several years before they fall off.
Ivy only flowers in autumn and is then a late source of food for insects.

teile.einleitung: Jupiter is the largest planet in our Solar System. It is a huge gas planet into which the Earth would fit more than 1,000 times. With its colourful bands of cloud, the Great Red Spot and almost a hundred moons, it is an exciting target for researchers.
wichtigste: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System.
It is the fifth planet counting from the Sun.
Jupiter is a gas planet and has no solid surface.
It consists mainly of hydrogen and helium.
A day on Jupiter lasts only just under 10 hours.
It needs almost 12 years for one lap around the Sun.
Jupiter has very many moons, and the four largest were discovered by Galileo Galilei.
The Great Red Spot is a huge storm on Jupiter.

abschnitte.text: Jupiter has a diameter of about 143,000 kilometres, which is around eleven times as much as the Earth. It is about 318 times as heavy as the Earth. That makes it heavier than all the other planets put together. Jupiter is one of the **gas planets**, together with Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

On average, Jupiter is about 778 million kilometres from the Sun, so around five times as far as the Earth. For one **orbit** around the Sun it needs just under 12 Earth years. But it spins very fast around itself, and one day lasts only just under 10 hours. Because of this fast spin, Jupiter is slightly flattened at the poles.

Jupiter consists mainly of **hydrogen** and helium. The surface that we see is a thick blanket of cloud with light and dark stripes. Huge storms rage in it. The best known is the **Great Red Spot**, a cyclone that is larger than the Earth and has been observed for almost 200 years. Jupiter also has a strong magnetic field and faint rings of dust.

Jupiter has more than 90 known moons, and new ones are still being discovered. The four largest are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. They are called the **Galilean moons**, because Galileo Galilei discovered them in 1610 with his telescope. Ganymede is the largest moon in the whole Solar System and is even bigger than the planet Mercury. On Io there are active volcanoes, and under the ice of Europa, experts suspect an ocean of water.

The space probes Pioneer and Voyager flew past Jupiter in the 1970s and sent the first close-up pictures. From 1995 to 2003 the probe Galileo orbited the planet. Since 2016 the NASA probe **Juno** has been studying Jupiter from close by. The European probe Juice was launched in 2023 and is due to arrive in the early 2030s to explore the icy moons.

Jupiter is easy to see with the naked eye and often shines brighter than any star. It was named after the chief Roman god, who was called Zeus by the Greeks. Even with simple binoculars, you can make out its four large moons as small points of light. In Switzerland too it can be observed well on clear nights, for example at an **observatory**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large planet that consists mainly of gases and has no solid ground.
The four largest moons of Jupiter, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
An unmanned spacecraft that explores planets and radios data back to Earth.
An invisible zone of force around a planet that, for example, lines up compass needles.

gewusst: In 1994, fragments of Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crashed into Jupiter and left dark marks bigger than the Earth.
Jupiter spins faster around itself than any other planet in the Solar System.
Because of its enormous gravity, Jupiter deflects some comets and asteroids before they reach the inner Solar System.

teile.einleitung: Lianas are climbing plants. They root in the ground and climb up trees or walls towards the light. Many lianas grow in the rainforest, but there are also some in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Lianas climb up trees.
They want to reach the sunlight.
Lianas have no thick, strong trunk and need a support.
Ivy is a liana of our forests.
The grapevine is also a liana.
Monkeys use lianas as a path between the trees.

abschnitte.text: In the **rainforest** the trees stand close together. Down on the ground it is dark. **Lianas** root in the ground and climb up tree trunks, to bring their leaves to the **sunlight**. They have no thick, strong trunk. That is why they need a **support** to hold on to. In this way they save energy and grow quickly upwards.

Lianas have various tricks. Some **twine** round a trunk, like hops. Others hold on with **tendrils**, like the **grapevine**, which bears grapes. **Ivy** climbs up trees and walls with small **adhesive roots**. The bramble hooks itself onto other plants with its prickles.

In Switzerland too there are lianas. **Ivy** grows in many forests and on house walls. It stays green in winter. The **traveller’s joy** climbs over bushes at forest edges. In autumn it bears feathery, silvery fruit clusters. And in vineyards, for example in the Valais or on Lake Geneva, grapevines grow.

In the rainforest, **monkeys** like to use lianas as a path. They climb along them and so get from tree to tree without having to go down to the ground. Lianas are also known from stories: **Tarzan** is a character from books and films. He grows up in the jungle and swings through the trees on lianas.

gewusst: From the stems of the rattan palm, a liana, rattan furniture is woven.
An ivy plant can become several hundred years old.

teile.einleitung: Vascular bundles are the pipes of plants. In these long strands, water, minerals and sugar flow between root, stem and leaves. You can see them, for example, as veins in a leaf.
wichtigste: A vascular bundle is a strand of transport tissues.
It consists of xylem and phloem.
Mosses have no true vascular bundles.
In dicotyledons, the vascular bundles in the stem lie in a ring.
In monocotyledons such as maize they are scattered.
The veins of a leaf contain vascular bundles.
Open vascular bundles have a cambium and allow growth in thickness.

abschnitte.text: Vascular bundles are long **strands** that connect root, shoot and leaves. Each vascular bundle has two parts. In the **xylem**, also called the wood part, **water and minerals** rise from the root upwards. In the **phloem**, the sieve part, **sugar** is carried from the leaves to other parts of the plant. Plants with vascular bundles are called **vascular plants**. These include ferns, conifers and flowering plants.

**Mosses** have no true conducting tissue. They take up water over their whole surface. That is why they stay small and need **damp places**. With vascular bundles, by contrast, plants can grow tall, because they conduct water far upwards. In this way trees reach heights of many metres.

If you cut a stem across, you see the vascular bundles as dots. In **dicotyledons** such as the sunflower they lie in a **ring**. In **monocotyledons** such as **maize** they are **scattered** over the whole cross-section. The visible **veins** in a leaf are also vascular bundles. They bring water into the leaf and carry sugar away.

If between xylem and phloem there lies a layer of cells that can divide, the **cambium**, people speak of **open vascular bundles**. The cambium constantly forms new cells. In this way a trunk can grow in thickness, as in trees. The **annual rings** in the wood arise from this as well. If the cambium is missing, the vascular bundles are called closed.

Vascular bundles are easy to make visible. You stand **celery** in water with **food colouring**. After a few hours the coloured water has risen in the vascular bundles. If you cut the stalk across, you see **coloured dots**. The strings that you can pull off celery also contain vascular bundles.

gewusst: The strings in celery are vascular bundles with firm supporting tissue.
The annual rings of a tree arise through the cambium in open vascular bundles.

teile.einleitung: Germination is the moment when a young plant wakes from a resting seed. The seed takes up water, swells and bursts its coat, and then root and shoot grow out. You can easily watch this at home with cress or beans.
wichtigste: In germination, a young plant, the seedling, grows from a seed.
To germinate, a seed needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
A seed does not necessarily need soil to germinate.
The first step is imbibition, in which the seed takes up water and swells.
Usually the radicle comes out of the seed coat first.
Until it has green leaves, the seedling lives on the stores in the seed.
Grasses such as maize and wheat have only one seed leaf, beans have two.

abschnitte.text: A seed is like a small packed lunch. Inside lies a tiny **embryo**, that is, the beginnings of root, stem and first leaves. Next to it are nutrients such as starch, protein and fat. In the bean, these stores are kept in the two thick **seed leaves**. On the outside, a hard seed coat protects everything from drying out and from injury.

A seed needs above all **water**, oxygen to breathe and suitable warmth. Soil is not necessary at the beginning, which is why cress also germinates on damp cotton wool. Some seeds need light to germinate. They are called light germinators, for example lettuce. Others germinate only in the dark. Many alpine plants germinate only after they have been through a cold winter.

First the dry seed takes up water and swells. This is **imbibition**. This wakes up the metabolism, and the seed begins to use its stores. Then the **radicle** usually bursts the seed coat and grows downwards. After that the shoot stretches upwards to the light. As soon as green leaves are there, the young plant can make food itself by photosynthesis.

Botanists divide flowering plants by the number of their seed leaves. **Monocotyledons** such as maize, wheat, grasses and tulips have only one seed leaf. Dicotyledons such as the bean, sunflower or beech have two. In the garden bean, the seed leaves are lifted above the soil during germination. In the pea, by contrast, they stay below ground in the soil.

Many seeds do not germinate at once, even if it is damp and warm. They are in **seed dormancy** and wait for the right moment, for example for spring after a winter. In this way the plant prevents its seedlings from growing in autumn and then freezing. Some seeds stay able to germinate for many years or even centuries.

abschnitte.titel: Trying it out and why it matters
abschnitte.text: You can sow cress on damp cotton wool, and after one or two days you will see the first radicles. Farmers and gardeners use germination tests to check how many seeds come up. Good germination is the basis for harvests of wheat, maize or vegetables. In seed banks, countries store seeds to keep old varieties for the future.

begriffe.erklaerung: The very young plant that has just grown out of the seed.
The first step of germination, in which the seed takes up water and becomes thick.
The first leaf in the seed, which often stores nutrients for the seedling.
The first root, which usually grows out of the seed first.
The way green plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide.

gewusst: When swelling, seeds can develop so much force that they even move stones or burst containers.
From a date seed about 2,000 years old from Israel, a new date palm grew in 2005.
The radicle always grows downwards, even if you stand the seed on its head, because it senses gravity.

teile.einleitung: No habitat can feed an unlimited number of animals. The carrying capacity states how large a population can become there in the long run. It is an important term in ecology and is abbreviated with the letter K.
wichtigste: The carrying capacity K is the largest population that a habitat can support permanently.
In German it is called “Kapazitätsgrenze”.
K depends on the resources of the habitat, such as food.
Competition for food is density-dependent.
A late frost is density-independent.
When a population reaches K, its growth is zero.
If K is exceeded, this is called overshoot.

abschnitte.text: The **carrying capacity** K states how many individuals of a species a habitat with its resources can feed **in the long term**. In German it is called **Kapazitätsgrenze**. K depends on the habitat: on food, water, space and hiding places. If there is more food, K can rise. A higher birth rate, by contrast, does not change K.

Many populations first grow quickly and then ever more slowly. This is called **logistic growth**, and the curve looks like an S. In the formula there is the **braking factor** (1 minus N/K), where N is the size of the population. With N = 750 and K = 1000 it is 1 minus 0.75 = 0.25. The population then grows at only a quarter of its greatest possible rate. When N = K, the factor becomes zero: births and deaths balance out.

Some factors act more strongly the denser a population is. They are called **density-dependent**. One example is **competition for food**: the more animals share the food, the harder it gets. Diseases and parasites also spread more easily at high density. Other factors are **density-independent**. A late frost in spring kills a similar share of the insects, no matter how many there are.

abschnitte.titel: When a population becomes too large
abschnitte.text: On **St Matthew Island** in Alaska, reindeer were introduced in 1944. There was plenty of food and no enemies. The herd grew to around 6,000 animals and ate almost all the **lichens**. In the winter of 1963/64 the great majority of the animals died. When a population clearly exceeds its capacity, this is called **overshoot**.

gewusst: With logistic growth, the increase is greatest when the population is exactly half as large as K.
The carrying capacity is not a fixed value: a dry year can lower it, a good year for food can raise it.

teile.einleitung: The tropical rainforest seems unbelievably fertile. Its soil, however, is often poor in nutrients. The secret is a **short-circuited nutrient cycle**: the nutrients are in the plants and are reused almost at once.
wichtigste: In the rainforest, nutrients from the leaf litter go almost directly back into the plants.
The litter layer is much thinner than in a deciduous forest in Switzerland.
Warmth and moisture all year round speed up the breakdown of the litter.
Most fine roots lie in the top layer of soil.
Mycorrhizal fungi help the trees to take up nutrients.
After slash-and-burn clearing, a field is often productive for only a few years.

abschnitte.text: In a forest, leaves, twigs and fruits are constantly falling to the ground. This layer is called **litter**. Fungi, bacteria and small animals break it down, and in the process nutrients are released. In the rainforest these nutrients go **almost directly back into the plants**, without being stored in the soil for long. The cycle is therefore very short, it is **short-circuited**. Most of the nutrients are in the living plants and not in the soil.

In the tropics it is **warm and damp all year round**. That is why fungi, bacteria, termites and other decomposers work without a break. A leaf is often broken down in a few weeks or months. The **litter layer** is therefore **much thinner** than in a deciduous forest in Switzerland. Here, the cold winter slows the breakdown, and the leaves stay lying longer.

So that the nutrients are not lost, most of the **fine roots** of many rainforest trees lie in the **top layer of soil**. Some even grow into the litter. **Mycorrhizal fungi** help with this. These are fungi that live together with the roots. Their fine threads take up nutrients directly from the decaying litter and pass them on to the tree. In return the fungi get sugar from the tree.

In **slash-and-burn clearing**, a piece of forest is cut down and burned. At first the ash contains many nutrients, and the field gives good harvests. But the heavy rains **quickly wash the nutrients out**. Because the soil can hardly store them, the field is often exhausted after a few years. Then new forest is cleared. In this way a lot of rainforest is lost.

A form of farming that imitates the rainforest is **agroforestry**. In it, trees, shrubs and crops grow together in several storeys, similar to the **layered structure** of the forest. Leaves and plant remains stay on the field and supply nutrients continually. The soil stays covered and is washed out less. Cocoa and coffee are often grown this way.

gewusst: In a rainforest, most of the nutrients are in the plants and not in the soil.
In the tropics, a fallen leaf can almost completely disappear in a few weeks.

teile.einleitung: In hydroponics, plants grow without soil. Their roots stand in water or in a substrate without nutrients, and everything they need they get from a nutrient solution.
wichtigste: Hydroponic plants grow without soil using a nutrient solution.
Indoors, expanded clay is often used as the substrate.
A water level indicator shows when to top up.
In the nutrient film technique, a thin film of nutrient solution flows past the roots.
In aeroponics, the roots are sprayed in the air.
The EC value measures the amount of dissolved nutrient salts.

abschnitte.text: Plants do not actually need soil, but **water**, **air**, **light** and **minerals**. In **hydroponics** they get the minerals from a **nutrient solution**. Around 1860, the researchers **Julius Sachs** and **Wilhelm Knop** grew plants in water cultures with exactly known salts. In this way they proved which minerals plants really need.

For houseplants, **expanded clay** is often used. These are baked, porous **clay pellets**. They give the plant support, store a little water and let air get to the roots. A **water level indicator** with a float shows how much solution is in the pot. When it is at minimum, you add more, but not above optimum, so that the roots get enough air.

In vegetable growing there are larger systems. In the **nutrient film technique**, NFT for short, the plants stand in slightly sloping **channels**. A thin film of nutrient solution flows constantly past the roots. That way they get nutrients and air at the same time. In **aeroponics**, the roots hang freely in a chamber and are sprayed regularly with a fine **mist** of nutrient solution.

Professionals measure their nutrient solution precisely. The **EC value** gives the **electrical conductivity**. Dissolved salts conduct electricity, so the value rises the more nutrient salts are in the solution. The **pH value** is important too. For most plants it is kept at about **5.5 to 6.5**, that is, slightly acidic. Then nutrients such as **iron** and **phosphate** are readily available.

gewusst: With hydroponics, lettuce and herbs can also be grown in buildings, stacked one above the other on shelves.
Expanded clay is made when clay is heated very strongly and puffs up as it does so.

teile.einleitung: Deciduous trees are trees with flat, broad leaves instead of needles. Here, most of them lose their leaves in autumn, after these have turned yellow and red. Beech, oak, maple and lime are among the best-known deciduous trees of Switzerland.
wichtigste: Deciduous trees have broad, flat leaves instead of needles.
Most deciduous trees here lose their leaves in autumn.
In autumn many leaves turn yellow and red.
Well-known deciduous trees are beech, oak, maple, lime, ash and birch.
The maple has fruits with wings that spin like propellers as they fall.
Deciduous trees are flowering plants and form flowers and fruits.
The beech is the most common deciduous tree in the forests of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A deciduous tree is a tree whose leaves are broad and flat. In German the leaves together are called **Laub**, hence the name “Laubbaum”. Deciduous trees belong to the **angiosperms**, which means that their seeds grow up well protected in a fruit. Conifers such as spruce and fir, by contrast, are gymnosperms and carry their seeds openly in cones.

In Switzerland the **beech** is the most common deciduous tree. It has smooth, grey bark and supplies beechnuts. The **oak** can be recognised by its lobed leaves and the acorns and can live for many hundreds of years. The lime has heart-shaped leaves and scented flowers from which tea is made. More widespread are sycamore, ash, birch, chestnut and willow.

In spring, deciduous trees put out new, tender green leaves and bloom. In summer, the leaves carry out photosynthesis with the green **chlorophyll** and make sugar. In autumn the tree breaks down the chlorophyll, so that yellow pigments become visible, and some species also make red pigments. After that most deciduous trees drop their leaves to save water in winter, which is called **leaf fall**.

Deciduous trees spread their seeds in quite different ways. The **maple** has winged fruits that spin like small propellers as they fall and so are carried away by the wind. Acorns and beechnuts are hidden by squirrels and jays and sometimes forgotten, so that new trees grow from them. Birches and willows form tiny, light seeds that the wind spreads far.

Deciduous trees offer insects, birds and mammals food and shelter, and an old oak is a habitat for hundreds of animal species. Their wood is often hard and is used for furniture, parquet, tool handles and as firewood. The fallen leaves break down into valuable **humus**. In towns, deciduous trees give shade and cool the air on hot days.

About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest. On the **Central Plateau** and in the Jura, many deciduous trees grow, and in the mountains conifers predominate. In Ticino, **sweet chestnuts** shape whole forests, and their fruits were once an important food. According to legend, in Fribourg a lime twig was planted that a messenger had brought back after the Battle of Murten in 1476, and from it grew the famous Murten lime.

begriffe.erklaerung: The leaves of trees and shrubs.
The green leaf pigment with which plants capture sunlight for photosynthesis.
Plants whose seeds grow up in a protective fruit.
A ring in the wood that is added every year, from which you can read the age of a tree.

gewusst: The larch is a conifer but, like a deciduous tree, drops its needles in autumn.
The holly is a deciduous-type tree that keeps its green leaves even in winter.
Children like to stick the winged maple fruits on their faces as noses.

teile.einleitung: In many places today there are clearly fewer insects than in the past. People speak of insect decline. This affects plants, birds and farming too.
wichtigste: The Krefeld study of 2017 showed a sharp fall in insect biomass.
Causes include pesticides, loss of habitat and artificial light.
Fewer insects mean less pollination for fruit and vegetables.
Many birds as a result lack food.
In Switzerland there are around 600 species of wild bee.
Native wild flowers in the garden help insects.

abschnitte.text: In **2017**, the so-called **Krefeld study** was published. An association from Krefeld in Germany had caught and weighed flying insects in protected areas over almost three decades. The **insect biomass** had fallen by more than three quarters in that time. The study drew attention to the problem around the world. Other studies also show a decline in many groups of insects.

There is not just one cause. Many **flower meadows**, hedges and wetlands have disappeared. **Pesticides** from farming also harm insects that are not pests. Meadows that are mown often and heavily fertilised have **hardly any flowers**, so butterflies find little food there. In addition there is **artificial light** at night: it attracts many insects, which then circle the lamp until they are exhausted.

Insects are important **pollinators**. If they are missing, there is less fruit, fewer berries and fewer seeds. That is a problem for farming. In addition, insects are **food** for many animals. Swallows, tits and other birds feed their young on insects. Bats, hedgehogs and frogs also depend on them.

Everyone can help. In the garden or on the balcony you can sow **native wild flowers**. One corner can be left wild, with leaves, branches and stones. An **insect hotel** offers wild bees **nesting places**. At night you should switch off unnecessary light. In Switzerland there are **around 600 species of wild bee**, and many of them depend on this kind of help.

gewusst: In the Krefeld study, volunteers collected insects in traps for almost 30 years.
Most animal species in the world are insects.

teile.einleitung: Carbon dioxide, CO2 for short, is a colourless and odourless gas that occurs in small amounts in the air. Humans and animals breathe it out, and plants need it to grow. At the same time, CO2 is largely responsible for the enhanced greenhouse effect and thus partly to blame for climate change.
wichtigste: Carbon dioxide consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
It is a colourless, odourless gas and heavier than air.
Humans and animals breathe out CO2, and plants take it up for photosynthesis.
When wood, coal, oil and natural gas are burned, CO2 is produced.
CO2 is largely co-responsible for the enhanced greenhouse effect.
The CO2 content of the air has risen by about half since the beginning of industrialisation.
Frozen CO2 is called dry ice.

abschnitte.text: Carbon dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula **CO2**. A molecule consists of one carbon atom in the middle and two oxygen atoms to the left and right of it. The gas is invisible, smells of nothing and is about one and a half times as heavy as air. In the air it makes up only about 0.04 per cent, which in 2024 was about 420 particles per million air particles, abbreviated **ppm**.

In **cell respiration**, humans and animals use oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Plants do it the other way round: in **photosynthesis** they take up CO2 and water and build sugar from them with the help of sunlight. In doing so they give off oxygen. So CO2 is an important part of the natural cycle of life.

CO2 lets sunlight through almost unhindered, but holds back the heat radiation that rises from the Earth. This natural **greenhouse effect** makes sure that the Earth is not ice cold. Since industrialisation, however, people have been burning large amounts of coal, oil and natural gas, as a result of which the CO2 content has risen from about 280 ppm to over 420 ppm. This strengthens the greenhouse effect and the Earth warms up.

The bubbles in mineral water and lemonade consist of carbon dioxide that has been pressed into the drink under pressure. In baking, CO2 is produced by **yeast** or baking powder and makes the dough rise. Some fire extinguishers contain CO2, because it takes the oxygen away from the fire. At minus 78.5 degrees Celsius, CO2 becomes solid and is then called **dry ice**, which turns directly into gas without melting.

In large amounts, CO2 can become dangerous for people, because it displaces oxygen. Since it is heavier than air, it collects in cellars, pits or well shafts. In **wine cellars** in particular, a lot of CO2 is produced during fermentation, which is why there are warning devices there. In the sea, additional CO2 dissolves and makes the water more acidic, which is called **ocean acidification**.

Switzerland wants to cut its greenhouse gas emissions sharply. In June 2023, voters accepted the **Climate and Innovation Act**, which sets the goal of net zero by 2050. Net zero means that no more greenhouse gases are emitted than are removed from the air again. A Swiss firm from Zurich, Climeworks, builds plants that filter CO2 directly out of the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen from CO2 and water.
Abbreviation for parts per million, used to measure very small amounts of a substance.
Frozen carbon dioxide, which is minus 78.5 degrees cold.
No more greenhouse gas is emitted than is removed from the air again.

gewusst: An adult breathes out about one kilogram of carbon dioxide per day.
Dry ice does not melt into a puddle but turns directly into gas, and it produces fog when you put it in water.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be about minus 18 degrees on average.

teile.einleitung: Loam is a soil made of very fine particles. When damp it can be shaped, and when it dries it becomes hard. People have been building with loam for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Loam is a mixture of clay, silt and sand.
Damp loam can be shaped well, for example into a sausage.
Dry loam becomes hard and cracked.
Loam lets water through only slowly, which is why puddles form.
In the past, houses and walls were built of loam.
Bricks are fired in a kiln from loam and clay.

abschnitte.text: Loam is a mixture of **clay**, **silt** and **sand**. Clay and silt are very fine particles, much finer than sand. They stick closely together. That is why loam is **mouldable**: with damp loam you can easily roll a **long sausage** between your hands. With sand this does not work. This simple test is called the finger test.

The fine loam particles hold **water** well. Plants therefore have water for longer in loamy soil than in sandy soil. At the same time loam lets water through only **slowly**. After heavy rain, **puddles** therefore often remain. If loam dries out completely, it shrinks. It becomes **hard and cracked**.

Loam is one of the oldest **building materials** in the world. Thousands of years ago people already made walls and whole **houses** from it. In many countries, loam bricks are simply dried in the sun. Here, the walls of **half-timbered houses** used to be filled with loam. Today loam is valued again, for example as **loam plaster**: it takes moisture from the air in a room and gives it back again.

Loam and clay can be shaped and fired in a **kiln**. In this way hard **bricks** for roofs and walls are made. In the garden, loamy soil is often hard to **dig**, because it is dense and heavy. Gardeners therefore like to mix compost or sand into it. In return, loamy soil is mostly rich in nutrients.

gewusst: Loam that has not been fired can be softened again with water and used anew.
Pottery too is made from clay that is fired in a kiln.

teile.einleitung: The nasturtium is a cheerful garden plant with bright flowers and round leaves. It comes from South America and tastes slightly hot. You can even eat the flowers and leaves.
wichtigste: The nasturtium comes from the Andes in South America.
Its flowers are often orange, yellow or red.
The leaves are round like little plates.
Water droplets roll off the leaves in beads.
It tastes slightly hot, like pepper.
Aphids often sit on it in swarms.
It twines and creeps, and also grows in a balcony box.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of the nasturtium shine in warm colours such as **orange, yellow and red**. At the back each flower has a long **spur** with nectar. The shape of the flower is reminiscent of the **hood** of Capuchin monks. That is where the German name “Kapuzinerkresse” comes from. The flowers attract many insects.

abschnitte.titel: Round leaves that do not get wet
abschnitte.text: The leaves are **round**, and the stalk sits exactly in the middle. They look like little plates or umbrellas. The leaves are **water-repellent**. Water droplets roll off and take dirt with them. This keeps the leaf clean.

The nasturtium tastes slightly **hot**, similar to cress or pepper. This comes from a substance in the plant. Flowers and young leaves can be put in salad. The flowers then make a colourful decoration. It is important to eat only plants that you know for certain.

abschnitte.titel: In the garden and on the balcony
abschnitte.text: The nasturtium originally comes from the **Andes** in South America. It forms long shoots, creeps over the ground or **climbs** up fences. It also grows well in pots and in the **balcony box**, where the shoots hang down prettily. **Black aphids** like it very much. That is why it is sometimes planted to lure aphids away from other plants.

gewusst: Here, the nasturtium does not survive frost. That is why it is usually sown anew every year.
The green buds and unripe fruits can be pickled in vinegar. They then taste similar to capers.

teile.einleitung: The liverwort is one of the first flowers in spring. It glows blue in the still bare deciduous forest. It gets its name from its special leaves.
wichtigste: The liverwort mostly blooms blue to blue-violet.
It blooms mainly in March and April.
Its leaves have three rounded lobes.
The leaves reminded people in the past of a liver.
In the middle of the flower sit many whitish stamens.
The fresh liverwort is poisonous.

abschnitte.text: The liverwort is an **early bloomer**. It blooms mainly in **March and April**, when the trees still carry no leaves. Then a lot of light falls on the forest floor. The flowers are mostly **blue to blue-violet**. Rarely you also find pink or completely **white** flowers. The liverwort likes to grow in deciduous forests on chalky soil, also in Switzerland.

Each leaf is divided into **three rounded lobes**. By this you can recognise the plant even without a flower. Underneath, the leaves are often **reddish**. In the past the shape reminded people of a **liver**. That is why people believed the plant helped against liver complaints. The old leaves stay **green** over the winter. After flowering, new leaves grow.

abschnitte.titel: A close look at the flower
abschnitte.text: In the middle of the flower sit **many whitish stamens**. They glow brightly out of the coloured flower. Under the flower stand three small green leaves that look like a calyx. In sun the flowers open, in rain and at night they close. The liverwort belongs to the **buttercup family**.

The fresh liverwort is **poisonous**. You should not put it in your mouth. It is most beautiful in the forest anyway. The plant grows slowly and has become rare in some places. So it is best to leave it standing and only look at it.

gewusst: Ants carry away the seeds of the liverwort, because a nutritious appendage sits on them.
In bad weather the flowers close like a small umbrella.

teile.einleitung: Currants are small, sharp-tasting berries that grow in bunches on bushes. In Switzerland they are often called “Meertrübeli”. There are red, black and white varieties.
wichtigste: Currants can be red, black or white.
They hang in small bunches on the bush.
In German they are named after St John’s Day.
In Switzerland people often say “Meertrübeli”.
The blackcurrant is also called cassis.
Blackcurrants contain a lot of vitamin C.

abschnitte.text: Currants grow on **bushes** that reach about one to two metres in height. The berries hang in **small bunches** on thin stalks. There are **red**, **black** and **white** currants. The white ones are a pale form of the red. The gooseberry is a close relative.

The first berries ripen around **St John’s Day** on 24 June. That is where the German name “Johannisbeere” comes from. In Switzerland people often say **“Meertrübeli”** or simply “Trübeli”, because the berries look like little grapes. In Austria they are called “Ribisel”, after the Latin name Ribes.

Redcurrants taste **sharp** and refreshing. They are eaten raw with sugar, in cakes or as jelly and jam. The blackcurrant is also called **cassis**. It has a strong, tart taste and contains especially much **vitamin C**. It is made into juice, syrup and jam.

The berries are small and hang on many stalks. Picking them off one by one takes a long time. With a **fork** it goes much faster: you run the prongs along the stalk, and the berries drop off. Currants are delicate and should be eaten or processed soon after harvesting.

gewusst: Blackcurrants contain more vitamin C than lemons.
Currant bushes bear plenty of fruit only a few years after planting.

teile.einleitung: Larch cones are the small cones of the larch. They stand upright on the twigs and often stay on the tree for years after the seeds are long gone.
wichtigste: Larch cones are small and egg-shaped.
They stand upright on the twigs like small candles.
Young cones glow pink to dark red in spring.
The seeds have a wing and fly on the wind.
Empty cones often stay on the twig for several years.

abschnitte.text: The cones of the larch are **small** and **egg-shaped**. They have rounded scales and look a little like small **wooden roses**. Unlike the hanging cones of the spruce, they sit **upright** on the twigs, like small candles. In the Swiss Alps the **European larch** grows. The Japanese larch is only sometimes planted in parks and forests.
In spring the larch forms young **female flowers**, from which the cones develop. They glow **pink to dark red** and look like tiny roses. With time the cones turn green and later brown and woody.

Between the scales lie the **seeds**. Each seed has a small, thin **wing**. When the scales open, the seeds fall out, and the **wind** carries them away. In this way the larch can multiply and settle new areas.

After the seeds have fallen out, the empty cones often stay on the twig for **several years**. In winter the larch drops its needles. Then you can see the many small, dark cones especially well on the bare twigs.

gewusst: Larch cones are good for crafts, because they are small and firm.
The larch is the only native conifer that is bare in winter.

teile.einleitung: The hydrangea is a popular garden shrub with large, round balls of flowers. What is especially interesting is that some hydrangeas bloom blue or pink depending on the soil.
wichtigste: Hydrangeas are shrubs and usually grow about one to two metres tall.
Many have large, round flower heads like balls.
Hydrangeas need a great deal of water.
They like best to stand in partial shade.
The garden hydrangea comes from Japan.
Hydrangeas flower in summer.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of many hydrangeas look like **big balls**. Each ball is made up of many small flowers. Hydrangeas bloom from **early summer** until late summer, and the flowers last a very long time. In **autumn** the balls of flowers often dry on the shrub and change colour. You can cut them for **dried bouquets**.

Hydrangeas need a great deal of **water**. Their scientific name **Hydrangea** means roughly **water vessel**. If the soil is too dry, they let their leaves and flowers **droop**. After watering they often recover quickly. In blazing sun they easily go limp. They feel most comfortable in **partial shade**.

In some hydrangeas the colour depends on the **soil**. In **acidic soil**, where the plant can take up **aluminium**, they flower **blue**. In **limy soil**, the flowers turn **pink**. Gardeners sometimes add special fertilisers to get blue flowers. White hydrangeas, by contrast, do not change their colour.

The popular **garden hydrangea** originally comes from **Japan**. From there, plant lovers brought it to Europe. Today it grows in many gardens and on balconies in Switzerland. Hydrangeas grow as **shrubs** with several woody shoots. They usually reach about one to two metres in height.

gewusst: In some hydrangeas, the showy coloured parts are not petals at all, but sepals.
The leaves and flowers of the hydrangea are mildly poisonous and do not belong in the mouth.

teile.einleitung: Hyaline cells are large, empty cells in the small leaves of peat mosses that fill with water. They make peat mosses into huge water stores and are one reason why raised bogs stay so wet.
wichtigste: Hyaline cells store water.
“Hyaline” means transparent like glass, from the Greek hyalos for glass.
Fully grown hyaline cells are dead and have no living contents.
Between them lies a network of green cells containing chlorophyll.
Water flows in through pores in the cell wall.
Ring-shaped or spiral reinforcements stop the cells from collapsing.

abschnitte.text: A small leaf of a **peat moss** consists of only one layer of cells. Under the microscope you can see two kinds of cell. The large, empty ones are called **hyaline cells**. Between them runs a narrow network of **cells containing chlorophyll**. These green cells contain **chloroplasts** and carry out **photosynthesis**. The hyaline cells are responsible for the water.

The word **hyaline** comes from the Greek **hyalos**, meaning glass. The cells are colourless and transparent. As they mature, they lose their living contents, the **protoplast**. All that is left is the **cell wall** as a hollow space. It is exactly this empty space that can take up a lot of water.

The hyaline cells have round **pores** in their wall. Water flows rapidly and directly in through these openings. So that the empty cells do not collapse when they dry out, **ring-shaped or spiral reinforcements** are built into the wall. They support the cell like rings in a hose. In this way the stores are always ready for new water.

When the hyaline cells are filled with **water**, they are transparent. The green of the other cells then shines through. When a cushion of peat moss dries out, the cells fill with **air**. The air scatters the light, and the moss looks **whitish**. The **white moss** (Leucobryum glaucum) also has large, empty cells in its many-layered leaves. That is why its cushions look light grey to bluish white.

gewusst: Thanks to the hyaline cells, peat mosses can take up many times their own dry weight in water.
Because of their absorbency, peat mosses used to be used as dressing material for wounds.
